### 4.1 Convergence to the Shear Flow as Pressure Goes to Zero

Since this “critical pressure” value approaches zero, it seems as if the two-sink solution should approach the power-law shear flow, which has identically zero pressure, as $\lambda\to 2$ .

To that end, we prove the following proposition, which shows convergence of the two-sink solution to the power-law shear flow at the velocity level when the critical pressure approaches zero.

#### Proposition 4.1.

Let $\psi_{P}$ be a positive solution to the ordinary differential equation in Equation (8) with pressure $P<0$ on the interval $[0,T_{+}(P)]$ corresponding to the stream function of a two-sink solution. Let $\psi_{S}(x)=\lambda^{-\lambda}\sin^{\lambda}(\theta)$ be the explicit shear flow solution to Equation (8) on the interval $[0,\pi]$ (with zero pressure). Then we have

$$ \lim_{P\to 0^{-}}\psi_{P}=\psi_{S} $$

in $C^{1,\gamma}$ on any compact subset of $[0,\pi)$ and any $\gamma<1-1/\lambda$ .

#### Proof.

In this proof, we fix some $\lambda\in(1,2)$ . In particular, when we say that a constant depends “only” on something else, we exclude from consideration the dependence on $\lambda$ .

We recall that the positive function $\psi_{P}$ satisfies Equation (8):

$$ (\psi_{P}^{\prime})^{2}=-2P+\psi_{P}^{2-\frac{2}{\lambda}}-\lambda^{2}\psi_{P}^{2}. $$

By the standard theory of ordinary differential equations, $\psi_{P}$ is smooth on $(0,T_{+}(P))$ and vanishes at the endpoints of the interval.

Suppose first that there exists a sequence $P_{n}\to 0^{-}$ such that the solutions $\psi_{n}:=\psi_{P_{n}}$ satisfy $\|\psi_{n}\|_{L^{\infty}}\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ . Since $1<\lambda<2$ we know $2-2/\lambda<2$ . Therefore, if $x_{n}$ is the number in the interval $[0,T_{+}(P_{n})]$ at which the $L^{\infty}$ bound for each $\psi_{n}$ is saturated and if $\psi_{n}(x_{n}):=A_{n}$ , we have

$$ 0\leq(\psi^{\prime}_{n})^{2}=-2P_{n}+A_{n}^{2-2/\lambda}-\lambda^{2}A_{n}^{2}<0, $$

if we take $n$ large enough. This is a contradiction, so we may conclude that

$$ A:=\sup_{-1<P<0}\|\psi_{P}\|_{L^{\infty}}<\infty, $$

or equivalently that the solutions $\psi_{P}$ are uniformly bounded in $P$ near zero. Since $1<\lambda<2$ , we know $2-2/\lambda>0$ , so we immediately conclude that

$$ \sup_{-1<P<0}\|\psi_{P}\|_{\text{Lip}}<L(A), $$

where $L(A)$ is a constant depending only on $A$ . Equivalently, the family of functions $\psi_{P}$ have Lipschitz constant uniform in $P$ near zero.

Since $\psi_{P}$ is Lipschitz, then $-2P+\psi_{P}^{2-\frac{2}{\lambda}}-\lambda^{2}\psi_{P}^{2}$ is $C^{0,2-2/\lambda}$ Hölder regular, with Hölder norm depending only on $L(A)$ , the uniform Lipschitz bound of $\psi_{P}$ . In addition, $\pm\sqrt{-2P+\psi_{P}^{2-\frac{2}{\lambda}}-\lambda^{2}\psi_{P}^{2}}$ is $C^{0,1-1/\lambda}$ Hölder regular, with Hölder norm depending only on $L(A)$ , the uniform Lipschitz bound of $\psi_{P}$ . We conclude that $\psi_{P}\in C^{1,1-1/\lambda}$ , with Hölder norm depending solely on $A$ , the uniform bound in $P$ on $\|\psi_{P}\|_{L^{\infty}}$ .

By (a straightforward modification of) the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem, we conclude that there exists a sequence $P_{m}\to 0^{-}$ such that $\psi_{m}:=\psi_{P_{m}}$ converges in $C^{1,\gamma}$ to some $C^{1,1-1/\lambda}$ function $\psi_{\infty}$ on any compact subset of $[0,\pi]$ . If we prove that the limit is unique, taking any sequence $P\to 0^{-}$ makes $\psi_{P}$ converge to $\psi_{\infty}$ . We also remark that since $\psi_{P}\geq 0$ for each $P$ , we certainly have $\psi_{\infty}\geq 0$ on $[0,\pi$ ]. It remains to show that $\psi_{\infty}=\psi_{S}$ .

By the convergence proven earlier, we know

$$ (\psi_{\infty}^{\prime})^{2}=\psi_{\infty}^{2-\frac{2}{\lambda}}-\lambda^{2}\psi_{\infty}^{2}. $$

Since $\psi_{\infty}\geq 0$ , we may assume that $\psi_{\infty}=f^{\lambda}$ for some function $f\geq 0$ . The ordinary differential equation satisfied by $f$ is precisely

$$ (f^{\prime})^{2}+f^{2}=\lambda^{-2}. $$

Since $f(0)=0$ and $f\geq 0$ , it is clear that $f(x)=\lambda^{-1}\sin(\theta)$ . We conclude that $\psi_{\infty}=\psi_{S}$ . ∎

#### Remark 4.2.

As noted earlier, the two-sink solution is more regular than the power-law shear flow, in a way that precludes analogous uniform convergence of the two-sink to the shear flow at the vorticity level.

## Appendix

### A The Mellin Transform and its Analytic Continuation

Suppose $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{C}$ is a function that for some $\alpha<\beta$ ,

$$ f(t)=O(t^{-\alpha})~\text{as}~t\to 0,\quad f(t)=O(t^{-\beta})~\text{as}~t\to\infty. $$

Then, the Mellin transform $M[f;z]$ is defined on a strip $\alpha<\text{Re}\,z<\beta$ as

$$ M[f;z]=\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{z-1}f(t)\,dt. $$

The Mellin transform $M[f;z]$ is a holomorphic function of $z$ on the strip $\alpha<\text{Re}\,z<\beta$ . The inverse Mellin transform is given by

$$ f(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}t^{-z}M[f;z]\,dz,\quad\alpha<c<\beta. $$

From this, it is possible to deduce the Parseval-Plancherel identity for the Mellin transform:

$$ \int_{0}^{\infty}f(t)g(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}M[f;z]M[g;1-z]\,dz. $$

Suppose $f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_{k}t^{a_{k}}$ as $t\to 0^{+}$ . Then, the Mellin transform $M[f;z]$ can be extended to a meromorphic function on a left half plane $\text{Re}\,z<\beta$ with simple poles at $z=-a_{k}$ for $k=1,2,\cdots$ , and $\text{res}_{z=-a_{k}}M[f;z]=c_{k}$ . Let $f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}c_{k}t^{a_{k}}1_{[0,1)}(t)+f_{N}(t)$ . Then, on the strip $\alpha<\text{Re}\,z<\beta$ , we get

$$ M[f;z]=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}c_{k}\int_{0}^{1}t^{z+a_{k}-1}\,dt+M[f_{N};z]=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{c_{k}}{z+a_{k}}+M[f_{N};z]. $$

The expression above is a meromorphic function on a strip $-a_{N}<\text{Re}\,z<\beta$ with simple poles at $z=-a_{0},\cdots,-a_{N-1}$ .

Similarly, if $f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}d_{k}t^{-b_{k}}$ as $t\to\infty$ . Then, the Mellin transform $M[f;z]$ can be extended to a meromorphic function on a right half plane $\text{Re}\,z>\alpha$ with simple poles at $z=b_{k}$ for $k=1,2,\cdots$ , and $\text{res}_{z=b_{k}}M[f;z]=-d_{k}$ .

### B Asymptotic Expansions for Integrals

Consider

$$ I(\lambda)=\int_{0}^{L}f(t)g(\lambda t)\,dt $$

as $\lambda\to\infty$ . From the Parseval-Plancherel identity for Mellin transform, we get

$$ \int_{0}^{L}f(t)g(\lambda t)\,dt=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}\lambda^{-z}M[f;1-z]M[g;z]\,dz. $$

Suppose

$$ f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_{k}t^{a_{k}}~\text{as}~t\to 0^{+},\quad g(t)=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}d_{l}t^{-b_{l}}~\text{as}~t\to\infty. $$

If there is no $a_{k}$ and $b_{l}$ such that $a_{k}+1=b_{l}$ , then simple poles of $M[f;1-z]$ and $M[g;z]$ does not overlap. By shifting the contour to right, we pick up residues and the following asymptotic expansion is obtained:

$$ I(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_{k}M[g;a_{k}+1]\lambda^{-a_{k}-1}+\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}d_{l}M[f;-b_{l}+1]\lambda^{-b_{l}}. $$

If $a_{k}+1=b_{l}=\gamma$ for some $k,l$ , then $M[f;1-z]M[g,z]$ has a double pole at $z=-\gamma-1$ . In this case, the corresponding term in the asymptotic expansion becomes

$$ c_{k}d_{l}\lambda^{-\gamma}\log\lambda-\Big(\underset{z=-\gamma-1}{\text{res}}M[f;1-z]M[g,z]\Big)\lambda^{-\gamma}. $$

Now, consider

$$ J(\lambda)=\int_{0}^{L}f(s)g(\lambda\phi(s))\,ds $$

where $\phi:[0,L]\to[0,M]$ be strictly increasing bijection. Then, substituting $t=\phi(s)$ gives

$$ J(\lambda)=\int_{0}^{M}\underbrace{\frac{f(s)}{\phi^{\prime}(s)}}_{=\,F(t)}g(\lambda t)\,dt. $$

An asymptotic expansion can be obtained by the computation above, while

$$ M[F;z]=\int_{0}^{M}t^{z-1}f(s)\frac{dt}{\phi^{\prime}(s)}=\int_{0}^{L}\phi^{z-1}(s)f(s)\,ds. $$

# Homothetic Self-Similar Solutions to the Incompressible Navier-Stokes Equations

**Authors:** Tim Binz & Matei P. Coiculescu

## Abstract

We investigate homothetic forward self-similar solutions of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations: the solutions $\overline{U}$ for which both $\overline{U}$ and $\beta\overline{U}$ are self-similar profiles for some nontrivial $\beta$ . Homothetic solutions are, in addition, the only solutions for which a singular limit argument can be used to prove non-uniqueness of Leray-Hopf solutions along the lines of the Jia-Šverák program. In three dimensions, and for sufficiently regular initial data, we prove a Liouville theorem that rules out the existence of non-trivial homothetic solutions. In two dimensions, our Liouville theorem reproves a result of Luo and Shvydkoy that the only decaying homothetic solution with continuous angular data is the Oseen vortex. In addition, we prove that the Euler equations linearized around the Oseen vortex are stable in some subspaces of $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , for example in the space of $2$ -fold rotationally symmetric functions. On the other hand, we also discover a homothetic solution for which an unstable approximate eigenvalue of the linearized Euler equations exists.

## 1. Introduction

We consider the initial value problem of the unforced, incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ :

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}u-\nu\Delta u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla p&=0\\
\textrm{div }u&=0\\
u(t=0)&=u_{0}.\end{aligned}\right. $$

Since its value will not concern us, we set the viscosity parameter $\nu=1$ . The existence of a global-in-time Leray-Hopf weak solution to Equation (1) is classical (see [30] for details), but the uniqueness question remains of contemporary interest.

One of the most promising avenues towards proving non-uniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions is the following program proposed by Jia and Šverák in [17]. Given $\sigma>0$ and any $(-1)$ -homogeneous weakly divergence free vector field $u_{0}(x)\in C^{\alpha}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\})\subset L^{3,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ , Jia and Šverák proved in [18] the existence of a spatially smooth, forward self-similar solution $U_{\sigma}(x,t)$ with initial data $\sigma u_{0}(x)$ . For sufficiently small $\sigma>0$ , the results of [18] guarantee the uniqueness of the solution $U_{\sigma}$ .

Following [17, 18] we consider the self-similar ansatz appropriate to the parabolic scaling of the Navier-Stokes equations,

$$ \xi=xt^{-1/2},\quad\tau=\log(t),\quad u(x,t)=t^{-1/2}U(\xi,\tau), $$

and obtain for $U$ independent of $\tau$

$$ \left\{\begin{aligned} -\Delta U-\frac{U}{2}-\frac{\xi}{2}\cdot\nabla U+U\cdot\nabla U+\nabla P&=0\\
\textrm{div }U&=0.\end{aligned}\right. $$

The initial data $u_{0}$ enters as a boundary condition at infinity given by

$$ U(\xi)=u_{0}(\xi)+o\left(\frac{1}{|\xi|}\right),\quad|\xi|\to\infty. $$

A forward self-similar solution $\bar{u}_{\sigma}$ corresponds to a self-similar profile $\overline{U}_{\sigma}$ , i.e. a steady solution of (2). Consider the linearization of Equation (2) around the self-similar profile $\overline{U}_{\sigma}$ :

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\sigma}U:=\Delta U+\frac{U}{2}+\frac{\xi}{2}\cdot\nabla U-\overline{U}_{\sigma}\cdot\nabla U-U\cdot\nabla\overline{U}_{\sigma}-\nabla P. $$

Jia and Šverák prove in [17] that under some spectral conditions on $\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}$ , the non-uniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions to Equation (1) is guaranteed. The general idea is that as $\sigma$ increases in magnitude, the spectrum of $\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}$ will eventually cross the imaginary axis, leading to a bifurcation and the existence of another scale-invariant solution. Then, if the data $u_{0}$ decays like $1/|x|$ , a truncation argument can be used to prove the non-uniqueness of Leray-Hopf solutions. We remark that Hou, Wang, and Yang have announced in [15] a computer assisted completion of the Jia-Šverák program. Very recently, Ionescu, Jia, and Palasek [16] have provided strong numerical evidence of the existence of an unstable axisymmetric self-similar solution, which would complete the Jia-Šverák program even in the axi-symmetric setting.

For more singular data than the class considered in [18] we use a distributional notion of boundary-value at infinity. Whenever $u_{0}$ is specified, the assertion that $U$ has boundary value $u_{0}$ means

$$ RU(R\,\cdot)\longrightarrow u_{0}\quad\hbox{in }\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\qquad R\to\infty. $$

For self-similar profiles with locally integrable angular data, we state a stronger local convergence wherever it is needed. We call a profile isotropically decaying when $|U(x)|\leq C(1+|x|)^{-1}$ for all $x$ for some constant $C$ . We also consider anisotropic profiles (i.e. profiles that are not isotropic) which need not satisfy this bound. The heuristic to keep in mind is that a more regular data $u_{0}$ leads to better decay for the profile $U$ . For the usual boundary conditions, data Hölder continuous away from the origin leads to isotropically decaying profiles, while in this work we construct smooth solutions from more singular $BMO^{-1}$ data that only decay in one direction.

Albritton, Brué, and Colombo were able to carry out the Jia-Šverák program in [2] by introducing a force. The force enabled them to consider the linearization $\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}$ around an arbitrary, smooth, divergence free vector field $\sigma\cdot\overline{U}$ for any positive number $\sigma>0$ , not necessarily around an exact self-similar profile. Then, by proving the existence of an unstable eigenvalue to the linearization of the Euler equations (for some particular choice of $\overline{U}$ ):

$$ L_{\phi}U:=-\overline{U}\cdot\nabla U-U\cdot\nabla\overline{U}-\nabla P, $$

they were able to prove the existence of an unstable eigenvalue for the linearization of the self-similar Navier-Stokes equations

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\sigma}U=\frac{U}{2}+\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla U+\Delta U+\sigma L_{\phi}U $$

around $\sigma\bar{U}$ for some $\sigma>0$ . Their proof relies on a singular limit argument: consider the operator

$$ \tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\sigma}U=\sigma^{-1}\mathcal{L}U=\sigma^{-1}\left(\frac{U}{2}+\frac{x}{2}\cdot\nabla U+\Delta U\right)+L_{\phi}U. $$

Albritton, Brué, and Colombo prove that

$$ \tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\sigma}\to L_{\phi}\quad\text{ as }\quad\sigma\to+\infty $$

in the strong resolvent sense uniformly on compact sets in $\{z:\textrm{Re}(z)>0\}\cap\rho(L_{\phi})$ , which implies the convergence of isolated eigenvalues. This allows the authors to conclude the existence of an unstable eigenvalue for $\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\sigma}$ , hence for $\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}$ , when $\sigma>0$ is sufficiently large. Our work is motivated by the following question: can the singular limit argument of Albritton, Brué, and Colombo work for the unforced Navier-Stokes equations?

One thing that is necessary for the argument to work is that $\bar{U}$ and $\beta\bar{U}$ are self-similar solutions for some non-trivial $\beta$ , which, we shall see, is far from being true for a generic self-similar solution. In addition, the singular limit argument from [2] relies heavily on the profile $\overline{U}$ having compact support, which is not feasible in the unforced case, since as we can see from the boundary conditions, any compactly supported self-similar solution corresponds to zero initial data at physical time $t=0$ .

Once again, our key observation is that the singular limit argument of [2] can only be carried through for a specific class of self-similar solutions:

#### Definition 1.

A self-similar solution $\bar{U}$ is called a homothetic self-similar solution if and only if there exists a real number $\beta$ with $\beta\neq 1,0$ such that $\beta\bar{U}$ is also a self-similar solution.

We shall often simply call such solutions homothetic solutions. As we shall see, for the Navier-Stokes equations, once $\bar{U}$ and $\beta\bar{U}$ are solutions for some $\beta\neq 1,0$ , $\beta U$ is a self-similar solution for all $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ . It is worth pointing out that homothetic solutions are uniquely determined by their boundary data: for a given (-1)-homogeneous divergence free $C^{\alpha}$ -vector-field $u_{0}$ we shall show that there exists at most one homothetic self-similar solution whose blow-down limit is $u_{0}$ . Therefore, non-uniqueness from such data necessarily leads to another profile breaking the homothetic property.

Our main result rules out the existence of sufficiently regular homothetic solutions. Indeed, we show the following Liouville type theorem:

#### Theorem 1.1.

Suppose $\bar{U}$ is a homothetic forward self-similar solution to the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations lying in the Morrey space $\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ for some $2<q\leq 3$ and corresponding to initial data

$$ u_{0}=\frac{\vec{v}+f\vec{n}}{|x|}\in\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3}), $$

where $\vec{n}$ is the unit normal to the sphere and $\vec{v}$ is a tangent vector field to the sphere. Suppose either

- (1) $\vec{v}\in W^{1,4/3}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ and $f\in L^{4}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$

- (2) $\vec{v},f\in C^{\alpha}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ , for some $\alpha>1/2$

then $f=0$ and the head pressure $|\vec{v}|^{2}+2p=0$ as well. In case (2) we get that $\vec{v}=u_{0}=\bar{U}=0$ with no additional assumptions. For case (1), if we assume that the set $\{\omega\in\mathbb{S}^{2}:\vec{v}(\omega)=0\}$ has measure zero or is closed with $C^{2}$ boundary, then $\vec{v}=u_{0}=\bar{U}=0$ .

For the reader’s benefit, we recall the definition of the Morrey spaces $\mathcal{M}^{p}_{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ where $1\leq q\leq p$ :

$$ f\in\mathcal{M}^{p}_{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\iff\exists C>0,\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{3},\forall R>0,\quad\int_{B_{R}(x)}|f(y)|^{q}dy\leq CR^{3-\tfrac{3q}{p}}. $$

Evidently, since $u_{0}\in\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ , we have $\vec{v},f\in L^{q}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ , so there is a gap between a reasonable class of data ( $L^{q}$ with $2<q\leq 3$ ) and the level at which the Liouville theorem can be proven ( $L^{4}$ ). Indeed, the existence of a unique mild solution to the Navier-Stokes equations has even been shown for small data $u_{0}\in\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ for any $q>1$ .

The main idea behind our proof of Theorem 1.1 is that the blow-down limit of a homothetic solution in three-dimensions lying in the Morrey space $\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}$ with $q>2$ is always a $(-1)$ -homogeneous weak stationary solution of the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations. The proof then continues by showing the nonexistence of nontrivial $(-1)$ -homogeneous Euler solutions in the regularity classes dealt with in Theorem 1.1. More precisely, we prove the following Liouville theorem for the stationary Euler equations:

#### Theorem 1.2.

Suppose $u_{0}$ is a $(-1)$ -homogeneous weak stationary solution of the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations,

$$ \operatorname{div}(u_{0}\otimes u_{0})+\nabla P_{0}=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}u_{0}=0\quad\hbox{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{3}), $$

of the form

$$ u_{0}(r\omega)=\frac{\vec{v}(\omega)+f(\omega)\vec{n}(\omega)}{r},\qquad P_{0}(r\omega)=\frac{p(\omega)}{r^{2}}, $$

where $\vec{n}$ is the unit normal to the sphere and $\vec{v}$ is a tangent vector field to the sphere. Suppose either

- (1) $\vec{v}\in W^{1,4/3}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ and $f\in L^{4}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$

- (2) $\vec{v},f\in C^{\alpha}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ , for some $\alpha>1/2$

then $f=0$ and the head pressure $|\vec{v}|^{2}+2p=0$ as well. In case (2) we get that $\vec{v}=u_{0}=0$ with no additional assumptions. For case (1), if we assume that the set $\{\omega\in\mathbb{S}^{2}:\vec{v}(\omega)=0\}$ has measure zero or is closed with $C^{2}$ boundary, then $\vec{v}=u_{0}=0$ .

Our Liouville theorem for the steady Euler equations is a generalization of the result of Shvydkoy [28], cf. our Proposition 3.4. We also mention that three-dimensional homogeneous Euler flows have been studied in [28] and [1], and two-dimensional Euler flows have been studied in [24] and [7].

Let us point out that while for the Jia-Šverák program the boundary data is allowed to be in $C^{\alpha}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ for any $\alpha>0$ , our Theorem 1.1 only presently rules out the existence of homothetic solutions with boundary data in $C^{\alpha}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ for $\alpha>\frac{1}{2}$ . Therefore, one may now wonder whether our Theorem 1.1 can be generalized to all $\alpha>0$ . The bottleneck in our proof is the Liouville theorem for $(-1)$ -homogeneous solutions to the steady Euler equations. It is unlikely that this result can be generalized to arbitrary $(-1)$ -homogeneous $C^{\alpha}$ -solutions below the Onsager threshold $\alpha=\frac{1}{3}$ . Instead, we expect the existence of wild solutions arising from convex integration in this regime. It is unknown to us whether such irregular boundary data can yield isotropically decaying homothetic self-similar solutions or not. We also remark that the Morrey space condition, at the very least, appears sharp. In this work we construct explicit nontrivial examples of homothetic solutions lying in $\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ for all $q<2$ . The question of uniqueness for these exact profiles remains open.

While the idea of Albritton, Brué, and Colombo only directly applies to homothetic solutions, a more general strategy applies to rescaled self-similar profiles that do not themselves have to solve the self-similar Navier-Stokes equations. For a more general family $U_{\beta}$ with boundary value $\beta u_{0}$ , let $V_{\beta}=U_{\beta}/\beta$ and rescale the pressure so that

$$ -\beta^{-1}\left(\Delta V_{\beta}+\tfrac{1}{2}(V_{\beta}+x\cdot\nabla V_{\beta})\right)+(V_{\beta}\cdot\nabla)V_{\beta}+\nabla Q_{\beta}=0. $$

A formal limit of $V_{\beta}$ to a solution $V_{\infty}$ of the steady Euler equations would require compactness sufficient to pass to the nonlinear term in the weak formulation. To guarantee that the limit $V_{\infty}$ has the same blowdown limit boundary value at infinity, we also would require a uniform in $\beta$ blowdown limit for the family $V_{\beta}$ . Note that although the equation satisfied by $V_{\beta}$ changes with $\beta$ , the boundary data, assuming a uniform in $\beta$ blowdown limit, is constant in $\beta$ . Inspired by the work in [17] and [2], we have investigated when a sufficient condition for non-uniqueness of Leray-Hopf solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations can be found in terms of the linearized Euler equations in the unforced case. In forthcoming work, we prove a conditional non-uniqueness theorem for Leray-Hopf solutions along the lines of this inviscid-limit argument (which we may contrast with the previous singular-limit argument as not requiring the rescaled profiles to solve the same PDE).

On the other hand, we are also able to rule out this inviscid-limit scenario for sufficiently regular data. Due to the scaling invariance of the Euler equations, the vector field $MV_{\infty}(M\cdot\xi)$ also solves the steady Euler equations with the same data. Under mild regularity assumptions on $V_{\infty}$ (e.g. it lies in the same Morrey space as in the statement of Theorem 1.1), and assuming strong local $L^{2}$ convergence of its blow-downs, by following the proof of our Proposition 3.1, we can obtain that the $(-1)$ -homogeneous data $u_{0}$ must be a steady-state of the Euler equations. Thus, our Theorem 1.2 applies, confirming the triviality of $u_{0}$ . Consequently, the inviscid singular limit argument is ruled out for (sufficiently regular) arbitrary nontrivial data.

This shows that the curve of self-similar solutions $U_{\beta}$ constructed by Jia and Šverák [18] cannot admit such an inviscid limit with nontrivial boundary data. This does not by itself imply stability for sufficiently large $\beta$ or restrict the desired instability to an intermediate regime of $\beta$ .

For anisotropically decaying homothetic solutions, in contrast with the work above, we are able to find examples with boundary data below the regularity threshold of Theorem 1.1, see Section 4. This confirms that the regularity conditions in Theorem 1.1 cannot be removed in general. Indeed, a few such homothetic solutions have been described previously in the work [26] of Okamoto, but we believe some of our examples are new self-similar solutions of the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations. The construction of these solutions is, surprisingly, more geometric than analytic in nature. Moreover, we shall prove that these solutions sometimes admit instabilities of the linearized Euler equations in the form of unstable normal modes, which can be used to make approximate eigenvalues via a wave-packet construction. As an example, we consider the shear flow described by Okamoto in [26]:

$$ \overline{U}_{1,\beta}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\beta\left(\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}e^{-\frac{\xi_{2}^{2}}{4}}\text{erfi}\left(\frac{\xi_{2}}{2}\right),0,0\right). $$

The vector field $\overline{U}_{1,\beta}$ is an anisotropically decaying homothetic self-similar solution to the Navier-Stokes equations from initial data:

$$ \overline{u}_{1,\beta}(x,y,z)=\textrm{P.V. }\left(\frac{\beta}{y},0,0\right). $$

Note that this solution is outside the regularity range of our previously discussed Liouville theorems, indeed the data lies in $BMO^{-1}$ , so the unique existence of a mild solution follows from the work done by Koch and Tataru in [20], as long as $\beta$ is sufficiently small. The second author and Palasek have proven in [8] that non-uniqueness can occur for data in the class $BMO^{-1}$ , but the uniqueness question for any particular initial data, such as $\overline{u}_{1,\beta}$ with large $\beta$ , remains open. Interestingly, we are able to prove the existence of an unstable element of the approximate point spectrum:

#### Theorem 1.3.

Let $\beta\neq 0$ and let $\overline{U}_{1,\beta}$ be the Okamoto shear flow described above. Let $L_{\beta}$ be the linearization of the Euler equations around $\overline{U}_{1,\beta}$ in velocity form on $L^{2}_{\sigma}(\mathbb{R}^{3};\mathbb{C}^{3})$ with dense maximal domain. Then $L_{\beta}$ has a positive real point in its approximate spectrum.

Although one may think that we should be able to improve Theorem 1.3 to a non-uniqueness result, there are clear technical obstacles to doing so. First, the singular limit argument that allows one to conclude the existence of an unstable eigenvalue of $\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}$ crucially depends on the existence of a discrete eigenvalue (rather than approximate point spectrum) to allow the instability to pass through the singular limit. Second, the lack of decay of the background profile makes several parts of the argument, for instance the truncation of the data, unfeasible. Third, attempts to use custom anisotropic function spaces for the singular limit argument are usually defeated by the drift operator $x\cdot\nabla$ , which behaves poorly on such spaces. Lastly, the existence of the unstable spectrum for all $\beta\neq 0$ suggests a dynamical behavior different than the discrete eigenvalue crossing bifurcation used in the program of [17].

Let us now discuss the analogous situation in two dimensions. We emphasize that, in contrast to the three-dimensional situation, the existence of an unstable self-similar profile for the two-dimensional self-similar Navier–Stokes equations would not imply non-uniqueness of Leray–Hopf solutions. Rather, the Jia–Šverák program would imply non-uniqueness in $\mathrm{L}^{p}_{t}\mathrm{L}^{q}_{x}$ with $\frac{2}{p}+\frac{2}{q}>1$ , which would confirm that Serrin’s condition is sharp. For a detailed discussion of the Jia–Šverák program in dimension two we refer to the recent work of Albritton et al. [3]. Again, we rule out the singular limit scenario by proving the following results. The first one shows that the Oseen vortex is the only isotropically decaying homothetic forward self-similar solution to the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with continuous angular data, which is a consequence of the following Liouville theorem for the stationary Euler equations:

#### Theorem 1.4.

Let $b\in C(\mathbb{S}^{1};\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and set $u_{0}(r\omega)=r^{-1}b(\omega)$ for $r>0$ . Suppose that $\operatorname{div}u_{0}=0$ in $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and that, for some scalar distribution $P_{0}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus\{0\}$ ,

$$ \operatorname{div}(u_{0}\otimes u_{0})+\nabla P_{0}=0\quad\hbox{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus\{0\}). $$

Then there is $A\in\mathbb{R}$ such that

$$ b(\omega)=A\omega^{\perp},\qquad u_{0}(r\omega)=\frac{A}{r}\omega^{\perp}. $$

For homothetic solutions, Theorem 1.4 and Lemma 2.5 give the following:

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $b\in C(\mathbb{S}^{1};\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and set $u_{0}(r\omega)=r^{-1}b(\omega)$ for $r>0$ . Suppose that $\operatorname{div}u_{0}=0$ in $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and that, for some scalar distribution $P_{0}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus\{0\}$ ,

$$ \operatorname{div}(u_{0}\otimes u_{0})+\nabla P_{0}=0\quad\hbox{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus\{0\}). $$

Let $U$ be a homothetic solution with $RU(R\,\cdot)\to u_{0}$ in $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ as $R\to\infty$ . Then there is $A\in\mathbb{R}$ such that

$$ b(\omega)=A\omega^{\perp},\qquad\bar{U}(r,\omega)=A\frac{1-e^{-r^{2}/4}}{r}\omega^{\perp}. $$

Moreover, this profile’s blow-down limit converges to $u_{0}$ in $L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ .

The proof of Theorem 1.4 more or less follows the outline of the analogous argument in [24]. The long-time stability of the Oseen vortex for the two-dimensional self-similar Navier–Stokes equations was established by [13]; however, their result does not directly apply to the Jia-Šverák program since their analysis is carried out in weighted function spaces. We prove the following stability result which rules out the singular-limit scenario in the two-dimensional case.

#### Theorem 1.6.

The linearization of the Euler equations in vorticity form around the Oseen vortex generates a strongly-continuous semigroup on the space $\mathrm{L}^{2}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and

$$ s(L_{\phi},L^{2}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))=\omega_{0}(L_{\phi},L^{2}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))=0. $$

Here $L^{2}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ denotes the complex space $\{g\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{C}):g(-x)=g(x)\}$ of square-integrable two-fold rotationally symmetric functions. Here $s(L,X)$ denotes the spectral bound of a closed, densely defined operator $L\colon D(L)\subset X\to X$ and $\omega_{0}(L,X)$ denotes the growth bound of the strongly continuous semigroup generated by $L$ .

The argument used in the proof of Theorem 1.4 also applies more generally to the inviscid limit, as previously discussed for the three-dimensional case. As before suppose $U_{\beta}$ is a solution to Equation (2) with boundary data $\beta u_{0}(\xi)$ at spatial infinity for some $\beta>0$ . Let $V_{\beta}(\xi)=U_{\beta}(\xi)/\beta$ . If we take the formal limit as $\beta\to\infty$ , then $V_{\infty}$ , the limit of $V_{\beta}$ as $\beta\to\infty$ , satisfies the steady Euler equations with $(-1)$ -homogeneous data $u_{0}$ . Due to the scaling invariance of the Euler equations, the vector field $MV_{\infty}(M\cdot\xi)$ also solves the steady Euler equations with the same data. From here, we can no longer argue completely analogously to the three-dimensional case, because $(-1)$ -homogeneous functions are not locally square-integrable and therefore cannot be weak solutions of the Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ (Proposition 3.1 does not directly apply). However, a similar argument under strong local $L^{2}$ convergence of the blow-down limits away from the origin can get that the $(-1)$ -homogeneous data $u_{0}$ must be a steady-state of the Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus\{0\}$ . Thus, our Theorem 1.4 applies, which shows that the boundary data must be the point vortex $u_{0}(r\omega)=A\omega^{\perp}/r$ . The corresponding homothetic self-similar solution is the Oseen vortex by Theorem 1.5. Now, due to the stability of the Oseen vortex as proven in Theorem 1.6, we can say that we rule out the homothetic singular-limit argument of [2] or [3] for non-uniqueness from any continuous angular data in two-dimensions within the two-fold rotationally symmetric space considered in Theorem 1.6. The Liouville theorem alone does not identify a general inviscid limit with the Oseen vortex or imply high-Reynolds stability. We contrast this stability result with the numerically discovered instability at intermediate Reynolds number, see [3].

In the course of proving the stability of the Oseen vortex, we rediscovered the following general stability criterion for the Euler equations on the whole plane, also found in a separate context by Gallay and Smets in [12].

#### Theorem 1.7.

Let $\overline{u}=u(r)e_{\theta}$ be a smooth real vector field on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ . Set $\Omega=u/r$ and $\overline{\omega}=u^{\prime}+u/r$ , and suppose that $\Omega$ is bounded and $\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(r)=O(r^{-3})$ as $r\to\infty$ . If either $\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(r)>0$ for every $r>0$ or $\overline{\omega}^{\prime}(r)<0$ for every $r>0$ , then the spectrum of the Euler equations in vorticity form linearized around $\overline{\omega}$ and densely defined on its maximal domain for the space $L^{2}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ is contained in the imaginary axis.

### 1.1. Announcement of Stronger Rigidity Results

In future work, we shall present proofs of the following improvements to the rigidity results in this paper. One important reason for separating the proof of the announced results from those within this paper is that the former are proven with LLM-assistance.

First, we shall prove

#### Theorem 1.8.

Let $U$ be a homothetic profile on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with data satisfying $u_{0}\in L^{q}(\mathbb{S}^{2},\mathbb{R}^{3})$ for any $q>2$ . Then $U=0$ .

This sharp result (we construct explicit examples in our work here when $q<2$ ) shows that the only plausible case remaining is if $u_{0}\in L^{q}(\mathbb{S}^{2},\mathbb{R}^{3})$ for $q\leq 2$ . Note that existence of smooth mild solutions in the Morrey space $\mathcal{M}^{3}_{q}$ is guaranteed for all $1<q\leq 2$ , so a non-uniqueness program may still be a possibility in these spaces. On the other hand, we have shown rigidity up to the space $L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ which is the borderline space for the truncation argument in [17] to have any chance at working. Moreover, the classical existence theory of [18] is completely excluded (since it deals with continuous spherical data) and we expect homothetic solutions from rough $L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ data, if they exist, to decay anisotropically. The proof of the theorem above no longer relies on a Liouville theorem for the stationary Euler equations. It therefore no longer applies to the inviscid limit. In order to rule out the inviscid limit we still rely on the strategy of this paper. Here, the result is improved by sharpening the Liouville result for the (-1)-homogeneous stationary Euler equations. Indeed Theorem 1.2 can be improved to the following result:

#### Theorem 1.9.

Suppose $u_{0}$ is a $(-1)$ -homogeneous solution of the steady Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ such that

$$ u_{0}=\frac{\vec{v}+f\vec{n}}{|x|}, $$

where $\vec{n}$ is the unit normal to the sphere and $\vec{v}$ is a tangent vector field to the sphere. If any of the following conditions hold:

- • $v,f\in C^{\alpha}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ with $\alpha>1/3$

- • $v\in c^{1/3}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ and $f\in C^{1/3}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$

- • $v,f\in L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ and axisymmetric

- • $f\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})$ and $v\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{S}^{2})\cap BV(\mathbb{S}^{2})$

then $u_{0}=0$ .

This result shows that the $(-1)$ -homogeneous solutions of the Euler equations must have regularity below the Onsager threshold, cannot be axisymmetric, and cannot be of bounded variation. Together, this result suggests a complicated geometric structure for these solutions, if such objects exist.

Following the strategy from this paper this implies for the inviscid limit:

#### Corollary 1.10.

Suppose $U_{\beta}$ is a family of solutions to Equation (2) on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with boundary data $\beta u_{0}$ , where $u_{0}=(\vec{v}+f\vec{n})/|x|$ and $\vec{v},f$ satisfy any one of the regularity conditions in the preceding theorem. Set $V_{\beta}=U_{\beta}/\beta$ . Suppose that, for some sequence $\beta_{j}\to\infty$ ,

$$ V_{\beta_{j}}\longrightarrow V_{\infty}\quad\hbox{strongly in }L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{3}), $$

and that the boundary data is attained uniformly along this sequence in the sense that, for every compact set $K\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}$ ,

$$ \lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_{j}\big\|RV_{\beta_{j}}(R\,\cdot)-u_{0}\big\|_{L^{2}(K)}=0. $$

Then $u_{0}=0$ . In particular, for nontrivial data satisfying any of these regularity conditions, no such inviscid limit exists.

Finally, in two dimensions we can show that any homothetic profile is either an Oseen vortex or an Okamoto shear flow, which sharpens the result from this work. This completely characterizes the homothetic profiles in two dimensions regardless of decay.
