This proves part (ii).

Lemma 5.12 shows that the activation cutoff equals one throughout $I_{q+1}$ . Oddness gives $X_{q+1}(0,t)=0$ , and (120) gives

$$ \nabla\zeta_{1}(0,t)=a_{q+1}(t)\lambda_{q+1}^{\beta_{q+1}}\nabla X_{q+1}(0,t). $$

Set

$$ A_{q+1}(t)=B_{q+1}(t):=a_{q+1}(t)\lambda_{q+1}^{\beta_{q+1}}|\nabla X_{q+1}(0,t)|. $$

Writing $\nabla X_{q+1}(0,t)/|\nabla X_{q+1}(0,t)|=e(\alpha_{q+1}(t))$ , the leading origin-jet identity gives

$$ D_{x}u^{[0]}[\zeta_{1}](0,t)=C_{0}B_{q+1}(t)\cos\alpha_{q+1}(t)\mathcal{M}(\alpha_{q+1}(t)). $$

The terminal normalization places both principal amplitudes in $[\frac{3}{4}\lambda_{q+1}^{\beta_{q+1}},\frac{5}{4}\lambda_{q+1}^{\beta_{q+1}}]$ above a finite threshold.

For $j\geq 2$ , the correction estimate and one oscillatory-factor derivative give

$$ |\nabla\zeta_{j}(0,t)|+\|D_{x}u^{[M]}[\zeta_{j}](0,t)\|\leq C_{\beta}L^{C}\lambda^{(2-j)\beta}\leq C_{\beta}L^{C}. $$

For the principal correction, every nonleading expansion term gains $\lambda^{-\beta}$ :

$$ \|D_{x}(u^{[M]}-u^{[0]})[\zeta_{1}](0,t)\|\leq C_{\beta}L^{C}\lambda^{-\beta}. $$

For every $1\leq j\leq M$ , the grouped exact velocity remainder satisfies

$$ \|D_{x}(u_{\mathbb{T}}-u^{[M]})[\zeta_{j}]\|_{C^{0}}\leq C_{\beta}L^{C}\lambda^{3-(j+2)\beta-M\beta}\leq C_{\beta}L^{C}\lambda^{-5}. $$

Thus the sum of the higher-correction density jets and all nonleading velocity jets is bounded by $C_{\beta}L^{C}$ . A final threshold makes this at most the errors required in (58)–(59), proving the complete origin geometry.

Finally, the $j=1,2$ , $m=0$ cases of (54) at the preceding stage give

$$ \|P_{q+1}\|_{C^{1}}+\|u_{\mathbb{T}}(P_{q+1})\|_{C^{1}}\leq C\lambda_{q}^{2}. $$

Equation (63) makes this fixed power at most $\lambda_{q+1}^{\beta_{q+1}/8}$ above a finite threshold. This is the cutoff-parent bound in (57).

Parent admissibility and the terminal-time separation give

$$ \widetilde{C}\lambda_{q+1}^{-3\beta_{q+1}/4}\leq\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{C}\lambda_{q}^{-3\beta_{q}/4}\leq\frac{1}{2}. $$

Thus (45) propagates to the child, so its terminal window also lies in $[0,1]$ .

Put $J_{*}=\min\{K_{q},k_{q+1}\}$ . If $1\leq j+2m\leq J_{*}$ , cutoff boundedness and (54) at level $q$ give

$$ \|S_{\mu}\partial_{t}^{m}\rho^{(q)}\|_{C^{j}}\leq 2C_{j}\Lambda^{j+2m}. $$

There are finitely many such pairs, so frequency separation makes this at most $\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{j+2m}$ simultaneously for all of them. The new-perturbation bound above supplies the other half. Hence (165) follows from (155), proving part (iii). The scale selection, angle law, activation-interval separation, derivative bounds, and origin geometry verified above establish every remaining clause of the admissible-family definition. ∎

## 6. Global iteration and blow-up

Retain the fixed cutoff $\chi$ , spatial profile $f$ , and activation profile $W$ from Sections 3 and 5. The initial base oscillation parameter will be chosen so that every perturbation support is contained in the coordinate chart of Proposition 3.4. The all-order mixed estimates used in the iteration are proved in Appendix A.

### 6.1. Initialization and the recursive exponent choice

Set

$$ \beta_{0}:=\frac{1}{8},\qquad k_{0}=K_{0}:=257=d(\beta_{0}),\qquad\alpha_{0}:=\frac{\pi}{2}+\lambda_{0}^{-1/64}. $$

For sufficiently large $\lambda_{0}$ , define in the central chart

$$ \theta_{0}(x):=\lambda_{0}^{-7/8}f(\lambda_{0}^{1/4}x)\sin\bigl(\lambda_{0}e(\alpha_{0})\cdot x\bigr),\qquad P_{0}:=0,\qquad\rho^{(0)}:=\theta_{0}, $$

and extend $\theta_{0}$ periodically by zero. Put

$$ F^{(0)}:=u_{\mathbb{T}}(\theta_{0})\cdot\nabla\theta_{0}. $$

#### Lemma 6.1 (Periodic base layer).

There is a finite threshold $\lambda_{*}(f,\chi)$ such that, whenever $\lambda_{0}\geq\lambda_{*}(f,\chi)$ , the fields in (170)–(171) form an admissible level-zero stage.

#### Proof.

Increase $\lambda_{*}(f,\chi)$ , if necessary, so that $\lambda_{*}(f,\chi)\geq e$ and, whenever $\lambda_{0}\geq\lambda_{*}(f,\chi)$ ,

$$ \widetilde{C}\lambda_{0}^{-3/32}\leq 1. $$

Since $\beta_{0}=1/8$ , this is (45) and gives $I_{0}\subset[0,1]$ . The envelope in (170) is supported strictly inside the coordinate chart. Hence its extension by zero is smooth even though the local phase covector need not belong to the integer lattice. The density is odd and therefore has zero mean. Its support lies in $B_{\lambda_{0}^{-1/4}}$ , and

$$ \|\theta_{0}\|_{C^{j}}\leq C_{f,j}\lambda_{0}^{j-7/8}\leq\lambda_{0}^{j}\qquad(0\leq j\leq 257), $$

above a finite threshold. The pair is stationary and satisfies the level-zero equation by (171). Moreover, $F^{(0)}$ is odd because $u_{\mathbb{T}}(\theta_{0})$ is odd and $\nabla\theta_{0}$ is even.

Since $f=1$ near the origin,

$$ \nabla\theta_{0}(0)=\lambda_{0}^{1/8}e(\alpha_{0}). $$

On $I_{0}$ , define the witnesses in the admissible origin geometry by

$$ \displaystyle A_{0}(t) \displaystyle=B_{0}(t)=\lambda_{0}^{1/8}, \displaystyle\alpha_{0}(t) \displaystyle\equiv\frac{\pi}{2}+\lambda_{0}^{-1/64}, \displaystyle E_{0}^{\rho}(t) \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle E_{0}^{u}(t) \displaystyle=D_{x}u_{\mathbb{T}}(\theta_{0})(0)-C_{0}\lambda_{0}^{1/8}\cos\alpha_{0}\,\mathcal{M}(\alpha_{0}). $$

For this application, set $P=0$ , $v:=u_{\mathbb{T}}(P)$ , and $\mathcal{G}:=\nabla P$ , so $v=\mathcal{G}=0$ . Apply Proposition 3.4 with this $P$ , the linear phase $e(\alpha_{0})\cdot x$ , and $\beta_{0}=1/8$ ; its hypotheses hold with $v=\mathcal{G}=0$ , exactly linear phase on the amplitude support, $\operatorname{supp}f(\lambda_{0}^{1/4}\,\cdot)\Subset B_{r_{0}}$ , and $\nu_{1}=\lambda_{0}\geq e$ , by Lemma 3.2 and Corollary 3.3. Its leading Euclidean term gives the shear matrix in (59). The smooth periodic-kernel contribution is absorbed into the grouped remainder after exactly $M_{0}$ integrations by parts. The nonleading expansion terms, grouped remainder, and smooth-kernel term contribute entrywise to the Jacobian error at most

$$ C_{f}\lambda_{0}^{-1/8},\qquad C_{f}\lambda_{0}^{-43/8},\qquad C_{f}\lambda_{0}^{-391/8}, $$

respectively. Thus, above a finite threshold, each of the four components of $E_{0}^{u}$ has absolute value at most $\lambda_{0}^{1/64}$ . Profile scaling gives the support condition and the sharp perturbation estimates, while stationarity gives every positive-time mixed bound. The preceding bounds verify the remaining level-zero clauses of Definition 4.1; in particular, $P_{0}=0$ gives the required previous-stage $C^{1}$ estimates and the constant reference-angle law. ∎

The exponent $\beta_{q}$ controls the size of the $q$ -th perturbation and the number of derivative estimates required at that scale. The integer $k_{q}$ is the largest prescribed weighted mixed-derivative order for that perturbation; $K_{q}$ is the largest weighted mixed-derivative order verified for the complete stage. At a fixed exponent we raise $k_{q}$ as the base oscillation parameters grow. Once $K_{q}$ is large enough to authorize the smaller exponent and the corresponding finite threshold has been reached, we replace $\beta_{q}$ by $\beta_{q}/2$ .

Fix a finite threshold function

$$ \lambda_{\mathrm{th},\mathbb{T}}(\beta,\beta^{\prime},k;f,\chi,W),\qquad 0<\frac{\beta}{2}\leq\beta^{\prime}\leq\beta\leq\frac{1}{8},\qquad k\geq d(\beta^{\prime}), $$

which is nondecreasing in $k$ and dominates every finite requirement in Proposition 5.13. With parent exponent $\beta$ and child exponent $\beta^{\prime}$ , it dominates

$$ \begin{gathered}\Lambda_{\rm sep}(\beta),\quad\Lambda_{\rm geom}(\beta,\beta^{\prime}),\quad\Lambda_{\rm flow}(\beta,\beta^{\prime}),\quad\Lambda_{\perp}(\beta,\beta^{\prime}),\\
\Lambda_{\rm gain}(\beta,\beta^{\prime}),\quad\Lambda_{\rm seed}(\beta,\beta^{\prime}),\quad\Lambda_{\rm pkt}(\beta,\beta^{\prime}),\quad\Lambda_{\rm cas}(\beta,\beta^{\prime}),\\
\Lambda_{\rm res}(\beta,\beta^{\prime}),\quad\Lambda_{\rm com}(\beta,\beta^{\prime}),\quad\Lambda_{\rm activation}(\beta,\beta^{\prime}),\end{gathered} $$

whenever the named threshold is used, together with the finite scale, support, profile, and mixed-order absorptions for $j+2m\leq k$ . Each depends only on $(\beta,\beta^{\prime},k;f,\chi,W)$ . The arbitrary fixed-order sharp estimates have order-dependent constants but impose no additional threshold. Increase $\lambda_{0}$ , if necessary, so that

$$ \lambda_{0}\geq\max\left\{\lambda_{*}(f,\chi),\lambda_{\mathrm{th},\mathbb{T}}(\beta_{0},\beta_{0},d(\beta_{0});f,\chi,W)\right\}. $$

Suppose that level $q$ has been constructed and write $\beta=\beta_{q}$ . If

$$ K_{q}\geq d(\beta/2)\quad\text{and}\quad\lambda_{q}\geq\max\left\{\lambda_{\mathrm{th},\mathbb{T}}(\beta,\beta/2,d(\beta/2);f,\chi,W),\lambda_{\mathrm{th},\mathbb{T}}(\beta/2,\beta/2,d(\beta/2);f,\chi,W)\right\}, $$

choose

$$ \beta_{q+1}:=\frac{\beta_{q}}{2},\qquad k_{q+1}:=d(\beta_{q+1}). $$

Otherwise choose

$$ \beta_{q+1}:=\beta_{q},\qquad k_{q+1}:=\max\left\{k\in\mathbb{N}:d(\beta_{q})\leq k\leq q+d(\beta_{q}),\ \lambda_{q}\geq\lambda_{\mathrm{th},\mathbb{T}}(\beta_{q},\beta_{q},k;f,\chi,W)\right\}. $$

The admissible set in (174) is nonempty. At $q=0$ , the candidate $d(\beta_{0})$ is authorized by the base threshold. If level $q$ follows a halving, the second threshold in (172) authorizes $d(\beta_{q})$ . If it follows a retention step, the previously chosen $k_{q}$ remains admissible: it lies below the enlarged cap, while

$$ \lambda_{q}\geq\lambda_{q-1}\geq\lambda_{\mathrm{th},\mathbb{T}}(\beta_{q},\beta_{q},k_{q};f,\chi,W). $$

Once $\beta_{q+1}$ has been fixed, define $\lambda_{q+1}$ by (63), apply Proposition 5.13, and define $K_{q+1}$ by (160).

#### Lemma 6.2 (Continuation).

Let the parameter and mixed-derivative-order sequences be generated from (169) by (172)– (174), (63), and (160). The recursion continues for every $q$ . On every infinite consecutive set of indices on which $\beta_{q}$ is constant, one has $k_{q}\to\infty$ .

#### Proof.

At a halving step, condition (172) authorizes both that step and the first retained step at the new exponent. The nonemptiness verified immediately after (174) handles every retention step. Thus the recursion cannot stop.

Fix $\bar{\beta}$ and a derivative order $k\geq d(\bar{\beta})$ . The number $\lambda_{\mathrm{th},\mathbb{T}}(\bar{\beta},\bar{\beta},k;f,\chi,W)$ is finite. By (48), $\lambda_{q+1}\geq 4\lambda_{q}$ , so $\lambda_{q}\to\infty$ ; the cap $q+d(\bar{\beta})$ also tends to infinity. Consequently $k_{q}\geq k$ at all sufficiently late indices of a constant- $\bar{\beta}$ block. ∎

### 6.2. Iterated cutoff formulas and parameter growth

The density formula (61) was derived directly from the finite-stage invariant. The same cutoff induction gives, for every $Q\geq 1$ ,

$$ F^{(Q)}=S_{\mu_{1}}F^{(0)}+\sum_{i=1}^{Q-1}S_{\mu_{i+1}}G_{i}+G_{Q}. $$

Indeed, $\mu_{j}\geq 2\mu_{i}$ whenever $j>i$ , so

$$ S_{\mu_{j}}S_{\mu_{i}}=S_{\mu_{i}}. $$

Thus every perturbation and every force increment is truncated exactly once and is then fixed. In particular,

$$ \operatorname{supp}\widehat{S_{\mu_{i+1}}\theta_{i}}\subset B_{2\mu_{i+1}},\qquad\operatorname{supp}\widehat{S_{\mu_{i+1}}G_{i}}\subset B_{2\mu_{i+1}}. $$

Moreover, (150) and $\mu_{i+1}\geq 4\mu_{i}$ imply

$$ S_{\mu_{i+1}}\mathcal{C}_{\mu_{i}}(\rho^{(i-1)})=\mathcal{C}_{\mu_{i}}(\rho^{(i-1)}). $$

#### Lemma 6.3 (Decay of the scale exponent).

For the parameter and mixed-derivative-order sequences generated by (172)–(174), (63), and (160), one has

$$ \beta_{q}\downarrow 0,\qquad x_{q}:=\beta_{q}\log\lambda_{q}\longrightarrow\infty. $$

After increasing the base threshold,

$$ x_{q+1}\geq 64x_{q},\qquad L_{q}^{4}\leq\lambda_{q}^{\beta_{q}},\qquad r_{q+1}\leq\lambda_{q}^{-8}. $$

Consequently $r_{q}\to 0$ , $\underline{t}_{q}\uparrow 1$ , and the intervals $[\underline{t}_{q},\underline{t}_{q+1}]$ cover a terminal neighborhood of one.

#### Proof.

If $\beta_{q}\not\to 0$ , then, because each step either retains $\beta_{q}$ or replaces it by $\beta_{q}/2$ , only finitely many halvings occur. Hence $\beta_{q}=\bar{\beta}>0$ for every sufficiently large $q$ . Since $\beta_{q+1}=\beta_{q}$ at every sufficiently late stage, the halving criterion fails there. Its frequency condition already holds, so its first condition fails and $K_{q}<d(\bar{\beta}/2)$ , hence

$$ K_{q}\leq D_{*}:=\left\lceil\frac{16}{\bar{\beta}^{2}}\right\rceil, $$

at all sufficiently late stages. Lemma 6.2 gives $k_{q}>D_{*}+1$ . Put $n=K_{q}+1$ . By maximality in (160), there are integers $j,m\geq 0$ with $j+2m=n$ , and a time $\tau_{q}$ , such that

$$ \|\partial_{t}^{m}\rho^{(q)}(\tau_{q})\|_{C^{j}}>2\lambda_{q}^{n}. $$

Choose $q_{0}$ so that $k_{i}>D_{*}+1$ for every $i\geq q_{0}$ . Let $C_{\rm head}$ bound the fixed contribution of indices $i<q_{0}$ , uniformly over the finitely many possible values of $n$ . The cutoff operators commute with $\partial_{t}$ and have a uniform $C^{j}$ -operator norm for each $j\leq D_{*}+1$ . Hence (61) and the perturbation mixed estimates (53) give

$$ \|\partial_{t}^{m}\rho^{(q)}(\tau_{q})\|_{C^{j}}\leq C_{\rm head}+C_{D_{*}}\sum_{i=q_{0}}^{q-1}\lambda_{i}^{n}+\lambda_{q}^{n}. $$

On a constant- $\bar{\beta}$ block, the deterministic frequency law implies $\lambda_{q}/\lambda_{q-1}\to\infty$ . Since $n$ ranges over the finite set $\{1,\ldots,D_{*}+1\}$ ,

$$ C_{\rm head}+C_{D_{*}}\sum_{i=q_{0}}^{q-1}\lambda_{i}^{n}=o(\lambda_{q}^{n}), $$

uniformly in the possible $n$ . This contradicts (178). Therefore $\beta_{q}\downarrow 0$ .

The selected frequency separation gives

$$ \lambda_{q+1}^{\beta_{q+1}/8}\geq 4\lambda_{q}. $$

Taking logarithms and using $\beta_{q}\leq 1/8$ yields

$$ x_{q+1}\geq 8\log\lambda_{q}=\frac{8}{\beta_{q}}x_{q}\geq 64x_{q}. $$

Equation (63) also gives

$$ L_{q+1}=\frac{\beta_{q+1}}{192\pi}\exp(x_{q}/8),\qquad\log L_{q+1}\leq\frac{x_{q}}{8}. $$

After arranging the base case, $4\log L_{q+1}\leq x_{q+1}$ , which proves $L_{q+1}^{4}\leq\lambda_{q+1}^{\beta_{q+1}}$ . Therefore

$$ r_{q+1}=\lambda_{q+1}^{-2\beta_{q+1}}L_{q+1}^{4}\leq\lambda_{q+1}^{-\beta_{q+1}}\leq\lambda_{q}^{-8}. $$

The remaining conclusions follow from (40) and the neighboring time-scale separation. ∎

### 6.3. The limiting density and force

Define

$$ \rho:=S_{\mu_{1}}\theta_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}S_{\mu_{i+1}}\theta_{i},\qquad F:=S_{\mu_{1}}F^{(0)}+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}S_{\mu_{i+1}}G_{i}. $$

#### Proposition 6.4 (Global limit).

For the admissible stages produced by the recursive exponent choice, let $\rho,F$ be defined by (179). Then $F\in C^{\infty}([0,1]\times\mathbb{T}^{2})$ . For every $T<1$ , the sequences $(\rho^{(q)})_{q}$ and $(F^{(q)})_{q}$ are eventually constant in the stage index on $[0,T]$ , the limiting density is smooth there, and

$$ \partial_{t}\rho+u_{\mathbb{T}}(\rho)\cdot\nabla\rho=F\quad\text{on }[0,T]\times\mathbb{T}^{2}. $$

The initial datum is

$$ \rho_{\rm in}=\rho(0)=S_{\mu_{1}}\theta_{0}. $$

The function $\rho_{\rm in}$ is smooth, odd, and has zero spatial mean. For every $t\in[0,1]$ , the function $F(t,\cdot)$ is odd and has zero spatial mean. There is one function

$$ \rho_{*}\in\bigcap_{0\leq\eta<1}C^{\eta}(\mathbb{T}^{2}) $$

such that, for every $0\leq\eta<1$ ,

$$ \rho(t)\longrightarrow\rho_{*}\quad\text{in }C^{\eta}(\mathbb{T}^{2})\quad\text{as }t\uparrow 1. $$

#### Proof.

For $\eta=0$ , cutoff boundedness follows from (196); for $0<\eta<1$ , it follows from (198). Interpolation between the two sharp estimates in (163) gives

$$ \|S_{\mu_{i+1}}\theta_{i}\|_{C^{\eta}}\leq C_{\eta}\lambda_{i}^{-1+2\beta_{i}+\eta}. $$

By (176), the exponent on the right is at most $-(1-\eta)/2$ for every sufficiently large $i$ . The first series in (179) therefore converges uniformly in $C^{\eta}$ , including at $t=1$ , because $\lambda_{i+1}\geq 4\lambda_{i}$ by (48). Set $\rho_{*}:=\rho(1)$ . Uniform smallness of the series tails and continuity of every finite head prove (182); this definition of $\rho_{*}$ is independent of $\eta$ .

Fix $m,k\geq 0$ . Since $\beta_{i}\to 0$ , choose $i_{0}=i_{0}(m,k)$ so that for every $i\geq i_{0}$ ,

$$ \beta_{i}\leq\frac{1}{40},\qquad m+k\leq m_{i}:=\left\lfloor\frac{1}{4\beta_{i}}\right\rfloor-10. $$

By admissibility and (156), the base term and the finitely many summands with $i<i_{0}$ , including every term formed while $\beta_{i}>1/40$ , are smooth and form a finite head of (179). On the remaining tail, Proposition 5.13 and (164) give

$$ \|\partial_{t}^{m}G_{i}\|_{C^{k}}\leq\lambda_{i}^{-1/4}, $$

throughout this tail. The second series in (179) therefore converges in $C_{t}^{m}C_{x}^{k}$ : the cutoffs are uniformly bounded on every fixed $C^{k}$ , commute with time derivatives, and $\lambda_{i+1}\geq 4\lambda_{i}$ makes $\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}^{-1/4}$ finite. Since $m,k$ are arbitrary,

$$ F\in C^{\infty}([0,1]\times\mathbb{T}^{2}). $$

Fix $T<1$ . Choose $q$ sufficiently large that every perturbation with index at least $q-1$ vanishes on $[0,T]$ . Then $\rho^{(q-1)}$ is already Fourier truncated to $B_{2\mu_{q-1}}$ , and (201) puts its nonlinearity in $B_{4\mu_{q-1}}$ . Consequently,

$$ S_{\mu_{q}}\rho^{(q-1)}=\rho^{(q-1)},\qquad\mathcal{C}_{\mu_{q}}(\rho^{(q-1)})=0\quad\text{on }[0,T]. $$

The perturbation residual $E_{q}^{\rm pert}$ also vanishes there.

The newest untruncated term of $F^{(q-1)}$ is then a cutoff commutator at scale $\mu_{q-1}$ , and (150) places it in $B_{4\mu_{q-1}}$ . Every older force piece already has a lower Fourier cutoff. Since $\mu_{q}\geq 4\mu_{q-1}$ ,

$$ S_{\mu_{q}}F^{(q-1)}=F^{(q-1)}\quad\text{on }[0,T]. $$

Equations (155) and (156) now show that

$$ \rho^{(q)}=\rho^{(q-1)},\qquad F^{(q)}=F^{(q-1)}\quad\text{on }[0,T]. $$

These identities propagate by induction. Suppose $n\geq q$ and $\rho^{(n)}=\rho^{(q-1)}$ , $F^{(n)}=F^{(q-1)}$ on $[0,T]$ . The common density and force have Fourier supports in $B_{2\mu_{q-1}}$ and $B_{4\mu_{q-1}}$ , respectively. Since $\mu_{n+1}\geq\mu_{q}\geq 4\mu_{q-1}$ , the next cutoff fixes both, $\mathcal{C}_{\mu_{n+1}}(\rho^{(n)})=0$ , and $\theta_{n+1}=E_{n+1}^{\rm pert}=0$ on $[0,T]$ . The two stage recursions therefore give the same identities at level $n+1$ . Thus both sequences are eventually constant in the stage index on $[0,T]$ . The corresponding partial sums in (179) are $\rho^{(Q)}-\theta_{Q}$ and $F^{(Q)}-G_{Q}$ . For sufficiently large $Q$ , both $\theta_{Q}$ and $G_{Q}$ vanish on $[0,T]$ , so the two series agree there with the eventual stages. The finite-stage equation then gives (180) without passage through a nonlinear limit.

Every perturbation after the base layer vanishes at $t=0$ , which proves (181). Each $\theta_{i}$ , $F^{(0)}$ , and $G_{i}$ is odd, and the even cutoffs preserve oddness. Uniform convergence therefore preserves oddness in both limiting series; every odd periodic scalar has zero spatial mean. The first cutoff also makes $\rho_{\rm in}$ smooth.

At time zero, $E_{1}^{\rm pert}=0$ , and

$$ S_{\mu_{1}}F^{(0)}+\mathcal{C}_{\mu_{1}}(\theta_{0})=u_{\mathbb{T}}(S_{\mu_{1}}\theta_{0})\cdot\nabla S_{\mu_{1}}\theta_{0}. $$

The commutator is supported in $B_{4\mu_{1}}$ , so $S_{\mu_{2}}\mathcal{C}_{\mu_{1}}(\theta_{0})=\mathcal{C}_{\mu_{1}}(\theta_{0})$ . For $i\geq 2$ , the density $\rho^{(i-1)}(0)$ is Fourier truncated to $B_{2\mu_{i-1}}$ , while $\mu_{i}\geq 4\mu_{i-1}$ . Thus the Fourier truncated commutator identity (151) gives $\mathcal{C}_{\mu_{i}}(\rho^{(i-1)})(0)=0$ ; moreover, $E_{i}^{\rm pert}(0)=0$ . Hence $G_{i}(0)=0$ for every $i\geq 2$ . Every perturbation with positive index and every force increment $G_{i}$ with $i\geq 2$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $t=0$ , so $\partial_{t}\rho(0)=0$ and

$$ F(0)=u_{\mathbb{T}}(\rho_{\rm in})\cdot\nabla\rho_{\rm in}. $$

Thus the limiting equation also holds at the initial time. ∎

### 6.4. Density-gradient lower bound on terminal intervals

For

$$ t\in[\underline{t}_{q},\underline{t}_{q+1}], $$

every perturbation above $q+1$ vanishes. The iterated cutoff formula therefore gives

$$ \rho(t)=P_{q}(t)+S_{\mu_{q+1}}\theta_{q}(t)+S_{\mu_{q+2}}\theta_{q+1}(t). $$

Set

$$ y_{q}(t):=2r_{q+1}e(\alpha_{q}(t)). $$

Since $\operatorname{supp}\theta_{q+1}(t)\subset B_{r_{q+1}}$ and $r_{q+1}\leq\lambda_{q}^{-8}$ , this point lies outside the support of $\theta_{q+1}$ , but remains close enough to the origin to retain the level- $q$ geometry. For the density estimate only the cutoff tail of $\theta_{q+1}$ remains; for the velocity estimate, $u_{\mathbb{T}}(\theta_{q+1})$ is nonlocal and must also be bounded. All constants in the cutoff-tail estimates below are absolute after the fixed cutoff is chosen; in particular, they are independent of $q$ , $\beta_{q}$ , and $\beta_{q+1}$ .

#### Proposition 6.5 (Density-gradient lower bound).

For the limiting density $\rho$ produced by the recursive exponent choice, there is $q_{*}\in\mathbb{N}$ such that, for every $q\geq q_{*}$ and every $t\in[\underline{t}_{q},\underline{t}_{q+1}]$ ,

$$ \|\nabla\rho(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\geq\frac{1}{8}\lambda_{q}^{\beta_{q}}. $$

Consequently,

$$ \lim_{t\uparrow 1}\|\nabla\rho(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}=\infty. $$

#### Proof.

For large $q$ , the point $y_{q}(t)$ lies in the fixed coordinate chart, and the child $\theta_{q+1}$ vanishes in a neighborhood of it.

Apply (197) with $j=1$ , $s=3$ , the perturbation $C^{7}$ estimate (53), and $\mu_{q+2}\geq\lambda_{q+1}^{4}$ . This gives

$$ \|\nabla(S_{\mu_{q+2}}-I)\theta_{q+1}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\lambda_{q+1}^{-5}. $$

The cutoff-tail estimate (72) gives

$$ \|\nabla(S_{\mu_{q+1}}-I)\theta_{q}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\lambda_{q}^{-4}. $$

By the mean-value theorem, (184), the $C^{2}$ case of (163), and (177),

$$ |\partial_{e(\alpha_{q}(t))}\theta_{q}(y_{q}(t),t)-\partial_{e(\alpha_{q}(t))}\theta_{q}(0,t)|\leq 2r_{q+1}\|\theta_{q}(t)\|_{C^{2}}\leq 2\lambda_{q}^{-6}. $$

The cutoff-parent bound (57) gives

$$ \|P_{q}(t)\|_{C^{1}}\leq\lambda_{q}^{\beta_{q}/8}. $$

Combining (183), the three preceding error estimates, and (58), we obtain

$$ |\partial_{e(\alpha_{q}(t))}\rho(y_{q}(t),t)|\geq\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{q}^{\beta_{q}}-C\lambda_{q}^{\beta_{q}/8}-C\lambda_{q}^{-4}-C\lambda_{q}^{-6}-C\lambda_{q+1}^{-5}. $$

This is at least $\lambda_{q}^{\beta_{q}}/8$ for all sufficiently large $q$ , uniformly throughout the interval. Lemma 6.3 proves (186). ∎

### 6.5. Velocity-gradient lower bound on terminal intervals

#### Proposition 6.6 (Velocity-gradient lower bound).

For the limiting density $\rho$ produced by the recursive exponent choice, there are $c>0$ and $q_{*}\in\mathbb{N}$ such that, for every $q\geq q_{*}$ and every $t\in[\underline{t}_{q},\underline{t}_{q+1}]$ ,

$$ \|D_{x}u_{\mathbb{T}}(\rho(t))\|_{L^{\infty}}\geq c\lambda_{q}^{7\beta_{q}/8}. $$

Consequently,

$$ \lim_{t\uparrow 1}\|D_{x}u_{\mathbb{T}}(\rho(t))\|_{L^{\infty}}=\infty. $$

#### Proof.

Since

$$ \mathcal{M}(\alpha)=-e^{\perp}(\alpha)e(\alpha)^{\mathsf{T}}, $$

its entry in the first row and second column is $\sin^{2}\alpha$ . The angle bounds in Lemma 4.4, the bound $B_{q}(t)\geq\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{q}^{\beta_{q}}$ from Definition 4.1, and (59) give

$$ C_{0}B_{q}|\cos\alpha_{q}|\sin^{2}\alpha_{q}\geq\frac{C_{0}}{4}(1-o(1))\lambda_{q}^{7\beta_{q}/8}, $$

uniformly in the terminal interval. Retaining fixed slack, we obtain

$$ |\partial_{2}u_{\mathbb{T},1}(\theta_{q})(0,t)|\geq\frac{C_{0}}{8\pi}\lambda_{q}^{7\beta_{q}/8}-\lambda_{q}^{\beta_{q}/8}. $$

The mean-value theorem, (195) applied to each $\partial_{a}\theta_{q}$ , the $C^{3}$ case of (163), and (177) give

$$ |D_{x}u_{\mathbb{T}}(\theta_{q})(y_{q}(t),t)-D_{x}u_{\mathbb{T}}(\theta_{q})(0,t)|\leq Cr_{q+1}\lambda_{q}^{3}\leq C\lambda_{q}^{-5}. $$

The cutoff tail (72) contributes at most $C\lambda_{q}^{-4}$ , while (57) bounds the cutoff-parent contribution by $\lambda_{q}^{\beta_{q}/8}$ .

Since $\lvert y_{q}(t)\rvert=2r_{q+1}$ and $\operatorname{supp}\theta_{q+1}(t)\subset B_{r_{q+1}}$ ,

$$ \operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb{T}^{2}}\bigl(y_{q}(t),\operatorname{supp}\theta_{q+1}(t)\bigr)\geq r_{q+1} $$

for all sufficiently large $q$ . The differentiated periodic kernel is the differentiated Euclidean kernel, bounded by $C|h|^{-3}$ , plus a smooth function. Integration over the child support therefore gives

$$ |D_{x}u_{\mathbb{T}}(\theta_{q+1})(y_{q}(t),t)|\leq C\frac{\|\theta_{q+1}(t)\|_{C^{0}}}{r_{q+1}}+C\|\theta_{q+1}(t)\|_{L^{1}}. $$

The perturbation-size estimate (163) and the definition of $r_{q+1}$ now give

$$ \displaystyle|D_{x}u_{\mathbb{T}}(\theta_{q+1})(y_{q}(t),t)| \displaystyle\leq CL_{q+1}^{-4}\lambda_{q+1}^{-1+4\beta_{q+1}}+C\|\theta_{q+1}(t)\|_{L^{1}} \displaystyle\leq 1, $$

for all sufficiently large $q$ , because $\beta_{q+1}\leq 1/8$ . Applying (197) with $j=2$ , $s=3$ , and the perturbation $C^{8}$ estimate (53), followed by the periodic Schauder estimate, gives

$$ \|D_{x}u_{\mathbb{T}}((S_{\mu_{q+2}}-I)\theta_{q+1})\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\lambda_{q+1}^{-4}. $$

Combining (183) with (191) and the preceding error estimates yields

$$ \|D_{x}u_{\mathbb{T}}(\rho(t))\|_{L^{\infty}}\geq c\lambda_{q}^{7\beta_{q}/8}, $$

for every sufficiently large $q$ , uniformly throughout the interval. Since the intervals cover a terminal neighborhood of one and $\lambda_{q}^{7\beta_{q}/8}\to\infty$ , this proves (190). ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 2.1.

Lemma 6.1, Proposition 5.13, and the recursive exponent choice construct admissible stages for every $q$ . Proposition 6.4 gives an odd smooth datum, an odd force in $C^{\infty}([0,1]\times\mathbb{T}^{2})$ , a classical solution on $[0,1)$ , and convergence to an endpoint in every $C^{\eta}$ , $0\leq\eta<1$ . Propositions 6.5 and 6.6 give the two gradient divergences asserted in the theorem. ∎

## Appendix A Mixed estimates and smoothness of the force

At the step from level $q$ to level $q+1$ , use the one-step aliases

$$ \begin{gathered}\beta=\beta_{q+1},\quad\lambda=\lambda_{q+1},\quad L=L_{q+1},\quad M=M_{q+1}=\lceil\beta^{-2}\rceil,\quad\mu=\mu_{q+1},\quad r=r_{q+1},\\
P=P_{q+1},\quad v=v_{q}=u_{\mathbb{T}}(P),\quad\Phi=\Phi_{q},\quad X=X_{q+1},\quad\alpha=\alpha_{q+1},\quad a=a_{q+1},\quad s=s_{q+1},\\
\gamma=1-2\beta,\qquad D=\partial_{t}+v\cdot\nabla.\end{gathered} $$

The estimates below distinguish derivatives of perturbation coefficients from derivatives of the oscillatory factor. A coefficient derivative costs only powers of $L$ and $\lambda^{2\beta}$ per spatial derivative, whereas an ordinary time derivative of the oscillatory factor costs $\lambda^{\gamma}$ .

We first derive all-order bounds for the cutoff parent and its normalized coefficient propagator. We then verify the endpoint and derivative-range details for the two-pass mixed-time induction stated in Lemma 5.8. The final subsection verifies the two finite uncut-parent ranges authorized by $K_{q}\geq d(\beta)$ : the final grouped velocity remainder and the cutoff commutator.

### A.1. All-orders parent estimates

#### Proof of Lemma 5.1.

At time order zero, the constant-free stage bound gives

$$ \|\rho^{(q)}\|_{C^{2}}\leq 2\lambda_{q}^{2}. $$

The transfer identity turns $\lambda_{q}^{2}$ into a power of the child logarithm $L$ , and the periodic Schauder estimate gives the corresponding velocity bound. If $q=0$ , all positive time derivatives vanish.

Now assume $q\geq 1$ and fix $1\leq p\leq T$ . Differentiating (61) and using commutation with the cutoffs gives

$$ \partial_{t}^{p}\rho^{(q)}=S_{\mu_{1}}\partial_{t}^{p}\theta_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{q-1}S_{\mu_{i+1}}\partial_{t}^{p}\theta_{i}+\partial_{t}^{p}\theta_{q}. $$

For every $0\leq i\leq q$ , (55) gives

$$ \|\partial_{t}^{p}\theta_{i}\|_{C^{2}}\leq C_{2,p}(\beta_{i})L_{i}^{N_{2,p}(\beta_{i})}\lambda_{i}^{1+\beta_{i}+p(1-2\beta_{i})}. $$

Monotonicity gives $\beta_{i}\in[\beta_{q},1/8]$ . The a priori envelope (56) therefore bounds all constants and logarithmic exponents in terms of $\beta_{q}$ and $p$ . Moreover,

$$ 1+\beta_{i}+p(1-2\beta_{i})\leq\frac{9}{8}+p. $$

Thus a single exponent may be used before summation. For fixed $A>0$ and $N\geq 0$ , lacunarity gives

$$ \sum_{i=0}^{q}L_{i}^{N}\lambda_{i}^{A}\leq C_{A,N}L_{q}^{N}\lambda_{q}^{A}. $$

Apply this with $A=9/8+p$ . The transfer identity (65) converts the resulting parent-frequency power into a power of the child logarithm $L$ , proving the density part of (110). The periodic Schauder estimate gives the velocity part.

Since $P=S_{\mu}\rho^{(q)}$ and $S_{\mu}$ commutes with ordinary time derivatives, the Fourier-cutoff Bernstein inequality and the preceding $C^{2}$ bound give

$$ \|\partial_{t}^{p}P\|_{C^{j+1}}+\|\partial_{t}^{p}v\|_{C^{j+1}}\leq C_{p,j}L^{C_{p,j}}\mu^{j}. $$

This proves (111)– (112). Oddness gives $v(0,t)=0$ , so the mean-value theorem proves (113).

Finally, induct on $p+j$ , using, for $\nu\in\{1,2\}$ , $[D,\partial_{x_{\nu}}]=-(\partial_{x_{\nu}}v)\cdot\nabla$ . All factors are evaluated on $B_{r}$ . The ordinary cutoff bounds control spatial derivatives, while the transport factor satisfies $\|v\|_{C^{0}(B_{r})}\leq CL^{C}r$ ; hence its extra derivative costs at most $r\mu\leq 1$ , up to a power of $L$ . This proves (114). Each positive material order uses ordinary parent time derivatives no higher than that order. In addition, $D^{p}v$ is odd, so it vanishes at the origin; its local $C^{0}$ bound follows from its $C^{1}$ bound and the mean-value theorem. ∎

The preceding lemma supplies arbitrary spatial orders from the Fourier cutoff and the a priori low-order parent bound. The inequality $K_{q}\geq d(\beta)$ is used only for the finite uncut-parent derivative ranges in the residual and cutoff-commutator estimates.

### A.2. The weighted coefficient propagator

#### Proof of Lemma 5.2.

Put $\widetilde{c}_{P}(x,t)=c_{P}(x,t)-c_{P}(0,t)$ . Since $P$ is odd, $\widetilde{c}_{P}$ is even and has zero constant and linear jets at the origin. Lemma 5.1 and Taylor’s theorem give, for $y\in B_{\rho_{\rm ch}}$ ,

$$ |\partial_{t}^{m}\widetilde{c}_{P}(y,t)|\leq C_{m}L^{C_{m}}\mu^{2}|y|^{2}, $$

whereas, globally,

$$ \|\partial_{t}^{m}\widetilde{c}_{P}\|_{C^{k}(\mathbb{T}^{2})}\leq C_{m,k}L^{C_{m,k}}\mu^{k}\qquad(k\geq 1). $$

Here $c_{P}=m_{0}(t)\cdot\nabla P$ . Differentiating the angle equation (90) and using Lemma 5.1 controls every time derivative of $m_{0}(t)$ by a power of $L$ ; at positive order $m$ , only parent time orders through $m-1$ occur. This proves the two displayed bounds. The same estimates hold with material derivatives in place of ordinary time derivatives. Indeed, material differentiation preserves evenness, and the material bounds in Lemma 5.1 give the same Taylor estimate at the origin. Let $\widetilde{\Phi}(\tau;t,x)$ denote the coordinate lift furnished by Lemma 4.5, invoked with $J\geq\max\{S+T+1,3\}$ , and use the same notation $\widetilde{c}_{P}$ for its periodic coordinate lift. For $x\in B_{r}$ and $\tau$ between $\sigma$ and $t$ , (77) gives

$$ |\widetilde{\Phi}(\tau;t,x)|\leq CL^{2}r. $$

The fixed threshold $\Lambda_{\rm flow}$ is chosen so that

$$ \sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in B_{r}\\
\tau\text{ between }\sigma\text{ and }t\end{subarray}}|\widetilde{c}_{P}(\widetilde{\Phi}(\tau;t,x),\tau)|\leq CL^{C}\mu^{2}r^{2}\leq 1. $$

For each fixed $m\geq 1$ , every required ordinary or material derivative satisfies

$$ \sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\Omega_{t}\\
\tau\text{ between }\sigma\text{ and }t\end{subarray}}|\mathcal{D}^{m}\widetilde{c}_{P}(\widetilde{\Phi}(\tau;t,x),\tau)|\leq C_{m}L^{C_{m}}\mu^{2}r^{2}\leq C_{m}L^{C_{m}},\qquad\mathcal{D}\in\{\partial_{t},D\}. $$

Here $\mu^{2}r^{2}=\lambda^{-3\beta}L^{8}$ ; no positive-order smallness is used. Also $\mu^{k}\leq\lambda^{2k\beta}$ . The characteristic formula is

$$ \widetilde{H}_{\sigma,t}[\varphi(\sigma)](x)=\varphi(\Phi(\sigma;t,x),\sigma)\exp\left(-\int_{\sigma}^{t}\widetilde{c}_{P}(\Phi(\tau;t,x),\tau)\,d\tau\right). $$

The tube estimate gives the zeroth-order exponential bound. On $\Omega_{\tau}\Subset B_{r}$ , the positive-order $C^{k}$ -bounds above for $\widetilde{c}_{P}$ , together with (79), control every spatial derivative of the exponential. Since $\varphi(\sigma)$ is compactly supported in $\Omega_{\sigma}\Subset B_{r}$ , its stated $B_{r}$ -bounds control every nonzero term after composition. Finally, $\Phi(t;\sigma,\Omega_{\sigma})=\Omega_{t}$ carries the support.

For a datum depending on the lower-endpoint variable $\sigma$ , set $U_{\sigma,t}=\widetilde{H}_{\sigma,t}[\varphi(\sigma)]$ . Write

$$ D_{\sigma}:=\partial_{\sigma}+v(\cdot,\sigma)\cdot\nabla $$

for the material derivative acting on the lower-endpoint datum, and set $\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}:=D_{\sigma}+\widetilde{c}_{P}(\cdot,\sigma)$ . The exact endpoint identities are

$$ \partial_{\sigma}U_{\sigma,t}=\widetilde{H}_{\sigma,t}[\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}\varphi(\sigma)],\qquad D_{t}U_{\sigma,t}=-\widetilde{c}_{P}(t)U_{\sigma,t}. $$

Iteration of the first identity gives

$$ \partial_{\sigma}^{n}U_{\sigma,t}=\widetilde{H}_{\sigma,t}[\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}^{n}\varphi(\sigma)]. $$

Every datum factor in $\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}^{n}\varphi$ is $D_{\sigma}^{m}\varphi$ with $m\leq n$ ; every differentiated parent factor has material order at most $n-1$ . Iteration of the second identity expresses $D_{t}^{p}\partial_{\sigma}^{n}U_{\sigma,t}$ as a finite sum of $\widetilde{H}_{\sigma,t}[\mathcal{L}_{\sigma}^{n}\varphi]$ multiplied by products of $\widetilde{c}_{P},D\widetilde{c}_{P},\ldots,D^{p-1}\widetilde{c}_{P}$ . Thus an output $C^{j}$ norm uses datum pairs only with $m\leq n$ and spatial order at most $j$ . The diagonal condition gives $m+j\leq n+j\leq p+n+j\leq S+T$ . Every parent factor has ordinary time order at most $p+n-1$ , and all needed spatial orders are at most $p+n+j\leq S+T$ . The preceding coefficient, flow, and product bounds therefore prove (123). The case $p=n=0$ uses only the characteristic formula and order-zero parent bounds. ∎

#### Proof of Corollary 5.3.

To pass from material to ordinary derivatives, use $\partial_{t}=D-v\cdot\nabla$ . On $B_{r}$ , a transport factor acting on a coefficient costs

$$ r\lambda^{2\beta}=L^{4}. $$

Commutators with spatial derivatives are controlled by (111), proving (124). If the derivative falls on the oscillatory factor, its cost is

$$ r\lambda=L^{4}\lambda^{1-2\beta}=L^{4}\lambda^{\gamma}. $$

The phase and parameter bounds in Lemma 3.2 prove (125). ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 5.4.

The identity

$$ H_{\sigma,t}[a(\sigma)\varphi(\sigma)]=a(t)\widetilde{H}_{\sigma,t}[\varphi(\sigma)] $$

shows that $g=aJ$ , where

$$ J(t)=\int_{s}^{t}\widetilde{H}_{\sigma,t}[\varphi(\sigma)]\,d\sigma. $$

Equivalently,

$$ (D+\widetilde{c}_{P})J=\varphi,\qquad J(s)=0. $$

For each $0\leq k\leq S+T$ , apply the fixed-endpoint case of Lemma 5.2 with output parameters $(T,S)=(0,k)$ . Its local datum dependence uses only the order-zero $C^{k}$ bound for the Duhamel source $\varphi$ . The resulting estimate is uniform in $\sigma$ , and integration over $[s,t]$ , whose length is at most one, gives

$$ \|J\|_{C^{k}(B_{r})}\leq C_{k}L^{C_{k}}\mathcal{A}\lambda^{2k\beta}\qquad(0\leq k\leq S+T). $$

For $m\geq 1$ , applying $D^{m-1}$ to the equation for $J$ gives the exact recurrence

$$ D^{m}J=D^{m-1}\varphi-\sum_{\ell=0}^{m-1}\binom{m-1}{\ell}(D^{\ell}\widetilde{c}_{P})D^{m-1-\ell}J. $$

Induction in $m$ , using the Duhamel-source hypotheses and the parent bounds, yields

$$ \|D^{m}J\|_{C^{k}(B_{r})}\leq C_{m,k}L^{C_{m,k}}\mathcal{A}\lambda^{2k\beta}\qquad(m\leq T,\ m+k\leq S+T). $$

Indeed, the Duhamel source term at this pair is $D^{m-1}\varphi$ in $C^{k}$ , so its time–space index satisfies $(m-1)+k\leq S+T-1$ .

To pass to ordinary time derivatives, use $\partial_{t}=D-v\cdot\nabla$ . An order- $p$ ordinary derivative in $C^{j}$ uses $D^{m}J$ through spatial order $j+p-m$ , $0\leq m\leq p$ . The term $m=0$ uses the undifferentiated Duhamel source $\varphi$ through order $j+p$ ; for $m\geq 1$ , the recurrence uses the Duhamel-source derivative pair $(m-1,j+p-m)$ . Each extra spatial derivative is paired with a transport coefficient. Equations (111) and (113), together with

$$ r\lambda^{2\beta}=L^{4}, $$

show that these conversions cost only powers of $L$ . This proves the material and ordinary bounds for $J$ . Finally, the amplitude equation gives $\lvert\partial_{t}^{m}a\rvert\leq C_{m}L^{C_{m}}a$ ; the product rule proves (127). Characteristic transport and (126) give

$$ \operatorname{supp}g(t)\subset\Phi(t;s,K_{\varphi})\Subset\Omega_{t}, $$

which is the support assertion. ∎

For requested output orders $T,K$ , the cutoff-parent estimates supply every spatial derivative through

$$ N_{\mathrm{prof}}=K+M+T+2,\qquad N_{\mathrm{phase}}=N_{\mathrm{prof}}+1. $$

The additional phase derivative is used when a differentiated phase term is formed; it is supplied by the cutoff before Proposition 3.4 is invoked.

## Appendix B Periodic multiplier, cutoff, and kernel estimates

#### Lemma B.1 (Parity and periodic Schauder bounds).

Let $\rho\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$ . If $\rho(-x)=-\rho(x)$ , then $u_{\mathbb{T}}(\rho)(-x)=-u_{\mathbb{T}}(\rho)(x)$ . In particular,

$$ \partial^{\gamma}\rho(0)=\partial^{\gamma}u_{\mathbb{T}}(\rho)(0)=0\qquad\text{when }|\gamma|\text{ is even}. $$

For every integer $j\geq 0$ , every $0<\eta<1$ , and every $f\in C^{j,\eta}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$ ,

$$ \|u_{\mathbb{T}}(f)\|_{C^{j,\eta}}\leq C_{j,\eta}\|f\|_{C^{j,\eta}}. $$

In particular,

$$ \|D_{x}u_{\mathbb{T}}(f)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\|f\|_{C^{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\mathfrak{R}f(x)=f(-x)$ . Evenness of this Fourier multiplier symbol gives $u_{\mathbb{T}}(\mathfrak{R}f)=\mathfrak{R}u_{\mathbb{T}}(f)$ , which proves the parity assertion. On each periodic dyadic annulus, the rescaled Fourier multiplier symbol has a smooth compactly supported extension. Let $K_{n}$ denote its periodized kernel. These kernels have uniformly bounded $L^{1}$ norm and integral zero, so

$$ (K_{n}*f)(x)=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{2}}K_{n}(y)\bigl(f(x-y)-f(x)\bigr)\,dy. $$

Applying this first-difference identity and treating the finitely many low modes proves (194). Apply that estimate to each $\partial_{a}f$ with Hölder exponent $1/2$ , and bound $\|\partial_{a}f\|_{C^{0,1/2}}$ by $C\|f\|_{C^{2}}$ , to obtain (195). ∎

#### Lemma B.2 (Cutoff tails and exact Fourier cutoffs).

Let $\mu\geq 1$ and $f,g\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$ . For integers $j,s\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|S_{\mu}f\|_{C^{j}} \displaystyle\leq C_{j}\|f\|_{C^{j}}, \displaystyle\|(I-S_{\mu})f\|_{C^{j}} \displaystyle\leq C_{j,s}\mu^{-s}\|f\|_{C^{j+s+3}}. $$

For every $0<\eta<1$ ,

$$ \|S_{\mu}f\|_{C^{\eta}}\leq C_{\eta}\|f\|_{C^{\eta}}. $$

The cutoff preserves parity and the spatial mean and commutes with spatial derivatives and $u_{\mathbb{T}}$ . On smooth time-dependent families, it also commutes with $\partial_{t}$ . Moreover,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{supp}\widehat{S_{\mu}f} \displaystyle\subset\{k:|k|\leq 2\mu\}, \displaystyle\nu\geq 2\mu \displaystyle\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S_{\nu}S_{\mu}=S_{\mu}. $$

If $\operatorname{supp}\widehat{f},\operatorname{supp}\widehat{g}\subset\{|k|\leq 2\mu\}$ , then

$$ \operatorname{supp}\widehat{u_{\mathbb{T}}(f)\cdot\nabla g}\subset\{|k|\leq 4\mu\}. $$

Consequently, when $\nu\geq 4\mu$ ,

$$ S_{\nu}\bigl(u_{\mathbb{T}}(f)\cdot\nabla g\bigr)=u_{\mathbb{T}}(f)\cdot\nabla g. $$

#### Proof.

Poisson summation represents the kernel of $S_{\mu}$ as a periodization of a Schwartz function at scale $\mu^{-1}$ . Its $L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$ norm is bounded uniformly in $\mu$ , which proves (196). The same kernel bound gives

$$ |S_{\mu}f(x)-S_{\mu}f(y)|\leq C[f]_{C^{\eta}}|x-y|^{\eta}, $$

and hence (198). For the tail, Fourier inversion and three integrations beyond the requested derivative order give

$$ \sum_{|k|\geq\mu}|k|^{j}|\widehat{f}(k)|\leq C_{j,s}\mu^{-s}\|f\|_{C^{j+s+3}}, $$

and on the transition support $\mu\leq|k|\leq 2\mu$ , we have the same estimate. This proves (197). Evenness gives parity preservation, $\chi(0)=1$ gives mean preservation, multiplier form gives commutation with spatial derivatives, scalarity gives commutation with $u_{\mathbb{T}}$ , and time independence gives commutation with $\partial_{t}$ .

The support assertion follows directly from (13). On that support, $|k|/\nu\leq 1$ when $\nu\geq 2\mu$ , proving exact nesting. The multiplier $u_{\mathbb{T}}$ does not enlarge Fourier support. Convolution of the two Fourier supports then gives (201), and the identity $\chi=1$ on $B_{1}$ gives (202). ∎

#### Lemma B.3 (Periodic kernel decomposition).

For $f\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$ supported in $U_{0}$ , one has on $U$

$$ V_{\mathbb{T}}f=V_{\mathbb{R}}f+\mathcal{H}_{0}f, $$

where $V_{\mathbb{R}}$ is defined by (15), and

$$ \mathcal{H}_{0}f(x)=\int_{U_{0}}H_{0}(x,y)f(y)\,dy\qquad\text{with }H_{0}\in C^{\infty}(U\times U_{0}). $$

There is also a kernel $H_{\rm far}$ , smooth on a neighborhood of $(\mathbb{T}^{2}\setminus U)\times\overline{U_{0}}$ , such that, for $x\notin U$ ,

$$ V_{\mathbb{T}}f(x)=\int_{U_{0}}H_{\rm far}(x,y)f(y)\,dy. $$

The same decomposition holds componentwise for $u_{\mathbb{T}}$ through (9).

#### Proof.

Let $\mathcal{G}_{\mathbb{T}}$ be the mean-zero Green function of $-\Delta$ on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ . In a coordinate neighborhood of the diagonal,

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\mathbb{T}}(x-y)=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\log|x-y|+h(x,y). $$

Indeed, subtracting the displayed logarithm cancels the delta mass in the Green equation; the difference solves a Poisson equation with smooth right-hand side, and interior elliptic regularity makes $h$ smooth. Since $V_{\mathbb{T}}=2\pi\partial_{1}(-\Delta)^{-1}$ , its local convolution kernel with respect to ordinary Lebesgue measure is

$$ -\frac{x_{1}-y_{1}}{|x-y|^{2}}+\widetilde{H}(x,y). $$

After the substitution $h=y-x$ , the singular term is exactly (15). Insert a cutoff equal to one near the diagonal. The difference between the cutoff singular kernel and the full Euclidean kernel is smooth on $U\times U_{0}$ . Since $\overline{U_{0}}\Subset U$ , the periodic kernel is smooth on a neighborhood of $(\mathbb{T}^{2}\setminus U)\times\overline{U_{0}}$ , which gives $H_{\rm far}$ . Finally, since $\operatorname{supp}f\Subset U_{0}$ , integration by parts in $y$ gives

$$ \bigl(-\mathcal{H}_{0}(\partial_{2}f),\mathcal{H}_{0}(\partial_{1}f)\bigr)=\int_{U_{0}}\bigl(\partial_{y_{2}}H_{0}(x,y),-\partial_{y_{1}}H_{0}(x,y)\bigr)f(y)\,dy. $$

The same identity with $H_{\rm far}$ proves the componentwise assertion; all resulting kernels are smooth. ∎

# Non-Uniqueness of Weak Solutions to the Unforced Two-Dimensional Euler Equations with Vorticity in $L^{1}\cap L^{p}$ , I: A Compactness Criterion and the Linear Analysis

**Authors:** Matei P. Coiculescu ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, New York University, Email: m.coiculescu@nyu.edu

## Abstract

This paper and its companion Part II prove that the incompressible Euler equations in the plane, without external force, admit two distinct renormalized weak solutions with the same initial vorticity $f$ , where $f$ is radial and nonnegative and lies in $(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ for every $q<\infty$ but is not bounded. One solution is radially symmetric and stationary. The other is $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric, is equimeasurable with $f$ at every time, and departs from $f$ in finite time; the two solutions are distinct in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{q})_{x}$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^{2}$ for every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ and every sufficiently large $T$ . In this first part we prove two ingredients. One is a compactness criterion: for a radial datum, a sequence of $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric solutions with converging data, whose non-radial moment is bounded below at some bounded time, has a subsequence converging to a second distinct renormalized weak solution. The other is the linear analysis for the building blocks of our multiscale datum. We show that the linearization of the Euler equations around the basic building block plus a small point vortex has an unstable eigenvalue in a space of $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric perturbations. This latter argument depends on rigorous interval arithmetic that we discuss more fully in Part II.

## 1 Introduction

We consider the incompressible Euler equations in the plane, in vorticity form:

$$ \partial_{t}\omega+v\cdot\nabla\omega=0,\qquad v=K_{BS}\ast\omega,\qquad\omega(t=0)=\omega_{0}. $$

Here $K_{BS}(x)=x^{\perp}/(2\pi|x|^{2})$ , $x^{\perp}=(-x_{2},x_{1})$ , denotes the Biot-Savart kernel, so that $v$ is divergence free and $\partial_{1}v_{2}-\partial_{2}v_{1}=\omega$ . There is no external force, and we call $\omega_{0}$ the datum.

For a smooth decaying datum, Equation (1) has a unique global smooth solution (Wolibner [22], Hölder [13]; see Kato [14]; a self-contained proof for compactly supported data is in Appendix B of Part II [8]). Yudovich proved in [23], for bounded domains, that a weak solution with bounded vorticity is unique: its velocity is log-Lipschitz, which closes an energy estimate for the difference of two solutions. For the plane, with vorticity in $(L^{1}\cap L^{\infty})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and square-integrable velocity, a complete proof is given in Theorem 0.3 and Appendix B.2 of [1]. For a datum in $(L^{1}\cap L^{p})(\Omega)$ , $1<p<\infty$ , global weak solutions exist (Yudovich for a bounded domain $\Omega$ [23], see the introduction of [24]; DiPerna and Majda for $\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{2}$ [11]). When $p>4/3$ the product $v\,\omega$ is locally integrable and Equation (1) has a weak formulation (Lemma 2.2, Definition 2.5), but the velocity is only Sobolev regular and Yudovich’s uniqueness argument does not apply. Whether his theorem extends to vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}_{x}$ , $p<\infty$ , is the question of Section 1.1.1 of [5]. This paper and Part II [8] prove that, without force in the plane, uniqueness fails among renormalized weak solutions with vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{q})_{x}$ , for every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ at once and for an explicit radial datum. The velocity of our datum is not square integrable (see below), whereas the planar theorem of [1] assumes it is, and the question of [5] is posed on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ .

Uniqueness is known in several classes of unbounded vorticity. Yudovich proved in Theorem 1 of [24], in a bounded domain $D$ , uniqueness among solutions whose vorticity lies in every $L^{p}(D)$ with $p<\infty$ , with $\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{p}(D)}$ bounded, for all large $p$ , by a constant multiple of a growth function of $p$ satisfying a divergence condition of Osgood type. Taniuchi introduced uniformly local versions of these spaces on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and constructed global solutions in them [18]; uniqueness there under the same kind of divergence condition is proved by Chen, Miao and Zheng [7] and stated as Theorem 1.4 of [9], both crediting Taniuchi, and Crippa and Stefani gave a Lagrangian proof of uniqueness in localized Yudovich spaces (Theorem 1.6 of [9]). Vishik proved uniqueness in Besov-type spaces containing the local space $\mathrm{bmo}$ , under an additional integrability condition [19]. Bernicot and Keraani [3], Bernicot and Hmidi [2], and Chen, Miao and Zheng [7] gave spaces of unbounded vorticity with global existence, uniqueness or propagation of the class; Elgindi, Murray and Said [12] gave a local-in-time existence and uniqueness class whose solutions can leave it in finite time. Our datum satisfies none of these uniqueness criteria: its $L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ norms grow exponentially in $p$ , it is not in $\mathrm{BMO}$ , its dyadic blocks grow too fast for the spaces of [19], and it is not odd in the angle. We leave the verification of these facts to the interested reader. So Theorem 1.1 contradicts none of these results.

With a radial force, Vishik [20], [21] proved non-uniqueness with vorticity in an $L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ space, breaking the radial symmetry. In the account of Albritton, Bruè, Colombo, De Lellis, Giri, Janisch and Kwon [1], for every $p\in(2,\infty)$ there are a datum in $(L^{1}\cap L^{p})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ (possibly zero) with velocity in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and a force in $L^{1}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{p})_{x}$ whose Biot-Savart velocity lies in $L^{1}_{t}L^{2}_{x}$ , with uncountably many solutions with vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{p})_{x}$ and velocity in $L^{\infty}_{t}L^{2}_{x}$ . The unstable manifold of a steady vortex gives non-uniqueness only at time $-\infty$ ; Vishik’s self-similar background moves time $-\infty$ to time $0$ , but it is not an exact solution and requires the force (Section 0.1 of [1]). Without force, convex integration gives non-uniqueness for vorticity in $L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and $L^{p}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$ : Mengual [15] showed, for $2<p<\infty$ , that a truncated power-law vortex, a steady solution with vorticity in $(L^{1}\cap L^{p})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , is the datum of infinitely many bounded admissible weak solutions, with velocity in $C_{t}L^{2}_{x}$ . In that result only the initial vorticity lies in $L^{p}$ : at positive times the vorticity of these solutions is known only as a distribution inside a growing disk, so they are not known to lie in the class $L^{\infty}_{t}L^{p}_{x}$ of the question above. Both solutions of Theorem 1.1, in contrast, have vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{q})_{x}$ for every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ , so Theorem 1.1 answers that question in the plane, in the class in which it is posed. Bruè, Colombo and Kumar (Theorem 1.2 of [5]) obtained, on $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ , for some $p>1$ and a dense set of initial velocities, infinitely many weak solutions with vorticity in $C([0,1];L^{p}(\mathbb{T}^{2}))$ , which do not conserve energy. Outside the $L^{p}$ scale, convex integration also gives unforced non-uniqueness: [4] ( $L^{1,\infty}$ vorticity, bounded energy) and [6] (Hardy spaces $H^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $2/3<p<1$ ).

In an instability construction without force, the background must be an exact solution. Ours is radial, hence stationary: infinitely many rescaled copies of one unstable vortex ring on disjoint annuli accumulating at the origin, with amplitudes increasing toward it. Inner rings rotate faster, and the task is to carry an instability from an inner ring outward through every ring in a time independent of the depth, uniformly in the number of interacting rings.

For $T>0$ and $1\leq q\leq\infty$ we write $X_{q}(T)$ for the space $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{q})_{x}$ of functions on $(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^{2}$ . Renormalized weak solutions in $X_{q}(T)$ , $q>4/3$ (after DiPerna and Lions [10]), and equimeasurability are defined in Definitions 2.5 and 2.4. The ring $\Phi$ of Definition 4.1 is a closed formula in $\log|y|$ times a fixed smooth cutoff; it is radial, $\Phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , $0\leq\Phi<1$ , $\Phi\not\equiv 0$ , and $\supp\Phi\subset\{a\leq|y|\leq 1\}$ for an explicit $a\in(0,1)$ (Lemma 4.2). For $A_{1}>0$ , $\mu\in(1,2]$ and $\bar{s}\in(0,a/16]$ we put

$$ \begin{gathered}f=\sum_{k\geq 1}A_{k}\,\Phi(\cdot/r_{k}),\qquad A_{k}=A_{1}\mu^{k-1},\\
r_{1}=1,\qquad r_{k+1}=s_{k}r_{k},\qquad s_{k}=\bar{s}(2\mu)^{-k}\qquad(k\geq 1).\end{gathered} $$

The main theorem of the two papers is the following.

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $\Phi$ and $a$ be as in Definition 4.1. There are $\mu\in(1,\frac{17}{16}]$ and $\bar{s}\in(0,a/16]$ such that, for every $A_{1}>0$ , the function $f$ of Equation (2) has the following properties. It is radial and nonnegative, $f\in(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ for every $q\in[1,\infty)$ , and $f\notin L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . There is $T_{\star}\in(0,\infty)$ such that, for every $T>T_{\star}$ and every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ , Equation (1) with $\omega_{0}=f$ has two distinct renormalized weak solutions in $X_{q}(T)$ , in the sense of Definition 2.5:

- (i) the stationary solution $\omega(t)=f$ , $t\in[0,T]$ ;

- (ii) a solution $\omega_{\infty}$ such that $\omega_{\infty}\in C([0,\infty);L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ for every $p\in[1,\infty)$ and, for every $t\geq 0$ , $\omega_{\infty}(t)$ is equimeasurable with $f$ and $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric.

More precisely, there is $t_{0}\in[0,T_{\star})$ such that $\omega_{\infty}$ and $f$ are distinct elements of $X_{q}(T^{\prime})$ for every $T^{\prime}>t_{0}$ and every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ .

We do not treat $q\leq 4/3$ . No symmetry is imposed on the class; the $3$ -fold rotational symmetry of $\omega_{\infty}$ comes from the construction, where it removes the angular modes $\ell\notin 3\mathbb{Z}$ , among them the modes $\ell=\pm 1$ that contain the translations of a ring, and leaves the modes $\ell\in 3\mathbb{Z}$ , whose spectra we control under Hypothesis 4.17.

Theorem 1.1 concerns one explicit family of data. It says nothing about the kinetic energy or the vanishing viscosity limit. The velocity of $f$ is not square integrable: by Lemma 3.6, since $\supp f$ lies in the closed unit disk, $|K_{BS}\ast f(x)|=(2\pi|x|)^{-1}\int f$ for almost every $x$ with $|x|\geq 1$ , and $\int f>0$ .

The proof of Theorem 1.1 is divided between this paper and Part II [8]. This paper proves a non-uniqueness criterion (Section 3) and the linear analysis of the ring (Section 4), and it uses no machine computation. Part II proves that (N1)–(N3) of Hypothesis 4.17 imply Theorem 1.1 (Proposition 1.2 there), by a nonlinear construction followed by the criterion of Section 3, and it proves (N1)–(N3) (Theorem 1.3 there): (N1) and (N2) with rigorous interval arithmetic and (N3) by hand, in its Appendix A. Its Appendix B gives the existence theory for the global smooth solutions that the proof uses.

Section 3 follows the compactness theory of DiPerna and Lions for sequences of renormalized solutions, in a self-contained form for vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{2})_{x}$ , and proves a compactness criterion for non-uniqueness (Theorem 3.8). The form of it that Part II uses is the following conditional non-uniqueness theorem (Corollary 3.9 and Remark 3.10).

#### Theorem 1.2 (Conditional non-uniqueness).

Let $f$ be radial with $f\in(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ for every $q\in[1,\infty)$ . Suppose that there are data $f^{(n)}\to f$ in $(L^{1}\cap L^{2})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and, for each $n$ , a $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric renormalized weak solution $\omega^{(n)}$ of Equation (1) on $[0,\infty)$ with datum $f^{(n)}$ and vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{2})_{x}$ , with the following property: for some integer $m\geq 1$ , some real $\chi\in C_{c}^{\infty}((0,\infty))$ , some $c_{0}>0$ and $\bar{T}\in(0,\infty)$ , and some times $T^{(n)}\in[0,\bar{T}]$ ,

$$ \Big|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\omega^{(n)}(T^{(n)},x)\,\chi(|x|)\,(\bar{x})^{m}\differential x\Big|\geq c_{0}\qquad\text{for all large }n, $$

with $x$ written as a complex number. Then Equation (1) with $\omega_{0}=f$ has, besides the stationary solution $\omega(t)=f$ , a renormalized weak solution $\omega_{\infty}$ with vorticity in $L^{\infty}_{t}(L^{1}\cap L^{2})_{x}$ that is $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric and equimeasurable with $f$ at every time and lies in $C([0,\infty);L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))$ for every $q\in[1,\infty)$ . For some $t_{0}\in[0,\bar{T})$ , $\omega_{\infty}$ and $f$ are distinct elements of $X_{q}(T^{\prime})$ for every $T^{\prime}>t_{0}$ and every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ .

Since the moment in Theorem 1.2 vanishes for the radial function $f$ , its hypothesis says that the approximate solutions leave $f$ by a fixed amount, in one non-radial moment, within a time bounded independently of $n$ . The second solution is a limit of a subsequence of the $\omega^{(n)}$ .

For the datum $f$ of Theorem 1.1, Part II takes for $f^{(n)}$ the partial sum of the first $n$ rings of $f$ , with the innermost ring replaced by a seeded ring: a $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric copy of $\Phi$ , equimeasurable with it and close to it, that carries a small component along the unstable eigenfunction of Theorem 1.3 below. Figure 1 shows, for $n=10$ , the partial sum $f_{10}=\sum_{k=1}^{10}A_{k}\Phi(\cdot/r_{k})$ of the actual datum $f$ from which non-uniqueness occurs; $f^{(10)}$ differs from it only by the seed, which is invisible at this scale.

Left: $f_{10}$ against $\log_{10}|y|$ ; the rings sit at the scales $r_{1}=1>r_{2}>\dots>r_{10}\approx 10^{-32}$ , and their amplitudes $A_{k}=\mu^{k-1}$ grow toward the origin. Right: the same ten rings in a logarithmic polar picture, in which the distance from the center is an affine function of $\log|y|$ , so that all of them are visible; each ring is drawn without its amplitude, darker where $\Phi(\cdot/r_{k})$ is larger. The proof of Theorem 1.1 uses three explicit statements, collected in Section 4 as Hypothesis 4.17: (N1) and (N2) locate the zeros in the mode $\ell=3$ of the Evans function of the ring, an explicit holomorphic function, for every $G\in[0,\frac{1}{50}]$ , where $2\pi G$ is the circulation of a point vortex at the origin in the reference units of Definition 4.1; (N3) is an inequality between explicit numbers controlling the modes $\ell=\pm 6$ and $|\ell|\geq 9$ . Apart from the thresholds stated in (N1)–(N3), the only explicit numbers that the computer-assisted proof of these statements uses are the constants of the ring in Definition 4.1, which fix the building block of the multiscale datum; all other constants of this paper are used only through their existence. Without this hypothesis, Section 4 decomposes the linearization into angular modes (Lemma 4.5), reduces each mode to a linear second-order equation in $\xi=\log r$ , and defines the Evans function of each mode $\ell\geq 1$ (Definition 4.4). The Evans function is, up to sign, the Wronskian of the solutions of this equation that decay at the two ends (Lemma 4.6), and its zeros in $\{\real\lambda>0\}$ are exactly the eigenvalues there (Lemma 4.7). A simple zero of the Evans function gives an algebraically simple eigenvalue with an explicit Riesz projection of rank one (Theorem 4.8). Section 4 also bounds the real part of every unstable eigenvalue of the mode $\ell$ , for a radial vorticity that increases and then decreases in $r$ , by half the square root of an explicit double integral of the radial derivative of the vorticity over the region where it increases and the region where it decreases, which is nonincreasing in $\ell$ (Lemma 4.10). For the ring this integral is computed in closed form (Lemma 4.11), and (N3) makes the bound smaller than $\frac{9}{200}$ for $\ell=\pm 6$ and $|\ell|\geq 9$ . The section also proves a semigroup bound, uniform in $G$ , for all sufficiently large $|\ell|$ (Proposition 4.15), and constructs the semigroup of the linearization (Lemma 4.14).

The main result of the linear analysis is the linear instability of the ring, in the ring units of Definition 4.1, in the presence of a point vortex of small circulation $2\pi G$ at the origin, which stands for everything inside the ring. For an integer $s\geq 0$ let $X^{s}$ be the space of $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric $w\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{C})$ supported in the annulus $\{\frac{a}{2}\leq|y|\leq 2\}$ .

#### Theorem 1.3 (Linear instability of the ring).

Assume (N1)–(N3) of Hypothesis 4.17, which Part II proves. For $G\geq 0$ let

$$ L(G)w=-\Big(K_{BS}\ast\Phi+\frac{G\,y^{\perp}}{|y|^{2}}\Big)\cdot\nabla w-(K_{BS}\ast w)\cdot\nabla\Phi $$

be the linearization of Equation (1) at the steady state $\Phi$ plus a point vortex of circulation $2\pi G$ at the origin. Let $\overline{G}\approx 0.006024$ be the constant of Definition 4.1. Then, for every $G\in[0,\overline{G}]$ and every integer $s\geq 0$ :

- (i) $L(G)$ , defined on $X^{s+1}$ , extends to the generator of a $C_{0}$ -semigroup $e^{tL(G)}$ on $X^{s}$ . Its spectrum in $\{\real\lambda>\frac{9}{200}\}$ is $\{\lambda_{*}(G),\overline{\lambda_{*}(G)}\}$ , with $\real\lambda_{*}(G)>\frac{211}{2500}$ . The eigenvalue $\lambda_{*}(G)$ has the eigenfunction $\phi_{*}(G)=g(|y|)e^{3i\theta}$ , with $g$ smooth and supported in $[a,1]$ and $\|\phi_{*}(G)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=1$ , and it is algebraically simple on the functions in $X^{s}$ of angular mode $3$ ; $\overline{\lambda_{*}(G)}$ has the eigenfunction $\overline{\phi_{*}(G)}$ , of angular mode $-3$ .

- (ii) $\lambda_{*}(G)$ depends continuously on $G$ .

- (iii) There is $C$ , depending only on $s$ , such that $\|e^{tL(G)}\|_{X^{s}\to X^{s}}\leq Ce^{\real\lambda_{*}(G)\,t}$ for $t\geq 0$ . For every $\sigma^{\prime}\in(\frac{9}{200},\min_{G^{\prime}}\real\lambda_{*}(G^{\prime}))$ there is $C^{\prime}$ , depending only on $s$ and $\sigma^{\prime}$ , such that $\|e^{tL(G)}(1-\Pi(G))\|_{X^{s}\to X^{s}}\leq C^{\prime}e^{\sigma^{\prime}t}$ for $t\geq 0$ , where $\Pi(G)$ is the spectral projection of $L(G)$ for $\{\lambda_{*}(G),\overline{\lambda_{*}(G)}\}$ , whose range is spanned by $\phi_{*}(G)$ and $\overline{\phi_{*}(G)}$ .

- (iv) The moment $\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\phi_{*}(G)(y)\,(\bar{y})^{3}\differential y$ , with $y$ written as a complex number, has modulus at least a constant $c>0$ independent of $G$ .

Theorem 1.3 collects Proposition 4.19, Lemma 4.7(2), Propositions 4.21 and 4.22, and Lemma 4.23. In Section 4 these are stated with the precise eigendata that Part II uses (Definition 4.20).

Part II uses these conclusions in a nonlinear construction, which we describe heuristically. Each ring of $f$ sees the rings inside it essentially as a point vortex of small circulation, so its linearization is the operator $L(G)$ of Theorem 1.3 for a small $G$ , and a perturbation along its unstable eigenfunction grows at a rate proportional to the amplitude of the ring: inner rings are faster. An approximation of $f$ that keeps finitely many rings carries a small multiple of the unstable eigenfunction on its innermost ring. This perturbation grows until the ring saturates; the non-radial moment of the saturated ring then kicks the next ring outward along its unstable eigenfunction, and that ring grows and saturates in turn. Ring $k$ needs a time of order $k/A_{k}$ to saturate, and $A_{k}$ grows geometrically toward the origin, so this relay reaches the outermost ring in a time bounded independently of the number of rings, and one bootstrap keeps every ring close to its expected evolution. This is why the datum is multiscale. A single unstable ring would not suffice: a perturbation of size $\varepsilon$ of a steady state needs a time of order $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ to reach a fixed size, which tends to infinity as $\varepsilon\to 0$ , so approximations that converge to the steady datum would not leave it in a bounded time; this is the reason why the unstable manifold of a steady vortex gives non-uniqueness only at time $-\infty$ . In our datum the approximation differs from $f$ only at the scale of its innermost ring, where the seed has a fixed size relative to the ring; it is small in $(L^{1}\cap L^{q})(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ only because that ring is small. So the instability starts at order one on the time scale of that ring, which tends to $0$ with the depth, and the relay carries it to the outermost ring in a bounded time. The instability is what produces a non-radial moment bounded away from zero. At saturation the perturbation of the outermost ring is, to leading order, a multiple of fixed size of its unstable eigenfunction and its conjugate, which lie in the angular modes $3$ and $-3$ . The moment $\int\omega\Psi$ with $\Psi(x)=\chi(|x|)(\bar{x})^{3}$ , where $\chi=1$ on the annulus of the ring, sees only the angular mode $3$ , like $p^{\mathrm{out}}_{3}$ (Definition 2.3), and on the unstable eigenfunction it is the moment of Theorem 1.3(iv), which is bounded away from zero uniformly in $G$ . So this moment of the outermost ring has modulus at least a constant $c_{0}>0$ independent of the number of rings, while it vanishes for the radial datum $f$ . This is the hypothesis of Theorem 1.2, which gives the second solution as a limit of the approximate solutions. Section 1.2 of Part II lists the definitions and results of this paper that it uses.

The main idea of a linear instability in physical coordinates driving the non-uniqueness mechanism, the use of non-monotone unstable radial vortices and of a multiscale datum, and the overall strategy of the proof are due to the author.
