#### Lemma 4.2.

A function $\chi$ as in Definition 4.1 exists. Moreover $a_{0}<0<d$ , $\xi_{L}<\xi_{a}\leq a_{0}/2\leq\xi_{b}<\xi_{R}$ , $\ell d<1$ for every integer $1\leq\ell\leq 9$ , and $0<a<1$ . The function $\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}$ lies in $C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , is radial, satisfies $0\leq\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}<1$ , and $\supp\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}\subset\{e^{\xi_{L}}\leq|x|\leq e^{\xi_{R}}\}$ . Consequently $\Phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ is radial, $0\leq\Phi<1$ , $\Phi\not\equiv 0$ , and $\supp\Phi\subset\{a\leq|y|\leq 1\}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $e(x)=e^{-1/x}$ for $x>0$ and $e(x)=0$ for $x\leq 0$ , and $S(x)=e(x)/(e(x)+e(1-x))$ . Then $S\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ is nondecreasing, $S=0$ on $(-\infty,0]$ and $S=1$ on $[1,\infty)$ . The function

$$ \chi(\xi)=S\Big(\frac{\xi-\xi_{L}}{\xi_{a}-\xi_{L}}\Big)\,S\Big(\frac{\xi_{R}-\xi}{\xi_{R}-\xi_{b}}\Big) $$

is smooth with values in $[0,1]$ . Its second factor is $1$ for $\xi\leq\xi_{b}$ and its first factor is $1$ for $\xi\geq\xi_{a}$ ; since $\xi_{a}\leq\xi_{b}$ , $\chi$ is the first factor on $(-\infty,\xi_{a}]$ , $1$ on $[\xi_{a},\xi_{b}]$ , the second factor on $[\xi_{b},\infty)$ , and $0$ outside $[\xi_{L},\xi_{R}]$ . It has the required properties once the order of the data is checked.

We compare the data as fractions with a common power of two. The signs of $a_{0}$ and $d$ are those of their numerators; $4528212286209965>4077852323472915$ gives $\xi_{L}<\xi_{a}$ ; $a_{0}/2=-7304210039150669\cdot 2^{-55}$ and $\xi_{a}=-32622818587783320\cdot 2^{-55}$ give $\xi_{a}<a_{0}/2<0<\xi_{b}$ ; and $\xi_{b}=4503599627370496\cdot 2^{-53}<\xi_{R}$ . ### 4.2 The Linearization and the Evans Function

#### Definition 4.3.

A mode setting consists of: a real radial function $\overline{\omega}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , written also as a function of $r=|x|$ ; numbers $0<r_{1}\leq r_{2}$ such that the radial derivative $\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}$ is supported in $[r_{1},r_{2}]$ , and $\xi_{1}=\log r_{1}$ , $\xi_{2}=\log r_{2}$ ; a number $G\in\mathbb{R}$ ; and an annulus $N_{*}=\{\rho_{-}\leq|x|\leq\rho_{+}\}$ with $0<\rho_{-}<r_{1}$ and $r_{2}<\rho_{+}$ . In a mode setting we put

$$ \begin{gathered}\Omega(r;G)=r^{-2}\Big(\frac{\Gamma_{\overline{\omega}}(r)}{2\pi}+G\Big),\qquad k_{\ell}(r)=\frac{i\ell\,\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}(r)}{r},\\
(\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g)(r)=-\frac{1}{2|\ell|}\int_{0}^{\infty}\Big(\frac{\min(r,\rho)}{\max(r,\rho)}\Big)^{|\ell|}g(\rho)\,\rho\differential\rho\end{gathered} $$

for $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ . For an integer $s\geq 0$ , $Y^{s}$ is the space of $w\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{C})$ with $\supp w\subset N_{*}$ , and $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ is the space of radial profiles $g$ with $\supp g\subset[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ and $g(r)e^{i\ell\theta}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , normed by $\|g(r)e^{i\ell\theta}\|_{H^{s}}$ . As a set, $Y^{0}_{\ell}=L^{2}([\rho_{-},\rho_{+}],r\differential r)$ , and the two norms differ by the factor $\sqrt{2\pi}$ . The linearization at $(\overline{\omega},G)$ , that is, the linearization of the Euler equations (1) at the steady state $\overline{\omega}$ plus a point vortex of circulation $2\pi G$ at the origin, is

$$ L(G)w=-\Omega(\cdot;G)\,\partial_{\theta}w-(K_{BS}\ast w)\cdot\nabla\overline{\omega}. $$

The mode operators are $L_{\ell}(G)g=-i\ell\Omega g+k_{\ell}\,\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g$ for $\ell\neq 0$ and $L_{0}=0$ . For $\ell\geq 1$ , $\real\lambda>0$ and $\xi\in\mathbb{R}$ , the Rayleigh potential is

$$ V_{\ell}(\xi;\lambda,G)=\ell^{2}+\frac{i\ell\,\nu(\xi)}{\lambda+i\ell\,\Omega(e^{\xi};G)},\qquad\nu(\xi)=r\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}(r)\big|_{r=e^{\xi}}, $$

and $M_{\lambda}=(\lambda+i\ell\Omega(\cdot;G))^{-1}$ . This is the resolvent at $\lambda$ of the transport part $-i\ell\Omega$ of $L_{\ell}(G)$ , well defined because $\Omega$ is real; with it, the equation $(\lambda-L_{\ell}(G))g=h$ reads $g=M_{\lambda}(h+k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g)$ . The equation $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi=V_{\ell}(\cdot;\lambda,G)\,\psi$ is the Rayleigh equation of the mode $\ell$ in the variable $\xi=\log r$ .

Here $\Gamma_{\overline{\omega}}(r)=\int_{B_{r}}\overline{\omega}=2\pi\int_{0}^{r}\overline{\omega}(\rho)\rho\differential\rho$ , so $\Omega(r;G)$ , smooth on $(0,\infty)$ , is the angular velocity of the flow of $\overline{\omega}$ and a point vortex of circulation $2\pi G$ at the origin. The mode profiles $g_{\ell}$ of $w\in Y^{0}$ are its angular modes (Section 2), $w=\sum_{\ell}g_{\ell}(r)e^{i\ell\theta}$ in $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and $P_{\ell}w=g_{\ell}(r)e^{i\ell\theta}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}e^{-i\ell\phi}\,w\circ\mathsf{O}_{\phi}\differential\phi$ . Rotations preserve $N_{*}$ and are bounded on $H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , uniformly in the angle: by the chain rule, for $|\gamma|=j$ the derivative $\partial^{\gamma}(w\circ\mathsf{O}_{\phi})$ is a sum of at most $2^{j}$ terms $c\,(\partial^{\beta}w)\circ\mathsf{O}_{\phi}$ with $|\beta|=j$ and $|c|\leq 1$ , so $\|w\circ\mathsf{O}_{\phi}\|_{H^{s}}\leq C_{s}\|w\|_{H^{s}}$ with $C_{s}$ depending only on $s$ . (For $s\geq 2$ they are in general not isometries of the norm of Section 2.) By Minkowski’s integral inequality, $P_{\ell}$ is therefore a bounded projection on every $Y^{s}$ , with norm at most $C_{s}$ , and $g_{\ell}\in Y^{s}_{\ell}$ for $w\in Y^{s}$ .

We work in the variable $\xi=\log r$ , the usual logarithmic change of variables, which maps the half-line $r>0$ onto $\mathbb{R}$ . Since $\partial_{\xi}=r\partial_{r}$ , the radial part of the Laplacian on the mode $\ell$ satisfies

$$ \partial_{r}^{2}\psi+r^{-1}\partial_{r}\psi-\ell^{2}r^{-2}\psi=r^{-2}\big(\partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi-\ell^{2}\psi\big). $$

So $r^{2}$ times this operator is $\partial_{\xi}^{2}-\ell^{2}$ , which has constant coefficients and no first-order term, and the singular point $r=0$ of the radial equation moves to $\xi=-\infty$ . Since $\nu$ vanishes outside $[\xi_{1},\xi_{2}]$ , so does $V_{\ell}-\ell^{2}$ ; there the solutions of the Rayleigh equation are the combinations of $e^{\ell\xi}=r^{\ell}$ and $e^{-\ell\xi}=r^{-\ell}$ . A dilation $x\mapsto cx$ becomes the translation $\xi\mapsto\xi+\log c$ ; this is how Equation (13) below compares the ring in reference units with the ring in ring units.

The Evans function of Definition 4.4 detects the eigenvalues of $L_{\ell}(G)$ in $\{\real\lambda>0\}$ , for $\ell\geq 1$ . If $L_{\ell}(G)g=\lambda g$ with $g\neq 0$ , then $g=M_{\lambda}k_{\ell}\psi$ for the stream function $\psi=\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g$ . By the proof of Lemma 4.7 below, $\psi$ , as a function of $\xi$ , is then a nonzero solution of the Rayleigh equation with $\psi=O(e^{\ell\xi})$ as $\xi\to-\infty$ and $\psi=O(e^{-\ell\xi})$ as $\xi\to+\infty$ ; these conditions say that $\psi(r)e^{i\ell\theta}$ is regular at the origin and decays at infinity. On $(-\infty,\xi_{1}]$ the first condition leaves only the multiples of $e^{\ell\xi}$ , whose Cauchy data at $\xi_{1}$ are multiples of $(1,\ell)$ ; this is the normalization of $\psi_{\ell}$ in Definition 4.4. On $[\xi_{2},\infty)$ , $\psi_{\ell}=Ae^{\ell(\xi-\xi_{2})}+Be^{-\ell(\xi-\xi_{2})}$ with $2\ell A=\partial_{\xi}\psi_{\ell}(\xi_{2})+\ell\psi_{\ell}(\xi_{2})$ , so $\psi_{\ell}$ satisfies the second condition exactly when $A=0$ . Thus $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda;G)=2\ell e^{-\ell(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1})}A$ measures the growing part $r^{\ell}$ of $\psi_{\ell}$ at infinity, and Lemma 4.7 shows that its zeros in $\{\real\lambda>0\}$ are exactly the eigenvalues there.

The factor $e^{-\ell(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1})}$ makes $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$ equal to minus the Wronskian of the solutions that equal $e^{\ell\xi}$ near $-\infty$ and $e^{-\ell\xi}$ near $+\infty$ (Lemma 4.6(2) below). So $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$ depends only on $\overline{\omega}$ , $G$ and $\lambda$ , not on the choice of $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ , and for $\overline{\omega}=0$ it equals $2\ell$ . Since $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$ is holomorphic in $\lambda$ (Lemma 4.6(1)) and is computed from an initial value problem on the compact interval $[\xi_{1},\xi_{2}]$ , its zeros can be counted with the argument principle. Part II verifies (N1) and (N2) of Hypothesis 4.17 below in this way, by certified winding numbers of $\mathcal{E}_{3}$ .

#### Definition 4.4.

In a mode setting, for an integer $\ell\geq 1$ and $\real\lambda>0$ , let $\psi_{\ell}(\cdot;\lambda,G)$ be the solution on $\mathbb{R}$ of $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi=V_{\ell}(\cdot;\lambda,G)\psi$ with $\psi(\xi_{1})=1$ , $\partial_{\xi}\psi(\xi_{1})=\ell$ , and put

$$ \mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda;G)=e^{-\ell(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1})}\big(\partial_{\xi}\psi_{\ell}(\xi_{2})+\ell\,\psi_{\ell}(\xi_{2})\big), $$

where $\psi_{\ell}=\psi_{\ell}(\cdot;\lambda,G)$ . We call $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$ the Evans function.

#### Lemma 4.5.

In a mode setting the following hold.

- (1) For $\ell\neq 0$ and $g\in Y^{0}_{\ell}$ , $\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g$ is the unique $\psi\in C^{1}((0,\infty))$ with $\partial_{r}\psi$ locally absolutely continuous that solves $\partial_{r}^{2}\psi+r^{-1}\partial_{r}\psi-\ell^{2}r^{-2}\psi=g$ almost everywhere on $(0,\infty)$ and is $O(r^{|\ell|})$ as $r\to 0$ and $O(r^{-|\ell|})$ as $r\to\infty$ ; equivalently, $(\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g)(r)e^{i\ell\theta}=\Delta^{-1}(g(r)e^{i\ell\theta})$ , where $\Delta^{-1}$ is the convolution with $\frac{1}{2\pi}\log|x|$ . The operator $\mathcal{G}_{\ell}$ is bounded from $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ to $C([\rho_{-},\rho_{+}])$ .

- (2) $L(G)$ preserves angular modes: for an integer $s\geq 0$ and $w=\sum_{\ell}g_{\ell}(r)e^{i\ell\theta}\in Y^{s+1}$ , $P_{\ell}L(G)w=(L_{\ell}(G)g_{\ell})(r)e^{i\ell\theta}$ for every $\ell$ ; for the coupling term this holds for every $w\in Y^{0}$ : $P_{\ell}\big(-(K_{BS}\ast w)\cdot\nabla\overline{\omega}\big)=(k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g_{\ell})(r)e^{i\ell\theta}$ . Moreover $L_{-\ell}(G)\bar{g}=\overline{L_{\ell}(G)g}$ , and the coupling term commutes with rotations.

- (3) For $\ell\geq 1$ and $\real\lambda>0$ , $|\lambda+i\ell\Omega(r;G)|\geq\real\lambda$ for every $r>0$ ; $V_{\ell}$ is smooth in $\xi$ , holomorphic in $\lambda$ , and equal to $\ell^{2}$ outside $[\xi_{1},\xi_{2}]$ .

- (4) For $\ell\neq 0$ , $L_{\ell}(G)$ is a bounded operator on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ . Consequently the series $e^{tL_{\ell}(G)}=\sum_{n\geq 0}t^{n}L_{\ell}(G)^{n}/n!$ converges in operator norm for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and defines a group of bounded operators on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ , continuous in $t$ in operator norm, with $\frac{\differential}{\differential t}e^{tL_{\ell}(G)}=L_{\ell}(G)e^{tL_{\ell}(G)}=e^{tL_{\ell}(G)}L_{\ell}(G)$ ; in particular $L_{\ell}(G)$ generates the $C_{0}$ -semigroup $(e^{tL_{\ell}(G)})_{t\geq 0}$ .

#### Proof.

(1) Write $n=|\ell|$ . For $g\in Y^{0}_{\ell}$ the integrals below converge absolutely by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and

$$ (\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g)(r)=-\frac{1}{2n}\Big[r^{-n}\int_{0}^{r}\rho^{n+1}g(\rho)\differential\rho+r^{n}\int_{r}^{\infty}\rho^{1-n}g(\rho)\differential\rho\Big] $$

is continuous in $r>0$ . The kernel has modulus at most $\frac{1}{2n}$ and $g$ vanishes outside $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ , so by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in $L^{2}([\rho_{-},\rho_{+}],\rho\differential\rho)$ , for every $r>0$ ,

$$ |(\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g)(r)|\leq\frac{1}{2n}\int_{\rho_{-}}^{\rho_{+}}|g|\rho\differential\rho\leq\frac{1}{2n}\Big(\int_{\rho_{-}}^{\rho_{+}}\rho\differential\rho\Big)^{1/2}\|g\|_{L^{2}(r\differential r)}\leq\frac{\rho_{+}}{2n}\|g\|_{L^{2}(r\differential r)}, $$

as $\int_{\rho_{-}}^{\rho_{+}}\rho\differential\rho=\frac{1}{2}(\rho_{+}^{2}-\rho_{-}^{2})\leq\rho_{+}^{2}$ ; this is the last assertion. Differentiating, the terms from the variable limits cancel, so $\psi=\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g\in C^{1}$ with $\partial_{r}\psi=\frac{1}{2}\big[r^{-n-1}\int_{0}^{r}\rho^{n+1}g-r^{n-1}\int_{r}^{\infty}\rho^{1-n}g\big]$ absolutely continuous, and $\partial_{r}^{2}\psi+r^{-1}\partial_{r}\psi-n^{2}r^{-2}\psi=g$ almost everywhere. Since $g$ vanishes outside $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ , for $r\leq\rho_{-}$ the first integral in the formula for $\psi$ vanishes and the second is $\int_{\rho_{-}}^{\rho_{+}}\rho^{1-n}g\differential\rho$ , and for $r\geq\rho_{+}$ the second vanishes and the first is $\int_{\rho_{-}}^{\rho_{+}}\rho^{n+1}g\differential\rho$ . So

$$ \psi(r)=c_{-}r^{n}\ (r\leq\rho_{-}),\qquad\psi(r)=c_{+}r^{-n}\ (r\geq\rho_{+}),\qquad c_{\mp}=-\frac{1}{2n}\int_{\rho_{-}}^{\rho_{+}}\rho^{1\mp n}g(\rho)\differential\rho, $$

and $\psi$ satisfies the growth conditions. For uniqueness, let $\tilde{\psi}$ be a second solution with these properties and $D=\psi-\tilde{\psi}$ . Then $D\in C^{1}$ , $\partial_{r}D$ is locally absolutely continuous, and $\partial_{r}^{2}D=-r^{-1}\partial_{r}D+n^{2}r^{-2}D$ almost everywhere; the right side is continuous, so $D\in C^{2}((0,\infty))$ solves the homogeneous equation classically. In the variable $\xi=\log r$ this equation reads $\partial_{\xi}^{2}D=n^{2}D$ (by the identity displayed before Definition 4.4), whose solutions are $Ae^{n\xi}+Be^{-n\xi}$ ; hence $D=Ar^{n}+Br^{-n}$ for constants $A$ and $B$ . As $r\to 0$ , $D=O(r^{n})$ , so $B=r^{n}(D-Ar^{n})=O(r^{2n})$ and $B=0$ ; then, as $r\to\infty$ , $Ar^{n}=D=O(r^{-n})$ , so $A=0$ . Thus $D=0$ . For the equivalence, let first $g\in C_{c}^{\infty}((\rho_{-},\rho_{+}))$ , $w=g(r)e^{i\ell\theta}$ , $\Psi=(\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g)(r)e^{i\ell\theta}$ and $\Psi_{0}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\log|\cdot|\ast w$ . Near the origin $\Psi$ is a multiple of the harmonic polynomial $x^{n}$ or $\bar{x}^{n}$ ( $x$ read as a complex number), so $\Psi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ , and $\Delta\Psi=w$ because $\Delta(\psi(r)e^{i\ell\theta})=(\partial_{r}^{2}\psi+r^{-1}\partial_{r}\psi-\ell^{2}r^{-2}\psi)e^{i\ell\theta}$ . Also $\Delta\Psi_{0}=w$ , and $\Psi_{0}(x)=O(|x|^{-1})$ as $|x|\to\infty$ . Indeed, since $\ell\neq 0$ , $\int w=\int_{0}^{\infty}g(r)r\differential r\int_{0}^{2\pi}e^{i\ell\theta}\differential\theta=0$ , so

$$ \Psi_{0}(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int\big(\log|x-y|-\log|x|\big)\,w(y)\differential y. $$

Read $x$ and $y$ as complex numbers and let $|x|\geq 2\rho_{+}$ . On $\supp w$ , $|y|\leq\rho_{+}\leq|x|/2$ , so $s=|1-y/x|\geq\frac{1}{2}$ and $|s-1|\leq|y|/|x|$ ; since $|\log s|\leq 2|s-1|$ for $s\geq\frac{1}{2}$ , we get $|\log|x-y|-\log|x||=|\log s|\leq 2|y|/|x|$ and $|\Psi_{0}(x)|\leq\frac{\rho_{+}}{\pi|x|}\|w\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ . So $\Psi-\Psi_{0}$ is harmonic and tends to $0$ at infinity, and Liouville’s theorem gives $\Psi=\Psi_{0}$ . General $g\in Y^{0}_{\ell}$ follow by density, both sides being continuous from $L^{2}([\rho_{-},\rho_{+}],r\differential r)$ into $L^{2}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ .

(2) With the conventions of Section 2, $K_{BS}\ast w=\nabla^{\perp}\Delta^{-1}w$ and $(K_{BS}\ast w)\cdot\textbf{e}_{r}=-r^{-1}\partial_{\theta}\Delta^{-1}w$ . For $w=g(r)e^{i\ell\theta}$ , $g\in C_{c}^{\infty}((\rho_{-},\rho_{+}))$ , $\ell\neq 0$ , part (1) gives $-(K_{BS}\ast w)\cdot\nabla\overline{\omega}=-\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}(r)\,(K_{BS}\ast w)\cdot\textbf{e}_{r}=\frac{i\ell\,\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}}{r}(\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g)e^{i\ell\theta}=(k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g)e^{i\ell\theta}$ ; for $\ell=0$ , $\Delta^{-1}w$ is radial, so $K_{BS}\ast w=\nabla^{\perp}\Delta^{-1}w$ is a multiple of $\textbf{e}_{\theta}$ , while $\nabla\overline{\omega}=\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}\,\textbf{e}_{r}$ is a multiple of $\textbf{e}_{r}$ , and the term vanishes. Both sides are continuous from $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ into $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ . For the left side, $w$ vanishes outside $B_{\rho_{+}}$ and $\nabla\overline{\omega}$ is bounded and supported in $B_{\rho_{+}}$ , so Lemma 2.1(c) with $\rho=R=\rho_{+}$ gives $\|(K_{BS}\ast w)\cdot\nabla\overline{\omega}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\leq 2\rho_{+}\|\nabla\overline{\omega}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|w\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}$ ; for the right side, use (1). So the formula holds on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ . The coupling term commutes with rotations, since $K_{BS}(\mathsf{O}_{\phi}x)=\mathsf{O}_{\phi}K_{BS}(x)$ and $\nabla\overline{\omega}$ is radial times $\textbf{e}_{r}$ ; hence it commutes with $P_{\ell}$ , which gives the formula on $Y^{0}$ . For $w\in Y^{1}$ , $P_{\ell}(-\Omega\partial_{\theta}w)=-i\ell\Omega g_{\ell}e^{i\ell\theta}$ by integration by parts in $\theta$ . The conjugation relation holds because $\Omega$ , $\overline{\omega}$ , $K_{BS}$ and the kernel of $\mathcal{G}_{\ell}=\mathcal{G}_{-\ell}$ are real.

(3) $\real(\lambda+i\ell\Omega)=\real\lambda$ because $\Omega$ is real; $\nu$ is smooth and vanishes outside $[\xi_{1},\xi_{2}]$ , and $\Omega(e^{\xi};G)$ is smooth in $\xi$ .

(4) $\Omega(\cdot;G)$ and $k_{\ell}$ are bounded on $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ and $k_{\ell}$ vanishes outside $[r_{1},r_{2}]$ ; so multiplication by $\Omega$ , and $k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}$ by the last assertion of (1), are bounded on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ . Write $L=L_{\ell}(G)$ . The series converges absolutely in operator norm, since $\|t^{n}L^{n}/n!\|\leq(|t|\,\|L\|)^{n}/n!$ , uniformly for $t$ in compact sets. The group law $e^{(t+t^{\prime})L}=e^{tL}e^{t^{\prime}L}$ follows from the Cauchy product of these absolutely convergent series, and termwise differentiation of the power series in $t$ , which converges in operator norm, gives the derivative; so $L$ is the generator. ∎

Recall from Definition 4.4 that, for an integer $\ell\geq 1$ and $\real\lambda>0$ , $\psi_{\ell}(\cdot;\lambda,G)$ is the solution on $\mathbb{R}$ of the Rayleigh equation $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi=V_{\ell}(\cdot;\lambda,G)\,\psi$ with $\psi(\xi_{1})=1$ and $\partial_{\xi}\psi(\xi_{1})=\ell$ .

#### Lemma 4.6.

In a mode setting, let $\ell\geq 1$ .

- (1) $\psi_{\ell}(\xi;\lambda,G)$ and its $\xi$ -derivative are holomorphic in $\lambda\in\{\real\lambda>0\}$ , locally uniformly in $\xi$ , and so is $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\cdot;G)$ .

- (2) Put $\psi_{L}=e^{\ell\xi_{1}}\psi_{\ell}(\cdot;\lambda,G)$ , so that $\psi_{L}(\xi)=e^{\ell\xi}$ for $\xi\leq\xi_{1}$ , and let $\psi_{R}$ be the solution of $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi=V_{\ell}\psi$ with $\psi_{R}(\xi)=e^{-\ell\xi}$ for $\xi\geq\xi_{2}$ ( $L$ and $R$ for the left end $\xi\leq\xi_{1}$ and the right end $\xi\geq\xi_{2}$ , where these solutions are explicit and decay). The Wronskian $\mathcal{W}(\lambda)=\psi_{L}\,\partial_{\xi}\psi_{R}-\partial_{\xi}\psi_{L}\,\psi_{R}$ is independent of $\xi$ , and $\mathcal{W}(\lambda)=-\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda;G)$ .

For the ring in reference units, $\overline{\omega}=\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}$ , $(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})=(\xi_{L},\xi_{R})$ , the Evans function of Definition 4.4 is the function $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$ of Hypothesis 4.17 below.

#### Proof.

(1) On $(-\infty,\xi_{1}]$ , $V_{\ell}=\ell^{2}$ , so $\psi_{\ell}=e^{\ell(\xi-\xi_{1})}$ there, independently of $\lambda$ . On $[\xi_{1},\infty)$ , $Z=(\psi,\partial_{\xi}\psi)$ solves $\partial_{\xi}Z=AZ$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ V_{\ell}&0\end{pmatrix}$ ; let $Z_{0}=(1,\ell)$ and $Z_{n+1}(\xi)=Z_{0}+\int_{\xi_{1}}^{\xi}AZ_{n}$ . For compact $K\subset\{\real\lambda>0\}$ and $\bar{\xi}>\xi_{1}$ , Lemma 4.5(3) gives $|A|\leq C_{A}=1+\ell^{2}+\ell\|\nu\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})}/\min_{K}\real\lambda$ on $[\xi_{1},\bar{\xi}]\times K$ , and by induction $|Z_{n+1}-Z_{n}|\leq|Z_{0}|(C_{A}(\xi-\xi_{1}))^{n+1}/(n+1)!$ . The iterates are continuous in $(\xi,\lambda)$ and holomorphic in $\lambda$ and converge uniformly on $[\xi_{1},\bar{\xi}]\times K$ , so their limit $(\psi_{\ell},\partial_{\xi}\psi_{\ell})$ is holomorphic in $\lambda$ , uniformly in $\xi\in[\xi_{1},\bar{\xi}]$ . The same holds for $\psi_{R}$ of (2), with data at $\xi_{2}$ .

(2) The equation has no first-order term, so $\partial_{\xi}\mathcal{W}=0$ . At $\xi_{2}$ , $\partial_{\xi}\psi_{R}=-\ell\psi_{R}=-\ell e^{-\ell\xi_{2}}$ , so $\mathcal{W}=-e^{-\ell\xi_{2}}(\partial_{\xi}\psi_{L}+\ell\psi_{L})(\xi_{2})=-e^{-\ell(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1})}(\partial_{\xi}\psi_{\ell}+\ell\psi_{\ell})(\xi_{2})=-\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda;G)$ .

For the last assertion, $\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}$ , $r_{1}=e^{\xi_{L}}$ , $r_{2}=e^{\xi_{R}}$ and $N_{*}=\{\frac{1}{2}e^{\xi_{L}}\leq|x|\leq 2e^{\xi_{R}}\}$ form a mode setting by Lemma 4.2; $\nu=\partial_{\xi}\varpi$ , and $\Gamma_{\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}}(e^{\xi})/(2\pi)=\int_{0}^{e^{\xi}}\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}(\rho)\rho\differential\rho=\int_{-\infty}^{\xi}\varpi(\xi^{\prime})e^{2\xi^{\prime}}\differential\xi^{\prime}$ , so $\Omega(e^{\xi};G)=\Omega_{G}(\xi)$ , with $\Omega_{G}$ as in Hypothesis 4.17. So on $[\xi_{L},\xi_{R}]$ the equation, the data and the formula for $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$ are those of Hypothesis 4.17. ∎

For a closed operator $A$ and an isolated point $\lambda_{0}$ of its spectrum, the Riesz projection at $\lambda_{0}$ is $\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|\lambda-\lambda_{0}|=\epsilon}(\lambda-A)^{-1}\differential\lambda$ , for any $\epsilon>0$ such that the closed disk of radius $\epsilon$ meets the spectrum only at $\lambda_{0}$ ; its rank is the algebraic multiplicity of $\lambda_{0}$ , and $\lambda_{0}$ is algebraically simple if this rank is $1$ .

#### Lemma 4.7.

In a mode setting, let $\ell\geq 1$ and $\real\lambda>0$ .

- (1) If $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda;G)\neq 0$ , then $\lambda-L_{\ell}(G)$ is invertible on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ and on every $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ , and for $g\in Y^{0}_{\ell}$ ,

$$ \begin{gathered}\big((\lambda-L_{\ell})^{-1}g\big)(r)=M_{\lambda}(r)\big(g(r)+k_{\ell}(r)\,\psi_{g}(\log r)\big),\\ \psi_{g}(\xi)=\frac{1}{\mathcal{W}(\lambda)}\Big[\psi_{R}(\xi)\int_{-\infty}^{\xi}\psi_{L}F\differential\xi^{\prime}+\psi_{L}(\xi)\int_{\xi}^{\infty}\psi_{R}F\differential\xi^{\prime}\Big],\end{gathered} $$

where $\psi_{L}$ , $\psi_{R}$ and $\mathcal{W}$ are as in Lemma 4.6(2), and $F(\xi)=e^{2\xi}(M_{\lambda}g)(e^{\xi})$ .

- (2) If $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda;G)=0$ , then $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $L_{\ell}(G)$ on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ and on every $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ , with eigenfunction $g_{\lambda}=M_{\lambda}k_{\ell}\,\psi_{\ell}(\log r;\lambda,G)\neq 0$ , which is smooth and supported in $[r_{1},r_{2}]$ .

In particular, for each $\ell\geq 1$ the spectrum of $L_{\ell}(G)$ in $\{\real\lambda>0\}$ is the zero set of $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\cdot;G)$ and does not depend on $s$ ; for $\ell\leq-1$ it is the complex conjugate of that of $L_{-\ell}(G)$ .

#### Proof.

For $\eta\in Y^{0}_{\ell}$ and $\psi=\mathcal{G}_{\ell}\eta$ , the equation $(\lambda-L_{\ell})\eta=g$ reads $\eta=M_{\lambda}(g+k_{\ell}\psi)$ . Put $\tilde{\psi}(\xi)=\psi(e^{\xi})$ . By the identity displayed before Definition 4.4, the radial equation of Lemma 4.5(1) reads $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\tilde{\psi}-\ell^{2}\tilde{\psi}=e^{2\xi}\eta(e^{\xi})$ . At $r=e^{\xi}$ , $e^{2\xi}k_{\ell}=r^{2}\cdot i\ell\,\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}/r=i\ell\nu$ , so $e^{2\xi}M_{\lambda}k_{\ell}=i\ell\nu M_{\lambda}=V_{\ell}-\ell^{2}$ , all read at $r=e^{\xi}$ ; hence $u=\tilde{\psi}$ solves

$$ \partial_{\xi}^{2}u-V_{\ell}u=F,\qquad u=O(e^{\ell\xi})\ (\xi\to-\infty),\qquad u=O(e^{-\ell\xi})\ (\xi\to+\infty). $$

Conversely, if $\tilde{\psi}$ solves (12), put $\psi(r)=\tilde{\psi}(\log r)$ and $\eta=M_{\lambda}(g+k_{\ell}\psi)$ . Then $\eta\in Y^{0}_{\ell}$ , and $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\tilde{\psi}-\ell^{2}\tilde{\psi}=e^{2\xi}\eta(e^{\xi})$ , so $\psi$ solves the radial equation of Lemma 4.5(1) with the growth conditions there; hence $\psi=\mathcal{G}_{\ell}\eta$ and $(\lambda-L_{\ell})\eta=g$ .

(1) By Lemma 4.6(2), $\mathcal{W}\neq 0$ . Put $A(\xi)=\int_{-\infty}^{\xi}\psi_{L}F\differential\xi^{\prime}$ and $B(\xi)=\int_{\xi}^{\infty}\psi_{R}F\differential\xi^{\prime}$ , so that $\mathcal{W}\psi_{g}=\psi_{R}A+\psi_{L}B$ , $\partial_{\xi}A=\psi_{L}F$ and $\partial_{\xi}B=-\psi_{R}F$ . Differentiating, the terms from the variable limits cancel: $\mathcal{W}\,\partial_{\xi}\psi_{g}=\partial_{\xi}\psi_{R}\,A+\partial_{\xi}\psi_{L}\,B+(\psi_{R}\psi_{L}-\psi_{L}\psi_{R})F=\partial_{\xi}\psi_{R}\,A+\partial_{\xi}\psi_{L}\,B$ . Differentiating again and using $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi_{L}=V_{\ell}\psi_{L}$ and $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi_{R}=V_{\ell}\psi_{R}$ ,

$$ \mathcal{W}\,\partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi_{g}=V_{\ell}(\psi_{R}A+\psi_{L}B)+(\psi_{L}\,\partial_{\xi}\psi_{R}-\partial_{\xi}\psi_{L}\,\psi_{R})F=\mathcal{W}\,(V_{\ell}\psi_{g}+F) $$

almost everywhere, by the definition of $\mathcal{W}$ ; so $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi_{g}=V_{\ell}\psi_{g}+F$ . Since $F$ vanishes outside $[\log\rho_{-},\log\rho_{+}]$ , $\psi_{g}$ is a multiple of $\psi_{L}=e^{\ell\xi}$ below $\min(\xi_{1},\log\rho_{-})$ and of $\psi_{R}=e^{-\ell\xi}$ above $\max(\xi_{2},\log\rho_{+})$ ; so $\psi_{g}$ solves (12). As shown at the start of the proof, this means that the function $r\mapsto M_{\lambda}(r)\big(g(r)+k_{\ell}(r)\psi_{g}(\log r)\big)$ solves the resolvent equation. If $(\lambda-L_{\ell})\eta=0$ , then $\xi\mapsto(\mathcal{G}_{\ell}\eta)(e^{\xi})$ solves (12) with $F=0$ , so it is $O(e^{\ell\xi})$ solving $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi=\ell^{2}\psi$ on $(-\infty,\xi_{1}]$ , hence a multiple of $\psi_{L}$ , and likewise of $\psi_{R}$ ; as $\mathcal{W}\neq 0$ , it vanishes, and $\eta=M_{\lambda}k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}\eta=0$ . For the bounds: $M_{\lambda}$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$ by Lemma 4.5(3), so it is a bounded multiplier on every $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ . Since $r\differential r=e^{2\xi}\differential\xi$ , $|M_{\lambda}|\leq 1/\real\lambda$ (Lemma 4.5(3)) and $g$ vanishes outside $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ , the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, as in the proof of Lemma 4.5(1), gives

$$ \|F\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R})}=\int_{0}^{\infty}|M_{\lambda}g|\,r\differential r\leq\frac{1}{\real\lambda}\int_{\rho_{-}}^{\rho_{+}}|g|\,r\differential r\leq\frac{\rho_{+}}{\real\lambda}\|g\|_{L^{2}(r\differential r)}=\frac{\rho_{+}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\real\lambda}\|g\|_{Y^{0}_{\ell}}, $$

Put $C_{L}=\sup_{\xi\leq\xi_{2}}(|\psi_{L}|+|\partial_{\xi}\psi_{L}|)$ and $C_{R}=\sup_{\xi\geq\xi_{1}}(|\psi_{R}|+|\partial_{\xi}\psi_{R}|)$ ; they are finite, as $\psi_{L}=e^{\ell\xi}$ for $\xi\leq\xi_{1}$ , $\psi_{R}=e^{-\ell\xi}$ for $\xi\geq\xi_{2}$ , and both are $C^{1}$ on $[\xi_{1},\xi_{2}]$ . For $\xi\in[\xi_{1},\xi_{2}]$ , $|A(\xi)|\leq C_{L}\|F\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R})}$ and $|B(\xi)|\leq C_{R}\|F\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R})}$ , so the formulas for $\mathcal{W}\psi_{g}$ and $\mathcal{W}\,\partial_{\xi}\psi_{g}$ above give $|\psi_{g}|+|\partial_{\xi}\psi_{g}|\leq 2C_{L}C_{R}|\mathcal{W}|^{-1}\|F\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R})}\leq C\|g\|_{Y^{0}_{\ell}}$ on $[\xi_{1},\xi_{2}]$ , with $C$ depending on $\lambda$ . If $g\in Y^{s}_{\ell}$ , then $g\in H^{s}((0,\infty))$ , polar coordinates being smooth near $N_{*}$ , so $\|F\|_{H^{s}([\xi_{1},\xi_{2}])}\leq C\|g\|_{Y^{s}_{\ell}}$ , and from $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi_{g}=V_{\ell}\psi_{g}+F$ by induction $\|\psi_{g}\|_{H^{s+2}([\xi_{1},\xi_{2}])}\leq C\|g\|_{Y^{s}_{\ell}}$ . As $k_{\ell}$ is smooth and supported in $[r_{1},r_{2}]$ , $\|k_{\ell}(r)\psi_{g}(\log r)e^{i\ell\theta}\|_{H^{s+2}}\leq C\|g\|_{Y^{s}_{\ell}}$ . Hence $(\lambda-L_{\ell})^{-1}$ is bounded on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ and on every $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ .

(2) Now $\mathcal{W}=0$ . The functions $\psi_{L}$ and $\psi_{R}$ solve the same linear second-order equation, and their Wronskian vanishes, so they are linearly dependent; as $\psi_{R}\neq 0$ , $\psi_{L}=c\,\psi_{R}$ for a constant $c$ . Hence $\psi_{\ell}=e^{-\ell\xi_{1}}\psi_{L}=c\,e^{-\ell\xi_{1}}e^{-\ell\xi}$ for $\xi\geq\xi_{2}$ , so $\psi_{\ell}=O(e^{-\ell\xi})$ as $\xi\to+\infty$ : the vanishing of $\mathcal{W}$ is what gives the decay at $+\infty$ . As $\psi_{\ell}=e^{\ell(\xi-\xi_{1})}$ for $\xi\leq\xi_{1}$ , the condition at $-\infty$ holds as well, so $\psi_{\ell}$ solves (12) with $F=0$ , that is, with $g=0$ . As shown at the start of the proof, if $u$ solves (12), then $\eta(r)=M_{\lambda}(r)\big(g(r)+k_{\ell}(r)\,u(\log r)\big)$ satisfies $(\lambda-L_{\ell})\eta=g$ and $(\mathcal{G}_{\ell}\eta)(r)=u(\log r)$ ; with $g=0$ and $u=\psi_{\ell}$ this gives $\eta=g_{\lambda}$ , so $L_{\ell}g_{\lambda}=\lambda g_{\lambda}$ and $(\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g_{\lambda})(r)=\psi_{\ell}(\log r;\lambda,G)$ , and $g_{\lambda}\neq 0$ since $\psi_{\ell}(\xi_{1})=1$ . As $g_{\lambda}$ is smooth and supported in $[r_{1},r_{2}]$ , it lies in every $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ .

The spectral statement for $\ell\geq 1$ follows from (1) and (2). For $\ell\leq-1$ , complex conjugation is an isometry of $Y^{s}_{-\ell}$ onto $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ that conjugates $\lambda-L_{\ell}$ to $\bar{\lambda}-L_{-\ell}$ , by Lemma 4.5(2). ∎

#### Theorem 4.8.

In a mode setting, let $\ell\geq 1$ and let $\lambda_{*}$ be a zero of $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\cdot;G)$ with $\real\lambda_{*}>0$ . Put $\psi_{*}=\psi_{\ell}(\cdot;\lambda_{*},G)$ , $g_{*}=M_{\lambda_{*}}k_{\ell}\,\psi_{*}(\log r)$ and

$$ J=\int_{0}^{\infty}g_{*}(r)\,\psi_{*}(\log r)\,M_{\lambda_{*}}(r)\,r\differential r=i\ell\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\nu(\xi)\,\psi_{*}(\xi)^{2}}{(\lambda_{*}+i\ell\Omega(e^{\xi};G))^{2}}\differential\xi. $$

- (1) $\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})\neq 0$ and $e^{\ell(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1})}\,\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})\,\partial_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda_{*};G)=-J$ .

- (2) If $\partial_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda_{*};G)\neq 0$ , then $J\neq 0$ by (1), and the Riesz projection of $L_{\ell}(G)$ at $\lambda_{*}$ , on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ and on each $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ , is

$$ \Pi g=\ell_{*}(g)\,g_{*},\qquad\ell_{*}(g)=\frac{1}{J}\int_{0}^{\infty}g(r)\,\psi_{*}(\log r)\,M_{\lambda_{*}}(r)\,r\differential r; $$

it has rank one, so $\lambda_{*}$ is an algebraically simple eigenvalue.

#### Proof.

The two expressions for $J$ agree because $r\differential r=e^{2\xi}\differential\xi$ and $e^{2\xi}g_{*}=i\ell\nu M_{\lambda_{*}}\psi_{*}$ . Write $M_{*}=M_{\lambda_{*}}$ .

(1) Put $\dot{\psi}=\partial_{\lambda}\psi_{\ell}(\cdot;\lambda,G)$ at $\lambda=\lambda_{*}$ . It vanishes on $(-\infty,\xi_{1}]$ , where $\psi_{\ell}(\xi;\lambda,G)=e^{\ell(\xi-\xi_{1})}$ for every $\lambda$ : there $V_{\ell}=\ell^{2}$ , and the data $\psi(\xi_{1})=1$ , $\partial_{\xi}\psi(\xi_{1})=\ell$ do not depend on $\lambda$ (proof of Lemma 4.6(1)). Moreover, since differentiation in $\lambda$ and in $\xi$ commute by Lemma 4.6(1) and the integral form of the equation, it solves $\partial_{\xi}^{2}\dot{\psi}=V_{\ell}\dot{\psi}+\partial_{\lambda}V_{\ell}\,\psi_{*}$ with $\partial_{\lambda}V_{\ell}=-i\ell\nu M_{*}^{2}$ . Hence $\partial_{\xi}(\partial_{\xi}\dot{\psi}\,\psi_{*}-\dot{\psi}\,\partial_{\xi}\psi_{*})=\partial_{\lambda}V_{\ell}\,\psi_{*}^{2}$ . Since $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda_{*};G)=0$ , $\partial_{\xi}\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})=-\ell\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})$ , so at $\xi_{2}$

$$ \partial_{\xi}\dot{\psi}\,\psi_{*}-\dot{\psi}\,\partial_{\xi}\psi_{*}=\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})(\partial_{\xi}\dot{\psi}+\ell\dot{\psi})(\xi_{2})=\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})e^{\ell(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1})}\partial_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda_{*};G), $$

while at $-\infty$ it vanishes. Integrating the identity $\partial_{\xi}(\partial_{\xi}\dot{\psi}\,\psi_{*}-\dot{\psi}\,\partial_{\xi}\psi_{*})=\partial_{\lambda}V_{\ell}\,\psi_{*}^{2}$ in $\xi$ from $-\infty$ to $\xi_{2}$ , as $\supp\nu\subset[\xi_{1},\xi_{2}]$ , gives $\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})e^{\ell(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1})}\allowbreak\partial_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda_{*};G)=-i\ell\int\nu M_{*}^{2}\psi_{*}^{2}\differential\xi=-J$ . If $\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})=0$ , then $\partial_{\xi}\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})=0$ and $\psi_{*}\equiv 0$ by uniqueness, contradicting $\psi_{*}(\xi_{1})=1$ .

(2) Let $D$ be a closed disk about $\lambda_{*}$ in $\{\real\lambda>0\}$ containing no other zero of $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\cdot;G)$ ; it exists because $\partial_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda_{*};G)\neq 0$ . By Lemma 4.7, $\lambda_{*}$ is isolated in the spectrum on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ and on each $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ . For $g\in Y^{0}_{\ell}$ and $\real\lambda>0$ let $\mathcal{N}(\lambda)g$ be the bracket in the formula for $\psi_{g}$ in Lemma 4.7(1), that is,

$$ (\mathcal{N}(\lambda)g)(\xi)=\psi_{R}(\xi)\int_{-\infty}^{\xi}\psi_{L}F\differential\xi^{\prime}+\psi_{L}(\xi)\int_{\xi}^{\infty}\psi_{R}F\differential\xi^{\prime},\qquad F(\xi)=e^{2\xi}(M_{\lambda}g)(e^{\xi}), $$

with $\psi_{L}$ , $\psi_{R}$ taken at $\lambda$ . Then $\mathcal{N}(\lambda)g=\mathcal{W}(\lambda)\psi_{g}=-\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda;G)\psi_{g}$ wherever $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda;G)\neq 0$ , so for $\lambda\in D\setminus\{\lambda_{*}\}$

$$ \big((\lambda-L_{\ell})^{-1}g\big)(r)=M_{\lambda}(r)g(r)-\frac{M_{\lambda}(r)k_{\ell}(r)\,(\mathcal{N}(\lambda)g)(\log r)}{\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda;G)}. $$

Unlike $\psi_{g}$ , $\mathcal{N}(\lambda)g$ involves no division by $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$ : for fixed $r$ , $M_{\lambda}(r)g(r)$ and $(\mathcal{N}(\lambda)g)(\log r)$ are holomorphic in $\lambda$ on all of $\{\real\lambda>0\}$ , across $\lambda_{*}$ too, because $\psi_{L}$ , $\psi_{R}$ and $F$ are, with integrable bounds. So the only singularity of the resolvent at $\lambda_{*}$ is the factor $1/\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$ . Since $D$ meets the spectrum only at $\lambda_{*}$ , the Riesz projection is $\Pi g=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial D}(\lambda-L_{\ell})^{-1}g\differential\lambda$ , the $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ -valued integral of a continuous function of $\lambda\in\partial D$ . For each $\lambda$ we use the representative of $(\lambda-L_{\ell})^{-1}g$ given by the formula above, which is defined at every $r$ and, for fixed $r$ , continuous in $\lambda\in\partial D$ . The Riemann sums of the $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ -valued integral converge to $\Pi g$ in $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ , hence almost everywhere along a subsequence; at each $r$ they are Riemann sums of the scalar integral $\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\partial D}((\lambda-L_{\ell})^{-1}g)(r)\differential\lambda$ and converge to it. So $(\Pi g)(r)$ equals this scalar integral for almost every $r$ . In it, $M_{\lambda}(r)g(r)$ is holomorphic on $D$ and contributes $0$ by Cauchy’s theorem. In the other term, the numerator $h_{r}(\lambda)=M_{\lambda}(r)k_{\ell}(r)(\mathcal{N}(\lambda)g)(\log r)$ is holomorphic on $D$ , and $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\cdot;G)$ is holomorphic on $D$ with the single zero $\lambda_{*}$ , which is simple; so the integrand has at most a simple pole at $\lambda_{*}$ , with residue $-h_{r}(\lambda_{*})/\partial_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda_{*};G)$ . By the residue theorem, for almost every $r$ ,

$$ (\Pi g)(r)=-\frac{M_{*}(r)k_{\ell}(r)\,(\mathcal{N}(\lambda_{*})g)(\log r)}{\partial_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda_{*};G)}. $$

At $\lambda_{*}$ , $\mathcal{W}=0$ , so $\psi_{R}=\kappa\psi_{L}$ with $\kappa=e^{-\ell\xi_{2}}/(e^{\ell\xi_{1}}\psi_{*}(\xi_{2}))$ , and

$$ \mathcal{N}(\lambda_{*})g=\kappa\psi_{L}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\psi_{L}F\differential\xi^{\prime}=\kappa e^{2\ell\xi_{1}}\psi_{*}\int_{0}^{\infty}g(\rho)\,\psi_{*}(\log\rho)M_{*}(\rho)\,\rho\differential\rho. $$

Therefore

$$ \Pi g=-\frac{e^{-\ell(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1})}}{\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})\,\partial_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda_{*};G)}\Big(\int_{0}^{\infty}g\,\psi_{*}M_{*}\,\rho\differential\rho\Big)g_{*}=\ell_{*}(g)\,g_{*}, $$

since $J=-e^{\ell(\xi_{2}-\xi_{1})}\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})\,\partial_{\lambda}\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda_{*};G)$ by (1). Since $\ell_{*}(g_{*})=J/J=1$ , $\Pi$ has rank one. The resolvents on $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ are restrictions of those on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ , so the Riesz projection on $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ is the restriction of $\Pi$ , which maps into $\mathrm{span}\{g_{*}\}\subset Y^{s}_{\ell}$ . ∎

#### Lemma 4.9.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.8, assume that $\lambda_{*}$ is a simple zero, and put $p^{\mathrm{out}}_{*}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\rho^{\ell+1}g_{*}(\rho)\differential\rho$ and $p^{\mathrm{in}}_{*}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\rho^{1-\ell}g_{*}(\rho)\differential\rho$ , so that $p^{\mathrm{out}}_{*}=p^{\mathrm{out}}_{\ell}[g_{*}e^{i\ell\theta}]$ and $p^{\mathrm{in}}_{*}=p^{\mathrm{in}}_{\ell}[g_{*}e^{i\ell\theta}]$ .

- (1) $\ell_{*}(g_{*})=1$ , $\ell_{*}(L_{\ell}g)=\lambda_{*}\ell_{*}(g)$ for $g\in Y^{0}_{\ell}$ , and $\ell_{*}(e^{tL_{\ell}}g)=e^{\lambda_{*}t}\ell_{*}(g)$ for $t\geq 0$ , where $e^{tL_{\ell}}$ is the semigroup generated by $L_{\ell}(G)$ on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ (Lemma 4.5(4)).

- (2) $p^{\mathrm{in}}_{*}=-2\ell e^{-\ell\xi_{1}}$ and $p^{\mathrm{out}}_{*}=-2\ell e^{\ell\xi_{2}}\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})$ .

- (3) Put $b(r)=-\frac{i}{2}r^{-\ell-1}\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}(r)$ and $\beta=\ell_{*}(b)$ . Then $\beta=-p^{\mathrm{in}}_{*}/(2\ell J)$ .

- (4) $p^{\mathrm{out}}_{*}\neq 0$ , $p^{\mathrm{in}}_{*}\neq 0$ and $\beta\neq 0$ .

#### Proof.

(1) Write $M_{*}=M_{\lambda_{*}}$ and put $X(r)=\psi_{*}(\log r)M_{*}(r)$ , so that $k_{\ell}X=g_{*}$ and $(\lambda_{*}+i\ell\Omega)X=\psi_{*}=\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g_{*}$ (see the proof of Lemma 4.7(2)), and $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\bar{g}\,r\differential r$ , which is $(2\pi)^{-1}$ times the inner product of $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ . By Definition 4.3, $(\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g)(r)=\int_{0}^{\infty}K_{\ell}(r,\rho)\,g(\rho)\,\rho\differential\rho$ with $K_{\ell}(r,\rho)=-\frac{1}{2|\ell|}\big(\min(r,\rho)/\max(r,\rho)\big)^{|\ell|}$ . This integral kernel, taken with respect to the measure $\rho\differential\rho$ , is real and symmetric, $K_{\ell}(r,\rho)=K_{\ell}(\rho,r)$ . As $K_{\ell}$ is bounded, Fubini’s theorem gives, for the operator $\mathcal{G}_{\ell}$ , $\langle\mathcal{G}_{\ell}f,h\rangle=\langle f,\mathcal{G}_{\ell}h\rangle$ for $f,h\in L^{2}([\rho_{-},\rho_{+}],r\differential r)$ , and $\overline{\mathcal{G}_{\ell}h}=\mathcal{G}_{\ell}\bar{h}$ . The operator $L_{\ell}$ is bounded on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ (Lemma 4.5(4)); we compute its adjoint $L_{\ell}^{*}$ for $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ . For $f,h\in Y^{0}_{\ell}$ , $\langle-i\ell\Omega f,h\rangle=\langle f,i\ell\Omega h\rangle$ as $\Omega$ is real, and $\langle k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}f,h\rangle=\langle\mathcal{G}_{\ell}f,\bar{k}_{\ell}h\rangle=\langle f,\mathcal{G}_{\ell}(\bar{k}_{\ell}h)\rangle$ . The function $\mathcal{G}_{\ell}(\bar{k}_{\ell}h)$ is defined on all of $(0,\infty)$ , but $f$ vanishes outside $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ , so only its restriction to $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ enters, and that restriction lies in $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ . Hence $L_{\ell}^{*}h=i\ell\Omega h+\mathbf{1}_{[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}(\bar{k}_{\ell}h)$ . Conjugating $(\lambda_{*}+i\ell\Omega)X=\mathcal{G}_{\ell}(k_{\ell}X)$ gives $L_{\ell}^{*}\bar{X}=\overline{\lambda_{*}}\bar{X}$ on $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ . Since $\ell_{*}(g)=J^{-1}\langle g,\bar{X}\rangle$ , we get $\ell_{*}(g_{*})=1$ and $\ell_{*}(L_{\ell}g)=J^{-1}\langle g,\overline{\lambda_{*}}\bar{X}\rangle=\lambda_{*}\ell_{*}(g)$ . The functional $\ell_{*}$ is bounded on $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ , that is, a continuous linear map $Y^{0}_{\ell}\to\mathbb{C}$ : $X$ is continuous on $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ , as $\psi_{*}$ is continuous and $|M_{*}|\leq 1/\real\lambda_{*}$ (Lemma 4.5(3)), so the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives $|\ell_{*}(g)|\leq|J|^{-1}\|X\|_{L^{2}([\rho_{-},\rho_{+}],r\differential r)}\|g\|_{L^{2}(r\differential r)}$ . By Lemma 4.5(4), $t\mapsto e^{tL_{\ell}}g$ is differentiable in $Y^{0}_{\ell}$ with derivative $L_{\ell}e^{tL_{\ell}}g$ , so the function $t\mapsto\ell_{*}(e^{tL_{\ell}}g)$ has derivative $\ell_{*}(L_{\ell}e^{tL_{\ell}}g)=\lambda_{*}\ell_{*}(e^{tL_{\ell}}g)$ , which gives the last identity.

(2) As in the proof of (1), $\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g_{*}=\psi_{*}(\log r)$ , and $g_{*}$ vanishes outside $[r_{1},r_{2}]$ . For $r\geq r_{2}$ the definition of $\mathcal{G}_{\ell}$ gives $\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g_{*}(r)=-\frac{1}{2\ell}r^{-\ell}\int\rho^{\ell+1}g_{*}\differential\rho$ , and for $r\leq r_{1}$ it gives $-\frac{1}{2\ell}r^{\ell}\int\rho^{1-\ell}g_{*}\differential\rho$ . Compare with $\psi_{*}(\xi)=e^{\ell(\xi-\xi_{1})}$ for $\xi\leq\xi_{1}$ and $\psi_{*}(\xi)=\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})e^{-\ell(\xi-\xi_{2})}$ for $\xi\geq\xi_{2}$ . The identities $p^{\mathrm{out}}_{*}=p^{\mathrm{out}}_{\ell}[g_{*}e^{i\ell\theta}]$ and $p^{\mathrm{in}}_{*}=p^{\mathrm{in}}_{\ell}[g_{*}e^{i\ell\theta}]$ follow from Definition 2.3 by integrating in $\theta$ .

(3) From $g_{*}=M_{*}k_{\ell}\psi_{*}$ , $(\partial_{r}\overline{\omega})\psi_{*}M_{*}=rg_{*}/(i\ell)$ , so

$$ \beta=\frac{1}{J}\int b\,\psi_{*}M_{*}\,r\differential r=-\frac{i}{2J}\int r^{-\ell}(\partial_{r}\overline{\omega})\psi_{*}M_{*}\differential r=-\frac{1}{2\ell J}\int r^{1-\ell}g_{*}\differential r=-\frac{p^{\mathrm{in}}_{*}}{2\ell J}. $$

(4) $p^{\mathrm{in}}_{*}\neq 0$ by (2). If $p^{\mathrm{out}}_{*}=0$ , then $\psi_{*}(\xi_{2})=0$ by (2), contradicting Theorem 4.8(1). As $\lambda_{*}$ is a simple zero, $J\neq 0$ by Theorem 4.8(1), and $\beta\neq 0$ by (3). ∎

### 4.3 An A Priori Bound for Unstable Eigenvalues

#### Lemma 4.10.

In a mode setting, let $\mathcal{U}_{+}=\{r:\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}(r)>0\}$ and $\mathcal{U}_{-}=\{r:\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}(r)<0\}$ , and assume that $r<\rho$ for all $r\in\mathcal{U}_{+}$ and $\rho\in\mathcal{U}_{-}$ . For $\ell\geq 1$ put

$$ Z_{\ell}=\int_{\mathcal{U}_{+}}\int_{\mathcal{U}_{-}}\Big(\frac{r}{\rho}\Big)^{2\ell}|\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}(r)|\,|\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}(\rho)|\differential\rho\differential r. $$

If $g\in Y^{0}_{\pm\ell}$ , $g\neq 0$ , $L_{\pm\ell}(G)g=\lambda g$ and $\real\lambda>0$ , then $\real\lambda\leq\frac{1}{2}Z_{\ell}^{1/2}$ , and $Z_{\ell}$ is nonincreasing in $\ell$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 4.7, the eigenvalues of $L_{-\ell}$ in $\{\real\lambda>0\}$ are the conjugates of those of $L_{\ell}$ , so we may take the sign $+$ . Let $\psi=\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g$ , which is continuous, and $\langle f,h\rangle=\int f\bar{h}\,r\differential r$ . Since $\real\lambda>0$ , $\lambda+i\ell\Omega\neq 0$ (Lemma 4.5(3)), so $g=M_{\lambda}k_{\ell}\psi$ vanishes outside $\{\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}\neq 0\}$ ; there put $W=r/|\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}|$ and $\|g\|_{W}^{2}=\int|g|^{2}Wr\differential r=\int\ell^{2}|\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}|\,|\psi|^{2}|\lambda+i\ell\Omega|^{-2}\differential r$ , which is finite, and positive as $g\neq 0$ . Multiplying $\lambda g=-i\ell\Omega g+k_{\ell}\psi$ by $\bar{g}Wr$ , integrating, and using $k_{\ell}Wr=i\ell\,(\sgn\partial_{r}\overline{\omega})\,r$ , we get $\lambda\|g\|_{W}^{2}=-i\ell\int\Omega|g|^{2}Wr\differential r+i\ell\int(\sgn\partial_{r}\overline{\omega})\,\psi\bar{g}\,r\differential r$ , and the first term is imaginary. With $g_{a}=g\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{U}_{+}}$ , $g_{b}=g\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{U}_{-}}$ ,

$$ \int(\sgn\partial_{r}\overline{\omega})\,\psi\bar{g}\,r\differential r=\langle\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g_{a},g_{a}\rangle-\langle\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g_{b},g_{b}\rangle+\langle\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g_{b},g_{a}\rangle-\langle\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g_{a},g_{b}\rangle. $$

The kernel $K_{\ell}$ of $\mathcal{G}_{\ell}$ is real and symmetric (proof of Lemma 4.9(1)), so the first two terms are real and the last is the conjugate of $X_{ab}=\langle\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g_{b},g_{a}\rangle$ ; hence $\real\lambda\,\|g\|_{W}^{2}=-2\ell\imaginary X_{ab}$ . For $r\in\mathcal{U}_{+}$ , $\rho\in\mathcal{U}_{-}$ we have $r<\rho$ , so $|K_{\ell}(r,\rho)|=\frac{1}{2\ell}(r/\rho)^{\ell}$ . Writing $|g_{a}|r=(|g_{a}|^{2}Wr)^{1/2}|\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}|^{1/2}$ , likewise for $g_{b}$ , the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality on $\mathcal{U}_{+}\times\mathcal{U}_{-}$ gives $|X_{ab}|\leq\frac{1}{2\ell}Z_{\ell}^{1/2}\|g_{a}\|_{W}\|g_{b}\|_{W}\leq\frac{1}{4\ell}Z_{\ell}^{1/2}\|g\|_{W}^{2}$ , by the AM-GM inequality $\|g_{a}\|_{W}\|g_{b}\|_{W}\leq\frac{1}{2}(\|g_{a}\|_{W}^{2}+\|g_{b}\|_{W}^{2})=\frac{1}{2}\|g\|_{W}^{2}$ ( $g_{a}$ and $g_{b}$ have disjoint supports and $g=g_{a}+g_{b}$ ); so $\real\lambda\leq\frac{1}{2}Z_{\ell}^{1/2}$ . Since $r/\rho<1$ on $\mathcal{U}_{+}\times\mathcal{U}_{-}$ , the integrand of $Z_{\ell}$ decreases in $\ell$ . ∎

#### Lemma 4.11.

Let $\chi$ , $\varpi$ and $\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}$ be as in Definition 4.1. Then:

- (1) $\partial_{\xi}\varpi\geq 0$ on $(-\infty,a_{0}/2)$ and $\partial_{\xi}\varpi\leq 0$ on $(a_{0}/2,\infty)$ ; so $\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}$ satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma 4.10;

- (2) for every integer $\ell\geq 1$ with $\ell d<1$ , the quantity $Z_{\ell}$ of Lemma 4.10 for $\overline{\omega}=\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}$ is $Z_{\ell}=Z^{a}_{\ell}Z^{b}_{\ell}$ with

$$ Z^{a}_{\ell}=\int_{\{\partial_{\xi}\varpi>0\}}e^{2\ell(\xi-a_{0}/2)}\partial_{\xi}\varpi(\xi)\differential\xi,\qquad Z^{b}_{\ell}=\int_{\{\partial_{\xi}\varpi<0\}}e^{-2\ell(\xi-a_{0}/2)}|\partial_{\xi}\varpi(\xi)|\differential\xi, $$

and $Z^{a}_{\ell},Z^{b}_{\ell}\leq e^{\ell a_{0}}\Theta_{\ell}+\epsilon_{*}$ , where $\Theta_{\ell}=\pi\ell d/\sin(\pi\ell d)$ and $\epsilon_{*}=\max\{H((\xi_{a}-a_{0})/d),\,H(-\xi_{b}/d)\}$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 4.2, $a_{0}<0<d$ and $\xi_{L}<\xi_{a}\leq a_{0}/2\leq\xi_{b}<\xi_{R}$ . Put $\xi_{c}=a_{0}/2$ and $P(\xi)=H(\frac{\xi-a_{0}}{d})H(-\frac{\xi}{d})$ , so $\varpi=\chi P$ . Since $H(x)=\frac{1}{2}(1+\tanh x)$ , $\partial_{x}H(x)=2H(x)H(-x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sech}^{2}x$ and $\partial_{\xi}\log P(\xi)=\frac{2}{d}\big[H(-\frac{\xi-a_{0}}{d})-H(\frac{\xi}{d})\big]$ , which is positive if and only if $-(\xi-a_{0})>\xi$ , i.e. $\xi<\xi_{c}$ , as $H$ is increasing. For $\xi<\xi_{c}$ , $\partial_{\xi}\chi\geq 0$ (by monotonicity on $(-\infty,\xi_{a}]$ , and $\partial_{\xi}\chi=0$ on $[\xi_{a},\xi_{c}]$ ), $\chi\geq 0$ and $\partial_{\xi}P>0$ , so $\partial_{\xi}\varpi=(\partial_{\xi}\chi)P+\chi\,\partial_{\xi}P\geq 0$ ; for $\xi>\xi_{c}$ likewise $\partial_{\xi}\varpi\leq 0$ . As $\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}(r)=(\partial_{\xi}\varpi)(\log r)/r$ , $\{\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}>0\}\subset(0,e^{\xi_{c}}]$ and $\{\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}<0\}\subset[e^{\xi_{c}},\infty)$ are disjoint; this proves (1).

(2) In the double integral defining $Z_{\ell}$ (Lemma 4.10), with $r\in\mathcal{U}_{+}$ and $\rho\in\mathcal{U}_{-}$ , substitute $\xi=\log r$ and $\xi^{\prime}=\log\rho$ . As $\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}(r)=(\partial_{\xi}\varpi)(\log r)/r$ , the sets $\mathcal{U}_{\pm}$ become $\{\pm\partial_{\xi}\varpi>0\}$ , $|\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}(r)|\differential r=|\partial_{\xi}\varpi(\xi)|\differential\xi$ , $|\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}(\rho)|\differential\rho=|\partial_{\xi}\varpi(\xi^{\prime})|\differential\xi^{\prime}$ and $r/\rho=e^{\xi-\xi^{\prime}}$ , so

$$ Z_{\ell}=\int_{\{\partial_{\xi}\varpi>0\}}\int_{\{\partial_{\xi}\varpi<0\}}e^{2\ell(\xi-\xi^{\prime})}\,|\partial_{\xi}\varpi(\xi)|\,|\partial_{\xi}\varpi(\xi^{\prime})|\differential\xi^{\prime}\differential\xi, $$

and the factorization follows from $e^{2\ell(\xi-\xi^{\prime})}=e^{2\ell(\xi-\xi_{c})}e^{-2\ell(\xi^{\prime}-\xi_{c})}$ . For the bound on $Z^{a}_{\ell}$ , write $\partial_{\xi}\varpi=(\partial_{\xi}\chi)P+\chi\,\partial_{\xi}P$ and bound the two terms on $(-\infty,\xi_{c}]$ , which contains $\{\partial_{\xi}\varpi>0\}$ . First, $\partial_{\xi}P=\frac{1}{d}(\partial_{x}H)(\frac{\xi-a_{0}}{d})H(-\frac{\xi}{d})-\frac{1}{d}H(\frac{\xi-a_{0}}{d})(\partial_{x}H)(-\frac{\xi}{d})$ . The second term is $\leq 0$ , as $H,\partial_{x}H\geq 0$ , and we drop it; in the first, $H(-\frac{\xi}{d})\leq 1$ and $\partial_{x}H=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sech}^{2}$ . So $\partial_{\xi}P\leq\frac{1}{2d}\operatorname{sech}^{2}\big(\frac{\xi-a_{0}}{d}\big)$ for every $\xi$ , and, as $0\leq\chi\leq 1$ , also $\chi\,\partial_{\xi}P\leq\frac{1}{2d}\operatorname{sech}^{2}\big(\frac{\xi-a_{0}}{d}\big)$ . Second, by Definition 4.1, $\chi$ is nondecreasing on $(-\infty,\xi_{a}]$ and equal to $1$ on $[\xi_{a},\xi_{b}]$ , which contains $[\xi_{a},\xi_{c}]$ ; so on $(-\infty,\xi_{c}]$ we have $\partial_{\xi}\chi\geq 0$ , and $\partial_{\xi}\chi\neq 0$ only for $\xi<\xi_{a}$ . For $\xi\leq\xi_{a}$ , $P(\xi)\leq H(\frac{\xi-a_{0}}{d})\leq H(\frac{\xi_{a}-a_{0}}{d})$ , as $H\leq 1$ and $H$ is increasing; so $(\partial_{\xi}\chi)P\leq H(\frac{\xi_{a}-a_{0}}{d})\,\partial_{\xi}\chi$ on $(-\infty,\xi_{c}]$ . Both bounds are nonnegative. We integrate the first, times $e^{2\ell(\xi-\xi_{c})}$ , over all of $\mathbb{R}$ , and for the second we use $e^{2\ell(\xi-\xi_{c})}\leq 1$ on $(-\infty,\xi_{c}]$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{\xi_{c}}\partial_{\xi}\chi\differential\xi=\chi(\xi_{c})=1$ . The substitution $\xi=a_{0}+dx$ gives

$$ Z^{a}_{\ell}\leq e^{2\ell(a_{0}-\xi_{c})}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{2\ell dx}\,\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{sech}^{2}x\differential x+H\Big(\frac{\xi_{a}-a_{0}}{d}\Big)=e^{\ell a_{0}}\Theta_{\ell}+H\Big(\frac{\xi_{a}-a_{0}}{d}\Big), $$

by $\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\alpha x}\operatorname{sech}^{2}x\differential x=\pi\alpha/\sin(\pi\alpha/2)$ for $0<|\alpha|<2$ , with $\alpha=2\ell d$ . As $\operatorname{sech}^{2}$ is even, $\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{\alpha x}\operatorname{sech}^{2}x\differential x=2\int_{0}^{\infty}\cosh(\alpha x)(\cosh x)^{-2}\differential x$ , which is $2B(1+\frac{\alpha}{2},1-\frac{\alpha}{2})$ by [16, (5.12.7)] with $a=1$ and $b=\frac{\alpha}{2}$ (admissible as $|\alpha|<2$ ). By [16, (5.12.1)], $2B(1+\frac{\alpha}{2},1-\frac{\alpha}{2})=2\Gamma(1+\frac{\alpha}{2})\Gamma(1-\frac{\alpha}{2})=\alpha\Gamma(\frac{\alpha}{2})\Gamma(1-\frac{\alpha}{2})$ , and the reflection formula $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\pi/\sin(\pi z)$ [16, (5.5.3)] gives $\pi\alpha/\sin(\pi\alpha/2)$ . The bound for $Z^{b}_{\ell}$ is the mirror image: on $[\xi_{c},\infty)$ , which contains $\{\partial_{\xi}\varpi<0\}$ , $-\partial_{\xi}P\leq\frac{1}{2d}\operatorname{sech}^{2}\big(\frac{\xi}{d}\big)$ (now the first term of $\partial_{\xi}P$ is $\geq 0$ and is dropped, and $H(\frac{\xi-a_{0}}{d})\leq 1$ ); $\partial_{\xi}\chi\leq 0$ there, and $\partial_{\xi}\chi\neq 0$ only for $\xi>\xi_{b}$ , where $P\leq H(-\xi_{b}/d)$ ; and with $\xi=dy$ , $e^{-2\ell(dy-\xi_{c})}=\penalty e^{\ell a_{0}}e^{-2\ell dy}$ . ∎

### 4.4 Mode Bounds and the Semigroup

For $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}$ and a profile $g$ supported in $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ put

$$ \|g\|_{k,\ell}^{2}=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(1+\ell^{2})^{k-j}\|\partial_{r}^{j}g\|^{2}_{L^{2}([\rho_{-},\rho_{+}],r\differential r)}, $$

and let $\|g\|_{k,\ell;[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]}$ be the same expression for a profile $g$ on $(0,\infty)$ that need not be supported in $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ .

#### Lemma 4.12.

In a mode setting, for every integer $k\geq 0$ there are $c^{\rm eq}_{k},C^{\rm eq}_{k}>0$ , depending only on $k$ , $\rho_{-}$ and $\rho_{+}$ , such that every $w=\sum_{\ell}g_{\ell}(r)e^{i\ell\theta}\in Y^{k}$ satisfies $c^{\rm eq}_{k}\sum_{\ell}\|g_{\ell}\|^{2}_{k,\ell}\leq\|w\|^{2}_{H^{k}}\leq C^{\rm eq}_{k}\sum_{\ell}\|g_{\ell}\|^{2}_{k,\ell}$ .

#### Proof.

Near $N_{*}$ , $\partial_{r}=\cos\theta\,\partial_{1}+\sin\theta\,\partial_{2}$ , $\partial_{\theta}=-x_{2}\partial_{1}+x_{1}\partial_{2}$ , $\partial_{1}=\cos\theta\,\partial_{r}-\frac{\sin\theta}{r}\partial_{\theta}$ and $\partial_{2}=\sin\theta\,\partial_{r}+\frac{\cos\theta}{r}\partial_{\theta}$ . Iterating, each $\partial^{\alpha}$ , $|\alpha|=j$ , is a combination of the $\partial_{r}^{i}\partial_{\theta}^{n}$ , $i+n\leq j$ , with coefficients bounded on $N_{*}$ in terms of $j$ , $\rho_{\pm}$ , and conversely. As $\supp w\subset N_{*}$ , $\|w\|_{H^{k}}^{2}$ is comparable to $\sum_{i,n\geq 0,\ i+n\leq k}\|\partial_{r}^{i}\partial_{\theta}^{n}w\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=2\pi\sum_{\ell}\sum_{i,n\geq 0,\ i+n\leq k}\ell^{2n}\|\partial_{r}^{i}g_{\ell}\|^{2}_{L^{2}(r\differential r)}$ (Parseval in $\theta$ ). Finally $2^{-p}(1+x)^{p}\leq\sum_{n=0}^{p}x^{n}\leq(1+x)^{p}$ for $x\geq 0$ , by the binomial theorem, as $1\leq\binom{p}{n}\leq 2^{p}$ ; take $x=\ell^{2}$ , $p=k-i$ . ∎

#### Corollary 4.13.

In a mode setting, let $s\geq 0$ be an integer. There is $C_{K}=C_{K}(s,\rho_{-},\rho_{+},\|\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}\|_{C^{s}})$ such that $\|k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g\|_{s,\ell}\leq C_{K}(1+\ell^{2})^{-1/2}\|g\|_{s,\ell}$ for every $\ell\neq 0$ , every $G$ , and every $g\in H^{s}((0,\infty))$ supported in $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\ell\neq 0$ and let $g\in H^{s}((0,\infty))$ be supported in $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ . We first bound $\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g$ . Put $\xi=\log r$ , $\tilde{g}(\xi)=g(e^{\xi})$ , $\tilde{\psi}(\xi)=(\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g)(e^{\xi})$ and $\Xi=e^{2\xi}\tilde{g}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R})$ , compactly supported. For $r=e^{\xi}$ and $\rho=e^{\eta}$ , the kernel of $\mathcal{G}_{\ell}$ (proof of Lemma 4.9(1)) is $K_{\ell}(r,\rho)=-\frac{1}{2|\ell|}\big(\min(r,\rho)/\max(r,\rho)\big)^{|\ell|}=-\frac{1}{2|\ell|}e^{-|\ell||\xi-\eta|}$ , since $\min(r,\rho)/\max(r,\rho)=e^{-|\xi-\eta|}$ , and $\rho\differential\rho=e^{2\eta}\differential\eta$ . So $\tilde{\psi}=-\frac{1}{2|\ell|}e^{-|\ell||\cdot|}\ast\Xi$ . We use the Fourier transform $\hat{u}(\zeta)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-i\xi\zeta}u(\xi)\differential\xi$ on $\mathbb{R}$ , for which $\frac{1}{2|\ell|}e^{-|\ell||\xi|}$ has Fourier transform $(\ell^{2}+\zeta^{2})^{-1}$ ; hence the Fourier transform of $\tilde{\psi}$ is $\zeta\mapsto-\hat{\Xi}(\zeta)/(\ell^{2}+\zeta^{2})$ . With this normalization, Plancherel’s theorem reads $\|u\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|\hat{u}|^{2}\differential\zeta$ , which is where the single factor $\frac{1}{2\pi}$ below comes from, and $\partial_{\xi}^{j}u$ has Fourier transform $(i\zeta)^{j}\hat{u}$ . For $u$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and an integer $k\geq 0$ put $|u|_{k,\ell}^{2}=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(1+\ell^{2})^{k-j}\|\partial_{\xi}^{j}u\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}$ ; then

$$ |u|^{2}_{k,\ell}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\sum_{j=0}^{k}(1+\ell^{2})^{k-j}\zeta^{2j}\,|\hat{u}(\zeta)|^{2}\differential\zeta. $$

Multiplying the inequality $2^{-k}(1+x)^{k}\leq\sum_{n=0}^{k}x^{n}\leq(1+x)^{k}$ of the proof of Lemma 4.12 by $A^{k}$ , with $x=B/A$ , gives $\sum_{j=0}^{k}A^{k-j}B^{j}\leq(A+B)^{k}\leq 2^{k}\sum_{j=0}^{k}A^{k-j}B^{j}$ for $A>0$ , $B\geq 0$ ; we take $A=1+\ell^{2}$ and $B=\zeta^{2}$ . The first of these inequalities, with $k=s+2$ , gives the first step below; the formula for the Fourier transform of $\tilde{\psi}$ and $1+\ell^{2}+\zeta^{2}\leq 2(\ell^{2}+\zeta^{2})$ (as $\ell\neq 0$ ) give the second; and the second inequality, with $k=s$ , gives the third:

$$ |\tilde{\psi}|^{2}_{s+2,\ell}\leq\frac{1}{2\pi}\int(1+\ell^{2}+\zeta^{2})^{s+2}\frac{|\hat{\Xi}|^{2}}{(\ell^{2}+\zeta^{2})^{2}}\differential\zeta\leq\frac{4}{2\pi}\int(1+\ell^{2}+\zeta^{2})^{s}|\hat{\Xi}|^{2}\differential\zeta\leq 4\cdot 2^{s}|\Xi|^{2}_{s,\ell}. $$

On $\tilde{I}=[\log\rho_{-},\log\rho_{+}]$ , $\partial_{r}=e^{-\xi}\partial_{\xi}$ and $\partial_{\xi}=r\partial_{r}$ , so $\partial_{r}^{j}$ is a combination of $\partial_{\xi}^{i}$ , $i\leq j$ , with coefficients bounded on $\tilde{I}$ , and conversely; with $r\differential r=e^{2\xi}\differential\xi$ and $(1+\ell^{2})^{k-j}\leq(1+\ell^{2})^{k-i}$ for $i\leq j$ , for every integer $k\geq 0$ the norms $\|\cdot\|_{k,\ell;[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]}$ and $|\cdot|_{k,\ell}$ restricted to $\tilde{I}$ are equivalent, with constants depending on $k$ , $\rho_{-}$ and $\rho_{+}$ . Multiplication by $e^{2\xi}$ is bounded for $|\cdot|_{s,\ell}$ on functions supported in $\tilde{I}$ , by the Leibniz rule and the same monotonicity of the weights. Therefore $\|\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g\|_{s+2,\ell;[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]}\leq C|\tilde{\psi}|_{s+2,\ell}\leq C|\Xi|_{s,\ell}\leq C|\tilde{g}|_{s,\ell}\leq C\|g\|_{s,\ell}$ , with $C=C(s,\rho_{-},\rho_{+})$ .

The operator $k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}$ does not involve $G$ , and $k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g$ is supported in $I_{A}=[r_{1},r_{2}]$ . Since $1/r\leq 1/\rho_{-}$ on $I_{A}$ , the Leibniz rule gives

$$ \|\partial_{r}^{j}(r^{-1}(\partial_{r}\overline{\omega})\psi)\|_{L^{2}(I_{A},r\differential r)}\leq C\sum_{i=0}^{j}\|\partial_{r}^{i}\psi\|_{L^{2}(I_{A},r\differential r)} $$

with $C$ depending on $s$ , $\rho_{-}$ and $\|\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}\|_{C^{s}}$ . Using $(1+\ell^{2})^{s-j}\leq(1+\ell^{2})^{s-i}$ for $i\leq j$ , and then $(1+\ell^{2})^{s+2-i}=(1+\ell^{2})^{2}(1+\ell^{2})^{s-i}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g\|_{s,\ell}^{2} \displaystyle\leq C\ell^{2}\sum_{i=0}^{s}(1+\ell^{2})^{s-i}\|\partial_{r}^{i}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g\|^{2}_{L^{2}(I_{A},r\differential r)} \displaystyle\leq C\ell^{2}(1+\ell^{2})^{-2}\|\mathcal{G}_{\ell}g\|^{2}_{s+2,\ell;[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]}\leq C(1+\ell^{2})^{-1}\|g\|^{2}_{s,\ell}, $$

since $I_{A}\subset[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ , and by the bound above. ∎

#### Lemma 4.14.

In a mode setting, let $s\geq 0$ be an integer and $G_{+}\geq 0$ , and let $|G|\leq G_{+}$ . Put $L^{\rm tr}=-\Omega\partial_{\theta}$ and $\mathcal{K}w=-(K_{BS}\ast w)\cdot\nabla\overline{\omega}$ .

- (1) $(e^{tL^{\rm tr}}w)(r,\theta)=w(r,\theta-\Omega(r;G)t)$ is a $C_{0}$ -group on $Y^{s}$ , and there is $C_{s}$ , depending only on $s$ , $\overline{\omega}$ , $\rho_{\pm}$ and $G_{+}$ , with $\|e^{tL^{\rm tr}}\|_{Y^{s}\to Y^{s}}\leq C_{s}(1+|t|)^{s}$ and $\|e^{-i\ell\Omega t}g\|_{s,\ell}\leq C_{s}(1+|t|)^{s}\|g\|_{s,\ell}$ for all $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}$ , $|G|\leq G_{+}$ and $t\in\mathbb{R}$ ; $\mathcal{K}$ is bounded on $Y^{s}$ .

- (2) The Dyson-Phillips series $e^{tL}=\sum_{n\geq 0}S_{n}(t)$ , $S_{0}(t)=e^{tL^{\rm tr}}$ , $S_{n+1}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}S_{0}(t-\tau)\mathcal{K}S_{n}(\tau)\differential\tau$ , converges in operator norm uniformly on compact $t$ -sets and defines a $C_{0}$ -semigroup on $Y^{s}$ that satisfies both Duhamel formulas and preserves each mode. Its generator $\hat{L}$ satisfies $Y^{s+1}\subset D(\hat{L})$ and $\hat{L}w=L(G)w$ for $w\in Y^{s+1}$ , with $\|L(G)w\|_{Y^{s}}\leq C\|w\|_{Y^{s+1}}$ .

- (3) On each mode, $e^{tL}|_{Y^{s}_{\ell}}=\exp(t\Lsec{\ell}(G))$ , the norm-continuous semigroup generated by the bounded operator $L_{\ell}(G)$ on $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ .

In (3), $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ is identified with $P_{\ell}Y^{s}$ through $g\mapsto ge^{i\ell\theta}$ ; $L_{\ell}(G)$ is bounded on $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ because multiplication by $\Omega$ is, and $k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}$ is by Corollary 4.13 and Lemma 4.12; so, by the argument in the proof of Lemma 4.5(4), $L_{\ell}(G)$ generates a norm-continuous group $\exp(t\Lsec{\ell}(G))$ on $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ , with derivative $L_{\ell}(G)\exp(t\Lsec{\ell}(G))=\exp(t\Lsec{\ell}(G))L_{\ell}(G)$ .

#### Proof.

(1) On $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ , $e^{tL^{\rm tr}}$ is multiplication by $e^{i\varphi}$ , $\varphi=-\ell\Omega(r;G)t$ . By the Leibniz and Faà di Bruno formulas, $\partial_{r}^{j}(e^{i\varphi}g)=e^{i\varphi}\sum_{i=0}^{j}\binom{j}{i}B_{i}\,\partial_{r}^{j-i}g$ , where the complete Bell polynomial $B_{i}=B_{i}(i\partial_{r}\varphi,\dots,i\partial_{r}^{i}\varphi)$ is a sum of at most $C_{i}$ products of at most $i$ factors $\partial_{r}^{q}\varphi=-\ell t\,\partial_{r}^{q}\Omega$ . On $[\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]$ , $\|\Omega(\cdot;G)\|_{C^{s}}\leq\|\Omega(\cdot;0)\|_{C^{s}}+G_{+}\|r^{-2}\|_{C^{s}}$ , so $|B_{i}|\leq C(1+|\ell||t|)^{i}\leq C2^{i/2}(1+|t|)^{i}(1+\ell^{2})^{i/2}$ and

$$ (1+\ell^{2})^{s-j}\|\partial_{r}^{j}(e^{i\varphi}g)\|^{2}\leq C(1+|t|)^{2s}\sum_{i=0}^{j}(1+\ell^{2})^{s-(j-i)}\|\partial_{r}^{j-i}g\|^{2}; $$

summing over $j\leq s$ gives the mode bound. The map $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r,\theta-\Omega(r;G)t)$ is a smooth diffeomorphism near $N_{*}$ preserving $N_{*}$ , so $e^{tL^{\rm tr}}$ maps $Y^{s}$ to itself, and Lemma 4.12 gives the bound on $Y^{s}$ after enlarging $C_{s}$ by the factor $(C^{\rm eq}_{s}/c^{\rm eq}_{s})^{1/2}$ . For $w\in Y^{s}$ and each $\ell$ , $\|(e^{-i\ell\Omega t}-1)g_{\ell}\|_{s,\ell}\to 0$ as $t\to 0$ by dominated convergence in the formula above, with the summable bound $(C_{s}(1+|t|)^{s}+1)^{2}\|g_{\ell}\|^{2}_{s,\ell}$ ; so $e^{tL^{\rm tr}}w\to w$ in $H^{s}$ by Lemma 4.12. The group law holds because $\Omega$ does not depend on $\theta$ . By Lemma 4.5(2), $\mathcal{K}$ acts on mode profiles as $k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}$ , so $\|\mathcal{K}w\|_{H^{s}}\leq(C^{\rm eq}_{s}/c^{\rm eq}_{s})^{1/2}C_{K}\|w\|_{H^{s}}$ by Corollary 4.13 and Lemma 4.12, and $\supp\mathcal{K}w\subset\supp\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}\subset N_{*}$ .

(2) By induction $\|S_{n}(t)\|\leq C_{s}^{n+1}(1+t)^{s(n+1)}\|\mathcal{K}\|^{n}t^{n}/n!$ , so the series converges in operator norm uniformly on compact sets, and its sum $T(t)$ is strongly continuous, as each $S_{n}$ is. Summing the recursion, $T(t)=S_{0}(t)+\int_{0}^{t}S_{0}(t-\tau)\mathcal{K}T(\tau)\differential\tau$ . Fix $t^{\prime}\geq 0$ ; we show that both $T(\cdot+t^{\prime})$ and $T(\cdot)T(t^{\prime})$ solve

$$ \Psi(t)=S_{0}(t)T(t^{\prime})+\int_{0}^{t}S_{0}(t-\tau)\mathcal{K}\Psi(\tau)\differential\tau\qquad(t\geq 0). $$

For $T(\cdot)T(t^{\prime})$ , multiply the identity for $T(t)$ on the right by $T(t^{\prime})$ . For $T(\cdot+t^{\prime})$ , write the identity at time $t+t^{\prime}$ and split the integral at $\tau=t^{\prime}$ . On $[0,t^{\prime}]$ , $S_{0}(t+t^{\prime}-\tau)=S_{0}(t)S_{0}(t^{\prime}-\tau)$ by the group law of $S_{0}$ , and the bounded operator $S_{0}(t)$ can be taken out of the integral; on $[t^{\prime},t+t^{\prime}]$ , substitute $\tau=t^{\prime}+\sigma$ . This gives

$$ T(t+t^{\prime})=S_{0}(t)\Big(S_{0}(t^{\prime})+\int_{0}^{t^{\prime}}S_{0}(t^{\prime}-\tau)\mathcal{K}T(\tau)\differential\tau\Big)+\int_{0}^{t}S_{0}(t-\sigma)\mathcal{K}T(\sigma+t^{\prime})\differential\sigma, $$

and the bracket is $T(t^{\prime})$ , which is the equation for $\Psi=T(\cdot+t^{\prime})$ . The difference $D$ of two strongly continuous, locally bounded solutions satisfies $\|D(t)w\|\leq C\int_{0}^{t}\|D(\tau)w\|\differential\tau$ , so $D=0$ by iteration; hence $T$ is a $C_{0}$ -semigroup. By induction and Fubini’s theorem, $S_{n}(t)$ is the integral of $S_{0}(t-\tau_{n})\mathcal{K}S_{0}(\tau_{n}-\tau_{n-1})\cdots\mathcal{K}S_{0}(\tau_{1})$ over $0<\tau_{1}<\dots<\tau_{n}<t$ , so also $S_{n+1}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}S_{n}(t-\tau)\mathcal{K}S_{0}(\tau)\differential\tau$ , which gives the second Duhamel formula $T(t)=S_{0}(t)+\int_{0}^{t}T(t-\tau)\mathcal{K}S_{0}(\tau)\differential\tau$ . The $P_{\ell}$ commute with $S_{0}$ and $\mathcal{K}$ , which commute with rotations ( $S_{0}$ because $\Omega$ is radial, $\mathcal{K}$ by Lemma 4.5(2)), hence with $T(t)$ . For $w\in Y^{s+1}$ , $\|L^{\rm tr}w\|_{H^{s}}\leq C\|w\|_{H^{s+1}}$ , as $\Omega$ and the coefficients of $\partial_{\theta}$ are smooth near $N_{*}$ , and $(e^{hL^{\rm tr}}w-w)/h=\frac{1}{h}\int_{0}^{h}e^{\tau L^{\rm tr}}L^{\rm tr}w\differential\tau\to L^{\rm tr}w$ in $Y^{s}$ , since $\Omega\partial_{\theta}$ commutes with $e^{\tau L^{\rm tr}}$ . By the second Duhamel formula, $(T(h)w-w)/h=(e^{hL^{\rm tr}}w-w)/h+\frac{1}{h}\int_{0}^{h}T(h-\tau)\mathcal{K}e^{\tau L^{\rm tr}}w\differential\tau\to L^{\rm tr}w+\mathcal{K}w=L(G)w$ .

(3) On $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ , $S_{0}(t)=\exp(-i\ell\Omega t)$ and $\mathcal{K}=k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}$ , so $T(t)|_{Y^{s}_{\ell}}$ solves the first Duhamel equation for these bounded operators. So does $\exp(t\Lsec{\ell})$ , since

$$ \tfrac{\differential}{\differential\tau}\big[\exp(-(t-\tau)i\ell\Omega)\exp(\tau\Lsec{\ell})\big]=\exp(-(t-\tau)i\ell\Omega)k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}\exp(\tau\Lsec{\ell}). $$

By uniqueness they coincide. ∎

#### Proposition 4.15.

In a mode setting, let $s\geq 0$ be an integer, $\gamma>0$ and $G_{+}\geq 0$ . Let $C_{s}$ be as in Lemma 4.14(1), $C_{K}$ as in Corollary 4.13, $c_{s}(\gamma)=\sup_{t\geq 0}(1+t)^{s}e^{-\gamma t}$ , and let $\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}\geq 1$ satisfy $C_{s}C_{K}(1+\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}^{2})^{-1/2}I_{s}(\gamma)\leq\frac{1}{2}$ , with $I_{s}(\gamma)$ as in Equation (3). Then for every $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $|\ell|\geq\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}$ , every $G$ with $|G|\leq G_{+}$ and every $t\geq 0$ , $\|e^{tL_{\ell}(G)}\|_{s,\ell\to s,\ell}\leq 2C_{s}\,c_{s}(\gamma)\,e^{\gamma t}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix such $\ell$ and $G$ . Since $L_{\ell}$ is bounded for $\|\cdot\|_{s,\ell}$ (remark after Lemma 4.14), $Y_{T}:=\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}e^{-\gamma t}\|e^{tL_{\ell}}\|_{s,\ell\to s,\ell}$ is finite for $T<\infty$ . By Lemma 4.14(3) and the first Duhamel formula, $e^{tL_{\ell}}=e^{-i\ell\Omega t}+\int_{0}^{t}e^{-i\ell\Omega(t-\tau)}k_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}e^{\tau L_{\ell}}\differential\tau$ , so for $t\leq T$ , by Lemma 4.14(1) and Corollary 4.13,

$$ \displaystyle e^{-\gamma t}\|e^{tL_{\ell}}\| \displaystyle\leq C_{s}(1+t)^{s}e^{-\gamma t}+\int_{0}^{t}C_{s}(1+t-\tau)^{s}e^{-\gamma(t-\tau)}\,\frac{C_{K}}{(1+\ell^{2})^{1/2}}\,e^{-\gamma\tau}\|e^{\tau L_{\ell}}\|\differential\tau \displaystyle\leq C_{s}c_{s}(\gamma)+\tfrac{1}{2}Y_{T}, $$

by the choice of $\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}$ and $\int_{0}^{t}(1+u)^{s}e^{-\gamma u}\differential u\leq I_{s}(\gamma)$ . Taking the supremum over $t\leq T$ gives $Y_{T}\leq 2C_{s}c_{s}(\gamma)$ , for all $T$ . ∎

For $\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathbb{Z}$ let $Y^{s}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ be the closed subspace of $w\in Y^{s}$ with $g_{\ell}=0$ for $\ell\notin\mathcal{Z}$ ; it is invariant under $e^{tL}$ by Lemma 4.14(2).

#### Lemma 4.16.

In a mode setting, let $s\geq 0$ be an integer, $G_{+}\geq 0$ , $|G|\leq G_{+}$ , $\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathbb{Z}$ , and let $\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ be the generator of the restriction of $e^{tL}$ to $Y^{s}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ . Then:

- (1) $w\in D(\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}})$ if and only if $w\in Y^{s}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ and $\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{Z}}\|L_{\ell}(G)g_{\ell}\|^{2}_{s,\ell}<\infty$ , and then $P_{\ell}\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}}w=(L_{\ell}(G)g_{\ell})e^{i\ell\theta}$ for every $\ell$ ;

- (2) let $\gamma>0$ , let $\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}$ be as in Proposition 4.15, and let $\real\lambda>\gamma$ . For $|\ell|\geq\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}$ , $\lambda$ lies in the resolvent set of $L_{\ell}(G)$ on $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ , and $\|(\lambda-L_{\ell}(G))^{-1}\|_{s,\ell\to s,\ell}\leq 2C_{s}c_{s}(\gamma)/(\real\lambda-\gamma)$ ;

- (3) for $\real\lambda>\gamma>0$ : $\lambda$ lies in the resolvent set of $\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ if and only if $\lambda$ lies in the resolvent set of $L_{\ell}(G)$ on $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ for every $\ell\in\mathcal{Z}$ with $|\ell|<\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}$ ; and then $P_{\ell}(\lambda-\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}})^{-1}w=((\lambda-L_{\ell}(G))^{-1}g_{\ell})e^{i\ell\theta}$ for every $\ell\in\mathcal{Z}$ ;

- (4) if $\sigma_{+}\subset\{\real\lambda>\gamma\}$ is a compact set that is open and closed in the spectrum of $\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ , then the Riesz projection $\Pi_{\sigma_{+}}$ of $\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ for $\sigma_{+}$ satisfies $P_{\ell}\Pi_{\sigma_{+}}w=(\Pi_{\ell}g_{\ell})e^{i\ell\theta}$ , where $\Pi_{\ell}$ is the Riesz projection of $L_{\ell}(G)$ on $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ for $\sigma_{+}\cap\spec L_{\ell}(G)$ (and $\Pi_{\ell}=0$ if this set is empty).

#### Proof.

(1) Since $P_{\ell}$ is bounded and commutes with $e^{tL}$ , for $w\in D(\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}})$ Lemma 4.14(3) gives $P_{\ell}\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}}w=\lim_{h\to 0}h^{-1}(\exp(h\Lsec{\ell})g_{\ell}-g_{\ell})e^{i\ell\theta}=(L_{\ell}g_{\ell})e^{i\ell\theta}$ , and $\sum_{\ell}\|L_{\ell}g_{\ell}\|^{2}_{s,\ell}\leq(c^{\rm eq}_{s})^{-1}\|\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}}w\|^{2}_{H^{s}}$ by Lemma 4.12. Conversely, if the sum is finite, $v:=\sum_{\ell}(L_{\ell}g_{\ell})e^{i\ell\theta}$ converges in $Y^{s}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ by Lemma 4.12, and for $t>0$

$$ e^{tL}w-w=\sum_{\ell}\Big(\int_{0}^{t}\exp(\tau\Lsec{\ell})L_{\ell}g_{\ell}\differential\tau\Big)e^{i\ell\theta}=\int_{0}^{t}e^{\tau L}v\differential\tau; $$

dividing by $t$ and letting $t\to 0$ shows $w\in D(\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}})$ .

(2) We use the semigroup formula for the resolvent. Let $A$ be a bounded operator with $\|e^{tA}\|\leq Ke^{\gamma t}$ for $t\geq 0$ , and let $\real\lambda>\gamma$ . Then $R=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}e^{tA}\differential t$ converges in operator norm, $\|R\|\leq K/(\real\lambda-\gamma)$ , and $R=(\lambda-A)^{-1}$ : integrating $\frac{\differential}{\differential t}\big(e^{-\lambda t}e^{tA}\big)=-e^{-\lambda t}e^{tA}(\lambda-A)=-(\lambda-A)e^{-\lambda t}e^{tA}$ over $[0,\infty)$ gives $R(\lambda-A)=(\lambda-A)R=1$ . By Proposition 4.15, $A=L_{\ell}(G)$ on $Y^{s}_{\ell}$ satisfies this with $K=2C_{s}c_{s}(\gamma)$ when $|\ell|\geq\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}$ , which gives (2).

(3) If $\lambda$ is in the resolvent set of $\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ , then by (1) $P_{\ell}$ maps $D(\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}})$ into itself and commutes with $\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ there, so $(\lambda-\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}})^{-1}$ commutes with $P_{\ell}$ and its restriction to the mode $\ell$ inverts $\lambda-L_{\ell}$ . Conversely, under the condition, (2) and the finiteness of $\{\ell\in\mathcal{Z}:|\ell|<\mathcal{M}_{\gamma}\}$ give $K:=\sup_{\ell\in\mathcal{Z}}\|(\lambda-L_{\ell})^{-1}\|_{s,\ell\to s,\ell}<\infty$ . For $w\in Y^{s}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ , $u=\sum_{\ell}((\lambda-L_{\ell})^{-1}g_{\ell})e^{i\ell\theta}$ converges in $Y^{s}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ , with $\|u\|_{H^{s}}\leq(C^{\rm eq}_{s}/c^{\rm eq}_{s})^{1/2}K\|w\|_{H^{s}}$ (Lemma 4.12). Since $L_{\ell}u_{\ell}=\lambda u_{\ell}-g_{\ell}$ , the sum in (1) is finite, so $u\in D(\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}})$ and $(\lambda-\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}})u=w$ ; and $(\lambda-\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}})u=0$ forces $(\lambda-L_{\ell})u_{\ell}=0$ for all $\ell$ by (1), so $u=0$ .

(4) Let $\Gamma\subset\{\real\lambda>\gamma\}$ be a contour in the resolvent set of $\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ winding once around $\sigma_{+}$ and not around the rest of the spectrum. Since $P_{\ell}$ is bounded, $P_{\ell}\Pi_{\sigma_{+}}w=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\Gamma}P_{\ell}(\lambda-\hat{L}_{\mathcal{Z}})^{-1}w\differential\lambda=\big(\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\Gamma}(\lambda-L_{\ell})^{-1}g_{\ell}\differential\lambda\big)e^{i\ell\theta}$ by (3). The spectrum of $L_{\ell}$ inside $\Gamma$ is $\sigma_{+}\cap\spec L_{\ell}$ , by (3), which gives the claim. ∎

### 4.5 The Numerical Hypothesis

The rest of the paper assumes the following statements, which are proved in Appendix A of Part II [8] (Theorem 1.3 there).

#### Hypothesis 4.17.

Let $a_{0},d,\xi_{L},\xi_{a},\xi_{b},\xi_{R}$ , $H$ , $\chi$ and $\varpi$ be as in Definition 4.1. For $G\geq 0$ and $\xi\in\mathbb{R}$ put

$$ \Omega_{G}(\xi)=e^{-2\xi}\Big(G+\int_{-\infty}^{\xi}\varpi(\xi^{\prime})e^{2\xi^{\prime}}\differential\xi^{\prime}\Big). $$

For an integer $\ell\geq 1$ , $G\geq 0$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\real\lambda>0$ , let $\psi=\psi_{\ell}(\cdot;\lambda,G)$ be the solution on $[\xi_{L},\xi_{R}]$ of

$$ \partial_{\xi}^{2}\psi=\Big(\ell^{2}+\frac{i\ell\,\partial_{\xi}\varpi(\xi)}{\lambda+i\ell\,\Omega_{G}(\xi)}\Big)\psi,\qquad\psi(\xi_{L})=1,\quad\partial_{\xi}\psi(\xi_{L})=\ell, $$

and put

$$ \mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda;G)=e^{-\ell(\xi_{R}-\xi_{L})}\big(\partial_{\xi}\psi(\xi_{R})+\ell\psi(\xi_{R})\big), $$

a holomorphic function of $\lambda$ in $\{\real\lambda>0\}$ (Lemma 4.6). Put $\Theta_{\ell}=\pi\ell d/\sin(\pi\ell d)$ and $\epsilon_{*}=\max\{H((\xi_{a}-a_{0})/d),\,H(-\xi_{b}/d)\}$ . Then:

- (N1) for every $G\in[0,\frac{1}{50}]$ , the function $\mathcal{E}_{3}(\cdot;G)$ has exactly one zero, counted with multiplicity, in the closed half-plane $\{\real\lambda\geq\frac{9}{200}\}$ ;

- (N2) for every $G\in[0,\frac{1}{50}]$ , the function $\mathcal{E}_{3}(\cdot;G)$ has no zero in the closed strip $\{\frac{9}{200}\leq\real\lambda\leq\frac{211}{2500}\}$ ;

- (N3) for $\ell\in\{6,9\}$ , $e^{\ell a_{0}}\Theta_{\ell}+\epsilon_{*}<\frac{9}{100}$ .

By Lemma 4.2, $6d<1$ and $9d<1$ , so $\Theta_{6}$ and $\Theta_{9}$ are finite positive numbers.

### 4.6 Consequences of the Numerical Hypothesis

We use the ring in both normalizations of Definition 4.1. In reference units the ring is $\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}(x)=\varpi(\log|x|)$ , given directly by the explicit profile $\varpi$ , and Hypothesis 4.17, which Part II verifies with computer assistance, is stated in these units, for $G\in[0,\frac{1}{50}]$ . In ring units the ring $\Phi$ is supported in $\{a\leq|y|\leq 1\}$ , with outer radius $1$ ; this is the normalization of the building block of the datum (2), whose rings are the rescaled copies $A_{k}\Phi(\cdot/r_{k})$ , and of the spaces $X^{s}$ and the operator $L(G)$ that Part II uses. Equation (13) below translates between the two.

In each case we fix a mode setting (Definition 4.3); recall that $(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})=(\log r_{1},\log r_{2})$ , where $[r_{1},r_{2}]$ contains the support of $\partial_{r}\overline{\omega}$ . In reference units, $\overline{\omega}=\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}$ , whose profile $\varpi$ is supported in $[\xi_{L},\xi_{R}]$ ; we take $(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})=(\xi_{L},\xi_{R})$ and $N_{*}=\{\frac{1}{2}e^{\xi_{L}}\leq|x|\leq 2e^{\xi_{R}}\}$ . In ring units, $\overline{\omega}=\Phi$ ; since $\log|x|=\log|y|+\xi_{R}$ , the profile of $\Phi$ in $\xi=\log|y|$ is $\varpi(\xi+\xi_{R})$ , supported in $[\xi_{L}-\xi_{R},0]$ , so we take $(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})=(\xi_{L}-\xi_{R},0)$ , that is $(r_{1},r_{2})=(a,1)$ , and $N_{*}=N$ . Since $\Phi=\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}(R_{\mathrm{c}}\,\cdot)$ , $\Gamma_{\Phi}(r)=R_{\mathrm{c}}^{-2}\Gamma_{\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}}(R_{\mathrm{c}}r)$ , so

$$ \Omega^{\Phi}(r;G)=r^{-2}\Big(\frac{R_{\mathrm{c}}^{-2}\Gamma_{\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}}(R_{\mathrm{c}}r)}{2\pi}+G\Big)=(R_{\mathrm{c}}r)^{-2}\Big(\frac{\Gamma_{\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}}(R_{\mathrm{c}}r)}{2\pi}+R_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}G\Big)=\Omega^{\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}}(R_{\mathrm{c}}r;R_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}G), $$

and $\nu^{\Phi}(\xi)=\nu^{\overline{\omega}_{\mathrm{c}}}(\xi+\xi_{R})$ , as $R_{\mathrm{c}}=e^{\xi_{R}}$ . $$ \mathcal{E}^{\Phi}_{\ell}(\lambda;G)=\mathcal{E}_{\ell}(\lambda;R_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}G)\qquad(\ell\geq 1,\ \real\lambda>0,\ G\in\mathbb{R}). $$

#### Corollary 4.18.

Assume (N1) and (N2). For every $G\in[0,\frac{1}{50}]$ , the function $\mathcal{E}_{3}(\cdot;G)$ of Hypothesis 4.17 has exactly one zero $\lambda_{*}^{\mathrm{c}}(G)$ in $\{\real\lambda\geq\frac{9}{200}\}$ ; it is simple and $\real\lambda_{*}^{\mathrm{c}}(G)>\frac{211}{2500}$ .

#### Proof.

By (N1), $\mathcal{E}_{3}(\cdot;G)$ has exactly one zero $\lambda_{*}^{\mathrm{c}}(G)$ in $\{\real\lambda\geq\frac{9}{200}\}$ , counted with multiplicity, so this zero is simple; by (N2), $\real\lambda_{*}^{\mathrm{c}}(G)>\frac{211}{2500}$ . ∎

For the rest of the paper, $X^{s}$ denotes the space of $3$ -fold rotationally symmetric $w\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{C})$ with $\supp w\subset N=\{\frac{a}{2}\leq|y|\leq 2\}$ ; thus $X^{s}=Y^{s}_{3\mathbb{Z}}$ for the ring in ring units, and $X^{s}_{\ell}=Y^{s}_{\ell}$ for $\ell\in 3\mathbb{Z}$ . On $X^{s}$ , $L(G)$ denotes the linearization at $(\Phi,G)$ in ring units, that is, the generator of the restriction of $e^{tL}$ to $X^{s}$ ; by Lemma 4.14(2) it extends the differential operator on $X^{s+1}$ , and Lemma 4.16 describes it mode by mode.

#### Proposition 4.19.

Assume (N1)–(N3), and for $G\in[0,\overline{G}]$ let $\lambda_{*}(G)=\lambda_{*}^{\mathrm{c}}(R_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}G)$ be as in Corollary 4.18. Then $\real\lambda_{*}(G)>\frac{211}{2500}$ , and for every $G\in[0,\overline{G}]$ and every integer $s\geq 0$ : $\spec(L_{3}(G)|_{X^{s}_{3}})\cap\{\real\lambda>\frac{9}{200}\}=\{\lambda_{*}(G)\}$ , and $\lambda_{*}(G)$ is an algebraically simple eigenvalue of $L_{3}(G)$ on $X^{s}_{3}$ ; $\spec(L_{-3}(G)|_{X^{s}_{-3}})\cap\{\real\lambda>\frac{9}{200}\}=\{\overline{\lambda_{*}(G)}\}$ ; $\spec(L_{\ell}(G)|_{X^{s}_{\ell}})\cap\{\real\lambda>\frac{9}{200}\}=\emptyset$ for $\ell\in 3\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{3,-3\}$ ;

$$ \spec(L(G)|_{X^{s}})\cap\{\real\lambda>\tfrac{9}{200}\}=\{\lambda_{*}(G),\overline{\lambda_{*}(G)}\}; $$

and the Riesz projection of $L(G)$ on $X^{s}$ for this set acts as the Riesz projection of $L_{3}(G)$ at $\lambda_{*}(G)$ on the mode $3$ , as the Riesz projection of $L_{-3}(G)$ at $\overline{\lambda_{*}(G)}$ on the mode $-3$ , and as $0$ on the other modes.

#### Proof.

Fix $G\in[0,\overline{G}]$ and $s\geq 0$ ; then $R_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}G\in[0,\frac{1}{50}]$ . For $\ell=\pm 3$ : by Lemma 4.7, run in the mode setting of $\Phi$ , the spectrum of $L_{\pm 3}(G)$ on $X^{s}_{\pm 3}$ in $\{\real\lambda>0\}$ consists of the zeros of $\mathcal{E}^{\Phi}_{3}(\cdot;G)$ and their conjugates respectively, all eigenvalues. By (13) and the last assertion of Lemma 4.6, $\mathcal{E}^{\Phi}_{3}(\cdot;G)$ is the function $\mathcal{E}_{3}(\cdot;R_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}G)$ of Hypothesis 4.17. So by Corollary 4.18 the part of this spectrum in $\{\real\lambda\geq\frac{9}{200}\}$ is $\{\lambda_{*}(G)\}$ for $L_{3}(G)$ and $\{\overline{\lambda_{*}(G)}\}$ for $L_{-3}(G)$ , where $\lambda_{*}(G)=\lambda_{*}^{\mathrm{c}}(R_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}G)$ is a simple zero of $\mathcal{E}^{\Phi}_{3}(\cdot;G)$ and $\real\lambda_{*}(G)>\frac{211}{2500}$ ; and Theorem 4.8(2) shows that $\lambda_{*}(G)$ is algebraically simple on $X^{s}_{3}$ .
